chapters.title: Week 1 · Introduction to Business Ethics
chapters.description: What business ethics is, why it is needed, Friedman, law v. ethics, and Core Reading 1 (Penneys). Lecturer-sample style: five options, some FALSE/NOT and combined-answer questions - keep answer shuffling OFF.

questions.stem: According to the definition from Crane and Matten (2016) used in the introductory lecture, 'business ethics' is:

options.text: The voluntary activities a company undertakes to improve its reputation with stakeholders.
The set of laws and regulations that govern how companies must behave in the markets in which they operate.
The codes of conduct published by professional bodies and trade organisations.
The personal moral compass that each manager brings to his or her work.
The study of business situations, activities and decisions where issues of right and wrong are addressed.

questions.explanation: The slide quotes Crane and Matten (2016): business ethics is the study of business situations, activities and decisions where issues of right and wrong are addressed. It is not the same thing as law, personal morality, CSR or a professional code.
questions.source: Week 1 lecture slides (Introduction to Business Ethics), slide 6

questions.stem: Milton Friedman argued that there is 'one and only one social responsibility of business'. Which of the following best completes his position, as quoted in the lecture?

options.text: To balance the interests of shareholders, employees, customers and the wider community.
To increase its profits by any means that are not explicitly prohibited by criminal law.
To increase its profits so long as it stays within the rules of the game, engaging in open and free competition without deception or fraud.
To increase its profits while voluntarily investing a fair share of those profits in social causes.
To provide employment and pay taxes in the communities in which it operates.

questions.explanation: Friedman's statement is qualified: profit maximisation 'so long as it stays within the rules of the game, which is to say, engages in open and free competition without deception or fraud'. He did not endorse profit by any means, nor a balancing of stakeholder interests.
questions.source: Week 1 lecture slides (Introduction to Business Ethics), slide 9

questions.stem: In the passages from Milton Friedman quoted in the lecture, the corporate executive is described as:

options.text: A representative of the employees and customers who depend on the corporation.
An employee of the owners of the business, acting as their agent, whose primary responsibility is to them.
A citizen who must put the public interest ahead of the wishes of stockholders.
An independent professional who is bound mainly by his or her own conscience.
A trustee for all of the stakeholders affected by the corporation.

questions.explanation: Friedman describes the executive as 'an employee of the owners of the business' and 'the agent of the individuals who own the corporation', with primary responsibility to them. Stockholders, customers or employees can spend their own money on social causes if they wish.
questions.source: Week 1 lecture slides (Introduction to Business Ethics), slide 10

questions.stem: Which of the following was NOT one of the reasons given in the introductory lecture for why we still need 'business ethics', despite all the regulation governing business?

options.text: Businesses are facing a trust deficit.
Business malpractice can inflict huge personal harm, for example through pollution or accidents.
Most business activity is still not covered by any consumer, employment or environmental legislation.
The power of modern businesses and their impact on the democratic process, for example through lobbying.
Employees face significant pressure to compromise ethical standards.

questions.explanation: The lecture listed extensive regulation already in place (consumer, environmental, workplace safety, employment, procurement, advertising standards). The case for business ethics rests on corporate power, expectations that business solves social problems, harm from malpractice, stakeholder demands, pressure on employees and the trust deficit - not on an absence of legislation.
questions.source: Week 1 lecture slides (Introduction to Business Ethics), slides 7 and 13

questions.stem: The introductory lecture used an example of pharmaceutical industry lobbying in Washington D.C. to illustrate the power of modern business. Which ONE of the following statements reflects that example?

options.text: There were approximately 800 pharmaceutical manufacturing company lobbyists on Capitol Hill, compared with 535 elected politicians.
Pharmaceutical lobbying had been banned by the U.S. Senate following the opioid crisis.
Pharmaceutical companies spent less on lobbying than any other major industry.
The industry body PhRMA did not lobby directly, leaving this to the individual drug companies.
There were approximately 535 pharmaceutical lobbyists, compared with around 800 elected politicians.

questions.explanation: The slide noted approx. 800 pharmaceutical manufacturing company lobbyists on Capitol Hill against 535 elected politicians, with the top ten spenders laying out nearly $31 million in the first quarter of 2019 and the industry body PhRMA itself spending over $11 million in that quarter.
questions.source: Week 1 lecture slides (Introduction to Business Ethics), slide 14

questions.stem: With regard to the difference between laws and ethics, as presented in the lecture, which of the following is / are TRUE?

options.text: Law can be seen as the 'minimal acceptable standard'.
Ethics is concerned with situations where 'values are in conflict' (Trevino and Nelson, 2014).
If an action is legal then, by definition, it is also ethical.
a) and b) above
a), b) and c) above

questions.explanation: The slide describes law as the minimal acceptable standard, notes that many laws cover behaviour rather than ethics, and that ethics is where 'values are in conflict' - 'ethics begins where the law ends'. Legality does not guarantee that conduct is ethical, so c) is false.
questions.source: Week 1 lecture slides (Introduction to Business Ethics), slide 16

questions.stem: The phrase 'ethics begins where the law ends', used in the lecture, is best understood to mean that:

options.text: Ethics deals with the grey areas that the law does not, or cannot, fully cover, so that legal compliance alone does not settle whether conduct is right.
Ethics is a branch of law that is enforced by professional bodies rather than by the courts.
Companies that comply with the law have no further ethical questions to consider.
Laws are always less strict than the ethical codes they are based upon.
Ethical questions only arise once a law has been broken.

questions.explanation: Law is the minimum standard. Ethics operates in the grey zone beyond it, where values conflict and legislation gives no clear answer - which is why being legal does not automatically make something right.
questions.source: Week 1 lecture slides (Introduction to Business Ethics), slide 16; Lecture 1 class notes

questions.stem: In discussing 'whose ethics do we need?', the lecture referred to research by McCabe et al. (1991). This research suggested that:

options.text: Business students are more likely to plagiarise than law students.
Women are consistently more ethical than men in business settings.
Students who take a business ethics module are less likely to plagiarise.
Nationality has no measurable impact on ethical behaviour.
Law students are more likely to plagiarise than business students.

questions.explanation: The 'Ethical Differences?' slide cites McCabe et al. (1991): business students are more likely to plagiarise than law students. The same slide notes that studies on gender are inconclusive and that nationality can have a significant impact on ethical behaviour.
questions.source: Week 1 lecture slides (Introduction to Business Ethics), slide 19

questions.stem: With regard to possible 'ethical differences' between groups of people, which ONE of the following reflects what was presented in the lecture?

options.text: Studies conclusively show that women behave more ethically than men.
Ethical behaviour is determined almost entirely by a person's choice of degree programme.
Studies are inconclusive, but indicate that women and men may approach ethical dilemmas differently, while nationality can have a significant impact on ethical behaviour.
Studies conclusively show that men and women approach ethical dilemmas in exactly the same way.
Nationality has been shown to have no impact on ethical behaviour once income is taken into account.

questions.explanation: The slide states that studies on gender are inconclusive but indicate men and women may approach dilemmas differently, and that nationality can have a significant impact (as international transparency rankings suggest).
questions.source: Week 1 lecture slides (Introduction to Business Ethics), slide 19

questions.stem: Which of the following were given in the lecture as examples of the regulation and bodies that already govern the conduct of business?

options.text: Consumer legislation and advertising standards.
Workplace safety legislation and employment legislation (WRC).
Procurement legislation (anti-corruption measures) and environmental legislation.
a) and b) above
a), b) and c) above

questions.explanation: The 'Do we need Business Ethics?' slide lists consumer legislation, trade unions, professional bodies and trade organisations, environmental legislation, advertising standards, workplace safety, procurement (anti-corruption) and employment legislation (WRC).
questions.source: Week 1 lecture slides (Introduction to Business Ethics), slide 7

questions.stem: The article 'Penneys shows paradox of consumers who talk about ethics but buy based on price' (a core reading) refers to the 'CSR Consumer Paradox', as outlined by Janssen and Vanhamme. This paradox refers to the finding that:

options.text: Consumers are willing to pay more for ethical products but cannot find them in the shops.
Consumers say they want companies to have higher standards of social responsibility, implying they would pay for it, but their subsequent buying behaviour usually proves otherwise.
The more a company advertises its ethical credentials, the less consumers trust it.
Companies that spend the most on corporate social responsibility tend to have the worst ethical records.
Consumers in wealthier countries care less about ethics than consumers in poorer countries.

questions.explanation: The article describes the gap between what consumers say (to researchers, in polite company, on social media) and what they do: most consumers, most of the time, choose low prices over 'ethical consumption'.
questions.source: Core Reading 1: 'Penneys shows paradox of consumers who talk about ethics but buy based on price' (Mark Paul, Irish Times)

questions.stem: In the core reading on Penneys / Primark, the author refers to a psychological phenomenon called 'diffusion of responsibility'. Which ONE of the following best describes it, as explained in the article?

options.text: It is part of the 'bystander effect': the more people there are who are aware of a problem, the less likely many of them are, individually, to address it.
Companies spread the blame for poor working conditions across many suppliers so that no single firm can be held responsible.
Consumers transfer responsibility for ethical standards to governments by voting for stricter regulation.
Responsibility for a decision is passed up the hierarchy to the most senior person in an organisation.
Shoppers feel less guilty about a purchase the more often they repeat it.

questions.explanation: The article describes diffusion of responsibility as part of the bystander effect: consumers 'hide with our consumer guilt in the foliage of the market', consoled by the belief that somebody else will step in.
questions.source: Core Reading 1: 'Penneys shows paradox of consumers who talk about ethics but buy based on price' (Mark Paul, Irish Times)

questions.stem: According to the core reading on Penneys / Primark, what happened to Primark's business in the year following the 2013 Rana Plaza factory collapse in Bangladesh, in which more than 1,100 people died?

options.text: The company was sold to a competitor because of the reputational damage.
Revenue was flat, and the company closed a number of stores.
Revenue and profit both rose and the company opened more stores.
A consumer boycott caused revenue and profit to fall sharply.
The company stopped sourcing clothing from Bangladesh and raised its prices.

questions.explanation: The article reports that the following year revenue rose 16 per cent, profit rose 28 per cent and 20 more stores opened - evidence for the author's argument that calls for boycotts 'die out soon enough' because consumers continue to choose low prices.
questions.source: Core Reading 1: 'Penneys shows paradox of consumers who talk about ethics but buy based on price' (Mark Paul, Irish Times)

questions.stem: With reference to the core reading on Penneys / Primark, which ONE of the following is FALSE?

options.text: The author suggests that companies whose business models rely on good quality at low prices know how consumers behave, which is why their models rarely change fundamentally.
Primark has codes of practice and argues that its suppliers provide much-needed employment, especially for women, who might otherwise be much worse off.
The article quotes Nick Clegg's view that consumers have more power than they think when choosing where to shop, which the author describes as ultimately naive.
The author argues that most consumers, most of the time, will choose low prices over what is perceived as 'ethical consumption'.
The author presents himself as an ethical shopper who has stopped buying from low-price retailers and airlines.

questions.explanation: The author explicitly says 'I am a sinner and I know it. I have not a single stone to cast' - he admits buying cheap Penneys clothes, air-freighted food and Ryanair flights. All of the other statements reflect the article.
questions.source: Core Reading 1: 'Penneys shows paradox of consumers who talk about ethics but buy based on price' (Mark Paul, Irish Times)

questions.stem: The author of the core reading on Penneys / Primark uses the growth of Ryanair to support his argument. The point being made is that:

options.text: German consumers, unlike Irish consumers, have stopped using low-cost airlines.
Consumers have successfully forced airlines to change their business models through boycotts.
Low-cost airlines have become more environmentally friendly as they have grown.
People may feel genuine when they say they care about the environment, but they will not stop flying - the airline has grown to almost ten times its size since 2002 despite concerns over emissions.
Aviation is an example of an industry in which regulation has made ethical consumption unnecessary.

questions.explanation: The Ryanair example parallels Primark: stated concern about the environment has not changed buying behaviour, illustrating the gap between attitudes and purchases.
questions.source: Core Reading 1: 'Penneys shows paradox of consumers who talk about ethics but buy based on price' (Mark Paul, Irish Times)

chapters.title: Week 2 · Ethics v. Morals and Why Good People Do Bad Things
chapters.description: Ethics v. morals, the Stanford Prison and Milgram experiments, behavioural biases, leadership and Core Reading 2 (Milgram). Includes official samples 2, 3 and 5. Keep answer shuffling OFF.

questions.stem:
In the ‘Capital Punishment Experiment’ (Lord et al., 1979), discussed in class, both supporters and opponents of capital punishment were presented with the same samples of research that showed that capital punishment can be an effective deterrent and also the same samples of research that showed that capital punishment is not an effective deterrent.
Which ONE of the following is TRUE:

options.text: By exposing both camps (those for and against capital punishment) to research that presented an opposing view to their own, it served to make both camps even more polarised in their positions regarding  their perceived effectiveness of capital punishment.

By exposing both camps (those for and against capital punishment) to research that presented an opposing view to their own, it served to make both camps narrow their positions (i.e. come closer) regarding their perceived effectiveness of capital punishment.

By exposing both camps (those for and against capital punishment) to research that presented an opposing view to their own, it made no difference to their perceived effectiveness of capital punishment that they held prior to reviewing any research, and both camps remained the same distance apart.
Those who support capital punishment only read the research that confirmed the effectiveness of the deterrent effect of capital punishment.
Those who oppose capital punishment only read the research that confirms that capital punishment has no deterrent effect

questions.explanation: Official sample question (answer inferred - no official key supplied). Lord et al. found that each side rated the evidence confirming its own beliefs as more convincing, so exposure to the same mixed evidence produced 'not a narrowing of disagreement but rather an increase in polarization'. Both groups read both studies.
questions.source: Official MG2008 lecturer sample question 2 (2026 Exam Instructions, Details and Sample MCQs). Wording and options unchanged; no official answer key was issued, so the answer is inferred from: Week 2 lecture slides, 'Capital Punishment Experiment' (Lord et al., 1979)

questions.stem: Which of the following is true?

options.text: The Milgram Shock Experiment was undertaken to explore the degree to which regular people would inflict pain on other regular people if instructed to do so by an authority figure.
The Stanford Prison Experiment was undertaken to explore the degree to which regular people would inflict pain on other regular people if instructed to do so by an authority figure.

The Milgram Shock Experiment transpired to be more effective than the Stanford Prison Experiment in showing that regular people would inflict pain on other regular people when instructed to do so by an authority figure, as there were more controls in the former on how much pain could be inflicted on the learners at each point, whereas in the latter experiment the research participants were just instructed to inflict pain on the prisoners as they saw fit.
a and b above
a, b and c above

questions.explanation: Official sample question (answer inferred - no official key supplied). Milgram's stated aim was to see how far people would go in obeying an instruction that involved harming another person. The Stanford Prison Experiment was set up to observe how people behave in assigned roles of guard and prisoner (situation and anonymity), not obedience to an instruction to inflict pain, so b) and c) are not accurate descriptions.
questions.source: Official MG2008 lecturer sample question 3 (2026 Exam Instructions, Details and Sample MCQs). Wording and options unchanged; no official answer key was issued, so the answer is inferred from: Core Reading 2 (Milgram) and the Week 2 lecture / Stanford Prison Experiment video

questions.stem:
Brian is a student, and he works part-time in the deli-counter of a busy city-centre shop.  Any left-over food is always given to the residents of a near-by hostel for the homeless.  On this particular Saturday evening, Brian is given a parcel of left-over sandwiches and asked to drop them off at the shelter on his way home.  Brian is feeling peckish after a long shift, and is heading out for the night with his friends.  He also knows that the food is intended for the residents of the homeless shelter, and it's 'not right' that he should take it for his himself.  He could have bought food for himself from the deli at a staff discount.  However, he also reasons that he already does more for the homeless than most other people, and certainly any of his friends, as he volunteers for a 'soup run' for the homeless every Thursday night (and has being doing this regularly for over two years now).  Having considered this, he doesn't think it's so bad that he should now take the sandwiches back to his house, and he walks straight past the shelter for the homeless.
This is an example of which ONE of the following:

options.text: Self-serving Bias
Instant-entitlement Bias
‘Bathsheba Syndrome’
Moral licence
Personal Positivity Bias

questions.explanation: Official sample question (answer inferred - no official key supplied). Brian draws on the moral 'credit' he feels he has built up through volunteering to permit himself a wrongful act - the 'running scoreboard' described as moral licence.
questions.source: Official MG2008 lecturer sample question 5 (2026 Exam Instructions, Details and Sample MCQs). Wording and options unchanged; no official answer key was issued, so the answer is inferred from: Week 2 lecture slides, 'Why do good people do bad things?' (moral licence)

questions.stem: According to the definitions from Crane and Matten (2016) presented in class, which ONE of the following is correct?

options.text: Ethics refers only to the law, while morality refers only to religious teaching.
Morality is the study of ethics and the application of reason to elucidate rules; ethics is concerned with norms, values and beliefs embedded in social processes.
Ethics and morality are identical concepts and cannot conflict with one another.
Morality is always external to the individual, while ethics is always internal.

Morality is concerned with the norms, values and beliefs embedded in social processes which define right and wrong for an individual or a community; ethics is concerned with the study of morality and the application of reason to elucidate specific rules and principles.

questions.explanation: Crane and Matten: morality concerns norms, values and beliefs embedded in social processes; ethics is the study of morality and the application of reason to elucidate rules and principles that determine morally acceptable courses of action. Ethical theories are the codifications of these rules and principles.
questions.source: Week 2 lecture slides (Ethical Behaviour: Stanford Prison Experiment v. Milgram Shock Experiment), slide 4

questions.stem: In the 'Ethics versus Morals' comparison chart shown in class, which ONE of the following is correct?

options.text: A person who strictly follows ethical principles must, by definition, have strong morals.
Ethics come from a social system (external), whereas morals come from the individual (internal).
Both ethics and morals come only from the legal system.
Ethics come from the individual (internal), whereas morals come from the social system (external).
Ethics never vary between contexts, whereas morals vary constantly.

questions.explanation: The chart describes ethics as rules of conduct recognised by a group or culture (social system - external) and morals as a personal compass of right and wrong (individual - internal). Ethics tend to be consistent within a context but vary between contexts, and a person strictly following ethical principles may not have any morals at all.
questions.source: Week 2 lecture slides (Ethical Behaviour: Stanford Prison Experiment v. Milgram Shock Experiment), slide 5

questions.stem: A barrister for the defence discovers that their client is guilty and tells the court. As discussed in class, this is an example of:

options.text: Moral licence, as the barrister has built up moral credit with the court.
Behaviour that is both ethical and moral, as justice is served.
Behaviour that is driven by morals (a desire to see justice done) but that could be considered unethical, as it breaches the barrister's professional relationship with the client.
Behaviour that is ethical, as it follows the professional code, but immoral.
The fundamental attribution error.

questions.explanation: The slide uses the barrister to show that 'ethics are not always moral, and vice versa': the barrister acts on personal morals, yet breaches professional ethics. Professional ethical codes can be separated from morality.
questions.source: Week 2 lecture slides (Ethical Behaviour: Stanford Prison Experiment v. Milgram Shock Experiment), slide 6

questions.stem: Which of the following were given in the lecture as reasons why people may behave unethically / immorally at work?

options.text: Bureaucracy, which distances us from the impact of our actions.
The use of language, such as 'facilitation payment' rather than 'bribe'.
Organisational culture: 'everyone does it'.
a) and b) above
a), b) and c) above

questions.explanation: The slide lists rewards / punishments, work roles ('tough at the top'), organisational culture ('everyone does it'), bureaucracy (distance from the impact of our actions) and language ('facilitation payment' v. 'bribe').
questions.source: Week 2 lecture slides (Ethical Behaviour: Stanford Prison Experiment v. Milgram Shock Experiment), slide 14

questions.stem: With regard to how people rate their own morality, which ONE of the following reflects what was presented in class?

options.text: People generally rate themselves as less moral than the average person.
People's moral behaviour is consistent across all situations, so there is only one 'ethical self'.
In studies, fewer than half of people describe themselves as 'good'.
People have only a handful of operative values, which never conflict.
In studies, generally over 90% of people say they are 'good', and people tend to rate themselves more highly than 'the average person'.

questions.explanation: The slide notes that over 90% of people say they are good, that individuals are not always as good as they think and rate themselves above the average person, that people have some seventy operative values (Rokeach, 1973) and multiple 'ethical selves'.
questions.source: Week 2 lecture slides (Ethical Behaviour: Stanford Prison Experiment v. Milgram Shock Experiment), slide 12

questions.stem: 'Loss aversion', as described in class as one reason why good people do bad things, refers to the idea that:

options.text: People take credit for their successes but blame others for their losses.
People avoid all risk whenever there is any chance of a loss.
People prefer a certain small loss to an uncertain large gain.
People suffer from a loss approximately twice as much as they enjoy an equivalent gain, and so will take risks to avoid a loss that they would not take to make a gain.
People are more averse to losing an argument than to being wrong.

questions.explanation: The slide states that suffering from loss is approximately twice the enjoyment from gain, so people take risks to avoid a loss (e.g. to save a job) that they would not take to make a gain (e.g. to get a job).
questions.source: Week 2 lecture slides (Ethical Behaviour: Stanford Prison Experiment v. Milgram Shock Experiment), slide 15

questions.stem: A sales manager takes personal credit when her team exceeds its targets, but when the team misses its targets she blames the weak economy and her staff. This is an example of:

options.text: Self-serving bias
Moral compensation
Conformity bias
False consensus effect
Loss aversion

questions.explanation: Self-serving bias (a form of confirmation bias): personal credit is taken for successes, but others or circumstances are blamed for failures, protecting self-esteem and identity, particularly under pressure.
questions.source: Week 2 lecture slides (Ethical Behaviour: Stanford Prison Experiment v. Milgram Shock Experiment), slide 15

questions.stem: In relation to 'moral licence', the lecture distinguished between 'moral licensing' and 'moral compensation'. Which ONE of the following is correct?

options.text: Moral licensing occurs when people feel they need to make up moral credit; moral compensation occurs when people feel they have built up moral credit.
Both terms refer to rationalising a decision that has already been made sub-consciously.
Both terms refer to over-estimating how many other people share your views.
Moral licensing refers to leaders; moral compensation refers to followers.
Moral licensing occurs when people feel they have built up moral credit; moral compensation occurs when people feel they need to make up moral credit.

questions.explanation: People keep a 'running scoreboard' of moral behaviour: licensing if they feel they have built up credit, compensation if they feel they need to make up credit (which is when it is easier to get people to donate to charity).
questions.source: Week 2 lecture slides (Ethical Behaviour: Stanford Prison Experiment v. Milgram Shock Experiment), slide 18

questions.stem: A chief executive who strongly supports a new strategy assumes that 'practically everybody in the industry' agrees with him, although surveys show that most of his peers disagree. This is an example of:

options.text: Instant-entitlement bias
The fundamental attribution error
The false consensus effect
Moral rationalisation
Loss aversion

questions.explanation: The false consensus effect is the over-estimation by some people that more people agree with them than actually do, or that their own beliefs and attitudes are more common among the general public than they are.
questions.source: Week 2 lecture slides (Ethical Behaviour: Stanford Prison Experiment v. Milgram Shock Experiment), slide 18

questions.stem: The 'fundamental attribution error' (also shown on the slides as 'false attribution error') refers to the tendency to:

options.text: Assume that people who do good things are good people (and vice versa), under-estimating how far the situation, rather than disposition, may drive behaviour.
Assume that most other people share our own opinions.
Attribute our own successes to skill and our failures to bad luck.
Rationalise a decision after it has been made sub-consciously.
Attribute too much responsibility to the authority figure giving the orders.

questions.explanation: We tend to assume those who do 'good things' are 'good people' and vice versa, making it hard to believe that good people do bad things - yet the organisational situation may overwhelm them (dispositional v. situational factors).
questions.source: Week 2 lecture slides (Ethical Behaviour: Stanford Prison Experiment v. Milgram Shock Experiment), slide 18 / PDF p. 17

questions.stem: According to the lecture, 'moral rationalisation' arises because:

options.text: People build up moral credit which they later spend.
People are hard-wired to obey authority figures.
People conform to whatever the group around them decides.

Most decision-making is automatic (sub-conscious) and heavily influenced by emotion rather than logic, so what feels like reasoning through a dilemma may just be rationalising a decision already made.
People deliberately calculate the costs and benefits of each ethical decision before acting.

questions.explanation: The slide explains that most decision-making is sub-conscious and emotional; our 'reasoning' may be rationalisation of a decision already made (the job-interview situation was used as an example in class).
questions.source: Week 2 lecture slides (Ethical Behaviour: Stanford Prison Experiment v. Milgram Shock Experiment), slide 18

questions.stem: The lecture used Bono and U2's tax arrangements as an example. Which ONE of the following best reflects how this example was used?

options.text: As an example of the Bathsheba Syndrome, as Bono believed the rules did not apply to him.
As an example of illegal tax evasion by a high-profile campaigner.
As an example of loss aversion, since U2 moved in order to avoid losing fans.
As an example of legal arrangements that nonetheless raise questions of moral licence, given Bono's anti-poverty campaigning, which Bono defended as 'sensible' cost control.
As an example of a celebrity who admitted that the band's tax arrangements were hypocritical.

questions.explanation: U2's arrangements were legal; Bono defended them as 'smart people ... trying to be sensible' and as a duty to control costs, pointing to his activism and charitable giving. In class this was discussed as an illustration of moral licence and of the gap between what is legal and what may be seen as ethical.
questions.source: Week 2 lecture slides (Ethical Behaviour: Stanford Prison Experiment v. Milgram Shock Experiment), slides 19-20; Lecture 3 class notes

questions.stem: The 'Bathsheba Syndrome', discussed in class in relation to leaders, refers to:

options.text: Leaders taking a greater share of resources once they are allocated a leadership role.
Leaders sub-consciously rationalising ethical decisions made quickly or impulsively.
Followers seeing only the good in the leaders they elect or support.
Leaders obeying a higher authority against their own conscience.
Leaders coming to believe that the rules only apply to others, and behaving in a deliberately outrageous / immoral way in the belief that they can manipulate any outcome to their benefit.

questions.explanation: Named after the moral lapse of King David: rules only apply to others, and the leader behaves in a deliberately outrageous way believing any outcome can be manipulated. Option a) describes instant-entitlement bias and c) personal positivity bias.
questions.source: Week 2 lecture slides (Ethical Behaviour: Stanford Prison Experiment v. Milgram Shock Experiment), slide 21

questions.stem: In experiments, people who are allocated a 'leadership' role take more for themselves when asked to share goods among a group. In the lecture this was called:

options.text: Personal positivity bias
Conformity bias
Self-serving bias
Instant-entitlement bias
Over-confidence

questions.explanation: Instant-entitlement bias: in experiments people take more when allocated a 'leadership' role when asked to share goods to a group.
questions.source: Week 2 lecture slides (Ethical Behaviour: Stanford Prison Experiment v. Milgram Shock Experiment), slide 21

questions.stem: With regard to psychopathy and leadership, as covered in the lecture, which ONE of the following is FALSE?

options.text: Research cited in class suggested that clinically significant psychopathy is found in about 1% of the general population.
Leadership positions (power) may attract or suit those with psychopathic tendencies.
Hare (2002) is quoted as saying 'Not all psychopaths are in prison. Some are in the boardroom.'
The research cited in class showed that psychopathy is less common among business leaders than in the general population.
Sociopaths and psychopaths are now collectively termed ASPD ('anti-social personality disorder').

questions.explanation: The slides cite Babiak's suggestion that up to 4% of US business leaders could be psychopaths and a study finding 3%-21% of supply chain managers with clinically significant psychopathy, compared with 1% of the general population - i.e. more common, not less.
questions.source: Week 2 lecture slides (Ethical Behaviour: Stanford Prison Experiment v. Milgram Shock Experiment), slides 23-25

questions.stem: In relation to the Stanford Prison Experiment (Zimbardo, 1971), shown on video and discussed in class, which ONE of the following is correct?

options.text: The guards were real prison officers and the prisoners were real inmates.
Volunteers chose for themselves whether to be guards or prisoners, and the study ran for its full planned duration.
The experiment showed that participants refused to take on the roles they were given.
Volunteers were randomly assigned to be guards or prisoners, and the study was ended early as the guards' treatment of the prisoners became increasingly abusive.
Volunteers were asked to give electric shocks of increasing voltage to a 'learner'.

questions.explanation: In the Stanford Prison Experiment student volunteers were randomly assigned to the roles of guard and prisoner in a mock prison; it was stopped early as guards became increasingly cruel. Electric shocks relate to Milgram, not Zimbardo.
questions.source: Week 2 lecture - Stanford Prison Experiment video (first 15 minutes) and Lecture 2 class notes

questions.stem: The Stanford Prison Experiment has been criticised in more recent years, as discussed in class. Which ONE of the following is a criticism that was raised?

options.text: The guards were given an orientation in which they were encouraged to be tough on the prisoners, so their behaviour may reflect what they thought the researchers wanted (a 'demand characteristic') rather than cruelty emerging naturally.
No prisoner showed any sign of distress, so the study demonstrated nothing.
The study used female participants only.
The experimenters never observed or recorded the participants.
The sample consisted of real convicted criminals, so it cannot be applied to regular people.

questions.explanation: The class discussion noted that the guards were coached / instructed to be tough and that at least one guard later said he was deliberately playing a role for the researchers, undermining the claim that cruelty emerged spontaneously from the situation.
questions.source: Lecture 2 class notes (Stanford Prison Experiment: original narrative and criticisms)

questions.stem: According to the core reading on the Milgram Shock Experiment, what was the main result of Milgram's original study?

options.text: 65% of participants refused to give any shocks at all.
65% of participants continued to the highest level of 450 volts, and all participants continued to 300 volts.
35% of participants continued to the highest level of 450 volts, and no participants went beyond 300 volts.
Less than 1% of participants continued to the highest level of 450 volts, as psychiatrists had predicted.
All participants continued to the highest level of 450 volts.

questions.explanation: The reading reports that 65% (two-thirds) of the 'teachers' continued to 450 volts and that all participants continued to 300 volts.
questions.source: Core Reading 2: 'The Milgram Shock Experiment' (McLeod, 2017)

questions.stem: With reference to the core reading on the Milgram Shock Experiment, which ONE of the following statements about the procedure is FALSE?

options.text: The shock generator had switches marked from 15 volts to 450 volts.
The sample was made up of equal numbers of men and women from across the United States.
The draw to decide who would be 'teacher' and 'learner' was fixed, so that the real participant was always the teacher.
The 'learner' was a confederate, and did not actually receive electric shocks.
Participants were recruited through a newspaper advertisement for a study of 'learning' at Yale University.

questions.explanation: The original participants were 40 males aged 20 to 50 from the New Haven area, paid $4.50 for turning up. The all-male, self-selected sample is one of the criticisms of the study.
questions.source: Core Reading 2: 'The Milgram Shock Experiment' (McLeod, 2017)

questions.stem: In Milgram's 'Agency Theory', as set out in the core reading, the 'agentic state' is one in which:

options.text: People rationalise their decisions after they have been made.
People direct their own actions and take responsibility for the results of those actions.
People allow others to direct their actions and then pass off the responsibility for the consequences to the person giving the orders.
People act against authority in order to protect another person.
People conform to the behaviour of their peers rather than an authority figure.

questions.explanation: Milgram contrasted the autonomous state (people direct their own actions and take responsibility) with the agentic state (people act as agents for another's will and pass responsibility to the person giving the orders).
questions.source: Core Reading 2: 'The Milgram Shock Experiment' (McLeod, 2017)

questions.stem: According to the core reading, Milgram suggested that two things must be in place for a person to enter the 'agentic state'. These are:

options.text: The person must be anonymous, and must be part of a large group.
The person must be paid, and must be told that no real harm will occur.
The person giving the orders is perceived as legitimate (qualified to direct others' behaviour), and the person being ordered believes that the authority will accept responsibility for what happens.
The victim must be out of sight, and the person must have built up moral credit.
The person must be in a prestigious location, and must be wearing a uniform.

questions.explanation: The reading states the authority must be seen as legitimate and the person must be able to believe the authority will accept responsibility. When participants were reminded they were responsible for their own actions, almost none were prepared to obey.
questions.source: Core Reading 2: 'The Milgram Shock Experiment' (McLeod, 2017)

questions.stem: Milgram carried out a number of variations of his experiment. According to the core reading, in which ONE of the following variations did obedience (shocking to the maximum 450 volts) INCREASE compared with the original study?

options.text: When the participant could instruct an assistant to press the switches, rather than pressing them personally.
When the experiment was moved from Yale University to a set of run-down offices.
When the teacher had to force the learner's hand onto a shock plate.
When the experimenter gave instructions by telephone from another room.
When two other 'teachers' (confederates) refused to obey.

questions.explanation: In the two-teacher condition 92.5% shocked to the maximum - with less personal responsibility, obedience increases. Obedience fell in the other variations: run-down offices 47.5%, absent experimenter 20.5%, touch proximity 30%, social support 10%.
questions.source: Core Reading 2: 'The Milgram Shock Experiment' (McLeod, 2017)

questions.stem: According to the core reading on the Milgram Shock Experiment, which of the following is / are valid criticisms or ethical issues that have been raised about the study?

options.text: Deception: participants believed they were shocking a real person.
Protection of participants: they were exposed to extremely stressful situations with the potential to cause psychological harm.
The right to withdraw: the experimenter's verbal 'prods' mostly discouraged withdrawal.
a) and b) above
a), b) and c) above

questions.explanation: The reading lists deception, protection of participants (many were visibly distressed) and the right to withdraw (the four prods discouraged withdrawal), alongside criticisms of the biased sample and of 'experimental realism' (Orne and Holland, 1968).
questions.source: Core Reading 2: 'The Milgram Shock Experiment' (McLeod, 2017)

questions.stem: In the core reading on the Milgram Shock Experiment, what is said about the 'social support' variation, in which two other teachers (confederates) refused to continue?

options.text: Obedience was unchanged at 65%.
Obedience fell to 10%, showing that the presence of others who are seen to disobey the authority figure reduces obedience.
Obedience fell to zero.
Obedience rose, as the real participant felt more pressure to complete the task alone.
The variation could not be completed for ethical reasons.

questions.explanation: With two confederates stopping at 150 and 210 volts, only 10% of participants continued to the maximum.
questions.source: Core Reading 2: 'The Milgram Shock Experiment' (McLeod, 2017)

chapters.title: Week 3 · The Business Environment: The World Around Us
chapters.description: Global conditions, inequality, externalities, corporate power and 'perception is reality', plus Core Readings 3 (woke-washing) and 4 (Wells Fargo). Keep answer shuffling OFF.

questions.stem: In the lecture on 'The World Around Us and the Impact of Business', what approximate figures were given for the number of births and deaths in the world each day?

options.text: Approx. 36,000 births and 18,000 deaths per day.
Approx. 362,000 births and 180,000 deaths per day.
Approx. 1 million births and 500,000 deaths per day.
Approx. 180,000 births and 362,000 deaths per day.
Approx. 362,000 births and 362,000 deaths per day.

questions.explanation: The slides gave approx. 362,000 births per day (about 4 per second) as of 2026 and approx. 180,000 deaths per day - so world population continues to grow by roughly 180,000 people a day.
questions.source: Week 3 lecture slides (The World Around Us and the Impact of Business), pp. 3 and 12

questions.stem: In relation to suicide worldwide, the lecture cited data (Ritchie, Roser and Ortiz-Ospina) showing that:

options.text: Close to 80,000 people die from suicide every year, around half as many as die from homicide.
Close to 800,000 people die from suicide every year, around twice as many as die from homicide.
Suicide is only a significant cause of death in high-income countries.
Suicide figures are likely to be an over-estimate because of how deaths are classified.
Suicide causes fewer deaths each year than commercial airplane accidents.

questions.explanation: The slide: close to 800,000 people die from suicide every year (one every 40 seconds), around twice as many as from homicide; the figure is likely to be an under-estimate because of stigma and because suicide is illegal in some countries.
questions.source: Week 3 lecture slides (The World Around Us and the Impact of Business), p. 16

questions.stem: With regard to modern-day slavery, as presented in class (Anti-Slavery International, 2020), which ONE of the following is FALSE?

options.text: It was suggested in class that there are more people in slavery today than at any point in history.
Modern slavery is confined to low-income countries and no potential victims have been identified in the UK.
An estimated 40 million people are trapped in modern slavery worldwide.
1 in 4 of those in modern slavery are children.
Almost three quarters (71%) are women and girls.

questions.explanation: The slide noted that over 10,000 potential victims were identified by the authorities in the UK in 2019. The other statements reflect the slide and the class discussion of when slavery was 'at its worst'.
questions.source: Week 3 lecture slides (The World Around Us and the Impact of Business), pp. 22-23; Lecture 3 class notes

questions.stem: The lecture referred to a 2025 Reuters report, 'The hidden cost of your smartphone', on mining around the town of Rubaya in the Democratic Republic of Congo. According to this report:

options.text: Coltan ore is processed locally in Congo into finished smartphones.
The United Nations has certified that Rubaya's coltan is conflict-free.
Rubaya produces around 15% of the world's coltan, dug manually by impoverished locals earning a few dollars per day, in an area seized by the M23 rebel group.
Coltan is no longer used in mobile phones or computers.
Rubaya's mines are fully mechanised and operated by multinational smartphone manufacturers.

questions.explanation: The report: coltan ore is processed (in Asia) into tantalum, a heat-resistant metal used in phones, computers, aerospace components and gas turbines. Rubaya produces around 15% of world supply, dug by hand; the UN says M23, backed by Rwanda, has plundered the area's riches to fund its insurgency.
questions.source: Week 3 lecture slides (The World Around Us and the Impact of Business), p. 27

questions.stem: According to a report cited in the lecture (The Guardian, 2022), which ONE of the following is true of food waste in the European Union?

options.text: The EU wastes about 153 million tonnes of food a year, which is more than it imports.
The EU imports twice as much food as it wastes.
The EU has eliminated on-farm food waste.
The EU wastes about 15 million tonnes of food a year, a small fraction of what it imports.
Food waste in the EU is roughly equal to the food dumped in landfills in a single U.S. city.

questions.explanation: The report estimated about 153m tonnes of food wasted in the EU each year - double previous estimates and 15m tonnes more than is imported. A further slide noted the U.S. Department of Agriculture estimate that $161 billion worth of food is dumped in U.S. landfills every year.
questions.source: Week 3 lecture slides (The World Around Us and the Impact of Business), pp. 33-34

questions.stem: The lecture contrasted images of extreme luxury (e.g. 'The Residence' by Etihad Airways, the American Express Centurion card) with images of deprivation (e.g. 'Skid Row', Los Angeles), and quoted Bernie Sanders (2022). According to the figures quoted from Sanders:

options.text: The bottom half of American society owns more wealth than the top 1%.
CEO pay has fallen to about 10 times what workers earn.
Three multibillionaires own more wealth than the bottom half of American society, and CEOs of large corporations make around 350 times what their workers earn.
Income inequality in the U.S. has narrowed steadily over the past 47 years.
Only 4.5% of new income goes to the top 1%.

questions.explanation: Sanders: three multibillionaires own more wealth than the bottom half of American society (160 million people), 45% of all new income goes to the top 1%, CEOs make a record 350 times what their workers earn, and $50tn has been redistributed from the bottom 90% to the top 1% over 47 years (Rand Corporation).
questions.source: Week 3 lecture slides (The World Around Us and the Impact of Business), p. 41

questions.stem: The lecture referred to a drought in the Mexican state of Nuevo Leon (Thomson Reuters Foundation, 2022). The ethical issue highlighted was that:

options.text: Water companies were prevented by law from selling bottled water.
Residents were wasting water, leaving none for industry.
The state had banned all industrial water use during the drought.

Residents were left with little option but to buy water from companies that were themselves using up much of the supply, with five big soda and beer companies alone extracting 16 per cent of the water allocated for industry.
Soft drinks companies had donated their water allocations to residents.

questions.explanation: The article describes anger over water inequality: taps running dry while companies including Heineken and Coca-Cola extract a significant share of industrial water. The slide also noted Constellation Brands scrapping a $1bn brewery in Mexicali after residents rejected it in a referendum.
questions.source: Week 3 lecture slides (The World Around Us and the Impact of Business), p. 42

questions.stem: The lecture cited the example of Costa Coffee and the proposed 25p 'latte levy' on single-use cups in the UK. This example was used to illustrate:

options.text: Consumers boycotting a company over its use of disposable cups.
A company lobbying government against a proposed environmental measure, shortly before the proposal was dropped against MPs' advice.
A company being fined for breaching environmental legislation.
A company voluntarily introducing an environmental charge ahead of legislation.
A government forcing a company to switch to reusable cups.

questions.explanation: According to a freedom of information request by Greenpeace's Unearthed, Costa - which sells nearly half a billion drinks in takeaway cups a year - 'obstructively lobbied' against the levy just before the Chancellor dropped the plan.
questions.source: Week 3 lecture slides (The World Around Us and the Impact of Business), p. 45

questions.stem: Which of the following environmental points was / were made in the lecture on 'The World Around Us and the Impact of Business'?

options.text: An analysis suggested there is far more plastic on the ocean floor than floating on the surface.
A study suggested that as much as 40% of the existing Amazon rainforest is at a point where it could exist as savannah instead of rainforest.
A report claimed that plastic pollution in the oceans had been eliminated by 2020.
a) and b) above
a), b) and c) above

questions.explanation: The slides cited an analysis estimating more than 14m tonnes of plastic at the bottom of the ocean (around thirty times more than at the surface) and a Nature Communications study on the Amazon tipping point from rainforest to savannah.
questions.source: Week 3 lecture slides (The World Around Us and the Impact of Business), pp. 43-44

questions.stem: In 2020 a report by a U.S. congressional committee, cited in the lecture, found that four major digital companies had used their market dominance in 'anti-competitive and abusive ways' that had 'weakened democracy'. The four companies were:

options.text: Apple, Microsoft, Nvidia and Tesla
Facebook, Twitter, TikTok and Snapchat
Microsoft, Netflix, Twitter and TikTok
Google, Microsoft, IBM and Oracle
Apple, Facebook, Google and Amazon

questions.explanation: The House Judiciary subcommittee on antitrust sought answers from the chief executives of Apple, Facebook, Google and Amazon, accusing them of being 'evasive and non-responsive' and of charging exorbitant fees, imposing oppressive contract terms and extracting valuable data.
questions.source: Week 3 lecture slides (The World Around Us and the Impact of Business), p. 48

questions.stem: The section of the Week 3 lecture headed 'Perception is Reality' compared data on crime rates and unemployment in the USA with people's perceptions of crime and of the economy. The point being made was that:

options.text: Official statistics are unreliable and should be ignored in favour of public opinion.
Crime and unemployment always move in the same direction.
Perceptions only matter in politics and have no relevance for business.
People's perceptions can differ markedly from what the data show, and people act on their perceptions.
People's perceptions are generally an accurate reflection of the underlying data.

questions.explanation: The charts showed that perceptions of crime and of economic performance can diverge from the recorded trends. For business ethics, what people believe (shaped by media coverage and 'bubbles') drives behaviour, whether or not it matches the evidence.
questions.source: Week 3 lecture slides (The World Around Us and the Impact of Business), pp. 49-53; Lecture 3 class notes

questions.stem: In class, the lecturer distinguished between a person who is 'immoral' and a person who is 'amoral'. Which ONE of the following reflects that distinction?

options.text: The two terms mean exactly the same thing.
An immoral person does not know right from wrong; an amoral person knows their actions are wrong.
An amoral person has built up moral credit; an immoral person has not.
An immoral person knows their actions are wrong; an amoral person does not care about morality at all.
An immoral person breaks the law; an amoral person breaks an ethical code.

questions.explanation: As discussed in class: the immoral person knows their action is wrong, whereas the amoral person is simply not interested in the question of morality and typically lacks empathy.
questions.source: Lecture 3 class notes (Immoral vs amoral)

questions.stem: According to the core reading 'Woke-washing - how brands are cashing in on the culture wars', the term 'woke-washing' refers to:

options.text: Companies donating all of the profits from a product to a social cause.
Profit-driven companies cynically cashing in on people's idealism, using progressive-orientated marketing campaigns to deflect questions about their own ethical records.
Companies removing all political messages from their advertising to avoid controversy.
Activists using social media to expose unethical companies.
Governments regulating the social claims that companies can make in advertisements.

questions.explanation: This is the counter-argument the author sets against the view that motive does not matter if a campaign raises awareness. It parallels 'greenwashing', e.g. Chevron's 1980s campaign flaunting dubious green credentials.
questions.source: Core Reading 3: 'Woke-washing - how brands are cashing in on the culture wars' (Owen Jones, The Guardian, 2019)

questions.stem: In the core reading on 'woke-washing', several companies are criticised for a disconnect between their marketing and their own behaviour. Which ONE of the following pairings is correctly described in the article?

options.text: Burger King ran a campaign against toxic masculinity after years of telling men to be clean-shaven.
Nike ran a campaign on endangered species, while selling leather goods.
Lush ran an advert backing equal pay, but did not pay its staff the living wage.
Lacoste ran a campaign on mental health, but its employees could not afford mental health care.
Audi ran a Super Bowl advert backing equal pay, but only two of the company's 14 executives were women.

questions.explanation: Audi's equal-pay advert met a backlash over its executive team. In the article Lacoste is linked to endangered species (while selling deer and cow leather goods), Burger King to mental health (#FeelYourWay), Gillette to toxic masculinity, and Nike to Kaepernick / Serena Williams while a sponsored runner criticised its lack of paid maternity leave.
questions.source: Core Reading 3: 'Woke-washing - how brands are cashing in on the culture wars' (Owen Jones, The Guardian, 2019)

questions.stem: In the core reading on 'woke-washing', which company is presented as a rare, more clear-cut exception - a company whose campaign offered no obvious commercial gain and which passes the 'integrity test' of 'deeds not words'?

options.text: Marks & Spencer
Starbucks
Pepsi
Lush
Gillette

questions.explanation: Lush's campaign highlighting the misconduct of undercover police officers offered no commercial gain (78% of people had confidence in their local police), and its owners are said to donate privately to causes without fanfare. TOMS is mentioned as a possible exception but 'even this is problematic'.
questions.source: Core Reading 3: 'Woke-washing - how brands are cashing in on the culture wars' (Owen Jones, The Guardian, 2019)

questions.stem: With reference to the core reading on 'woke-washing', which ONE of the following is FALSE?

options.text: The author concludes that there is clear evidence that cause-based advertising campaigns have significantly changed the world for the better.
JP Hanson is quoted as arguing that companies should pay their tax and 'walk the walk before they talk the talk'.
Sophie Lewis is quoted as being inspired by the motto 'deeds not words', arguing brands must work with integrity and consistency.
The author suggests that younger people's sense of grievance in a 'culture war' is there to be monetised by brands.
The article suggests that buying a 'cause' product can act like 'clicktivism', becoming a substitute for actually tackling a problem.

questions.explanation: The author writes that while such campaigns have 'demonstrably helped rake in billions of pounds for big corporates, there is no evidence any have significantly changed the world for the better' - progress comes through 'protest and struggle, not well-intentioned sandwiches'.
questions.source: Core Reading 3: 'Woke-washing - how brands are cashing in on the culture wars' (Owen Jones, The Guardian, 2019)

questions.stem: The core reading 'Evaluating the Nature of Business Ethics in Practice' uses the Wells Fargo scandal as its main example. What happened in that scandal?

options.text: Employees, under aggressive cross-selling targets backed by stern penalties, created millions of unauthorised bank and credit card accounts without customers' knowledge or consent.
The bank knowingly sold high-risk mortgages to customers who could not afford them.
The bank was found to have laundered money for criminal organisations.
Senior executives secretly sold their shares before announcing poor results.
Tellers stole cash directly from customers' accounts for personal enrichment.

questions.explanation: Aggressive cross-selling goals and penalties (up to losing one's job) led many employees to open fake accounts that technically counted as cross-sales. Wells Fargo was fined $185 million and about 5,300 employees were fired, for revenue estimated at only around $5 million.
questions.source: Core Reading 4: 'Evaluating the Nature of Business Ethics in Practice' (Kemeny)

questions.stem: In the core reading 'Evaluating the Nature of Business Ethics in Practice', the author considers how three classical approaches would have applied to Wells Fargo. Which ONE of the following correctly matches the thinker with the approach as described in the article?

options.text: Plato - look at the action; Kant - look at the results; Mill - look at the actor.
Plato - look at the actor (virtues); Kant - look at the action (categorical imperative); Mill - look at the results (utility).
Plato - look at the results; Kant - look at the action; Mill - look at the actor.
All three thinkers are described as focusing on results.
Plato - look at the results; Kant - look at the actor; Mill - look at the action.

questions.explanation: The article summarises: 'rather than looking at the actor (Plato), or the action (Kant), one should look at the results' (Mill). Plato's four virtues are given as temperance, fortitude, prudence and justice. The author concludes that each falls short as a practical solution in a large organisation.
questions.source: Core Reading 4: 'Evaluating the Nature of Business Ethics in Practice' (Kemeny)

questions.stem: The author of 'Evaluating the Nature of Business Ethics in Practice' argues that traditional ('singular') ethics is of limited use for large organisations and proposes concepts for thinking about 'organizational ethics'. Which of the following is / are among the concepts he proposes?

options.text: Organisational fairness - whether the organisation is perceived as doing the right thing by the individuals within it.
Organisational communicativeness - how freely information is exchanged between parties in the organisation.
Organisational principles, which can be explicit or tacit.
a) and b) above
a), b) and c) above

questions.explanation: After discussing agency (incentives), the author breaks 'culture' into fairness (a 'canary in the coal mine'), communicativeness (worry when people stop complaining; retaliation blocks oversight) and tacit or explicit organisational principles.
questions.source: Core Reading 4: 'Evaluating the Nature of Business Ethics in Practice' (Kemeny)

questions.stem: In 'Evaluating the Nature of Business Ethics in Practice', the author distinguishes between 'explicit' and 'tacit' organisational principles. Applied to Wells Fargo, his argument is that:

options.text: Management deliberately wrote an explicit principle instructing tellers to create fake accounts.
Tacit principles are always weaker than explicit principles, so the written code should have prevented the scandal.
The scandal was a genuine moral quandary, with good ethical arguments on both sides.
There was no explicit policy against creating unauthorised accounts, so employees could not have known it was wrong.

Although there was likely an explicit policy against unauthorised accounts, tellers - through observation and imitation - developed a more powerful tacit principle that it was OK, and management missed this.

questions.explanation: Explicit principles are codified and shared; tacit principles are held and reaffirmed by observation and imitation. The author also argues Wells Fargo was not a moral quandary at all: 'Creating the unauthorized accounts was wrong'.
questions.source: Core Reading 4: 'Evaluating the Nature of Business Ethics in Practice' (Kemeny)

chapters.title: Week 4 · Ethical Frameworks (1): Consequentialist Theories
chapters.description: Approaches to ethics, absolutism v. relativism, utilitarianism (Bentham, Mill), egoism, the Sandel video and Core Reading 5 (textbook, utilitarianism). Includes official samples 1 and 9. Keep answer shuffling OFF.

questions.stem: Which of the following is / are considered to be consequentialist ethical theories:

options.text: Utilitarianism
Egoism
Deontology
a) and b) above
a), b) and c) above

questions.explanation: Official sample question (answer inferred - no official key supplied). Consequentialist theories focus on outcomes: egoism (outcomes for the decision-maker) and utilitarianism (outcomes for the whole community). Deontology is non-consequentialist, focusing on duty and the action itself.
questions.source: Official MG2008 lecturer sample question 1 (2026 Exam Instructions, Details and Sample MCQs). Wording and options unchanged; no official answer key was issued, so the answer is inferred from: Week 4 lecture slides, Part One, 'Consequentialist v. Non-consequentialist Theories'

questions.stem: According to the prescribed (core) reading from the textbook for this module (‘Business Ethics’ OpenStax, 2018), with regard to the section on Utilitarianism, J S Mill’s ‘harm principle’ states that:

options.text: Any harm done by an action must be counter-weighed by any benefit that action has brought, and only then it can be determined if that action is ‘unethical’ or not.

You must never do any harm intentionally to anyone, under any circumstances, regardless of the outcome overall of that action for the population as a whole (as an exception to the overall philosophy of ‘utilitarianism’).
The only reason for power to be rightfully exercised over any individual against their will is to prevent harm to others, and not to the individual themselves.
Power can and should be rightfully exercised over individuals against their will if it will prevent harm to others and / or to the individual themselves.
The potential to cause harm is never reasonable grounds for power to be exercised over any individual against their will, as it can never be proven that any harm would definitely occur.

questions.explanation: Official sample question (answer inferred - no official key supplied). The textbook quotes Mill: the 'only purpose for which power can be rightfully exercised over any member of a civilized community, against his will, is to prevent harm to others. His own good, either physical or moral, is not a sufficient warrant.'
questions.source: Official MG2008 lecturer sample question 9 (2026 Exam Instructions, Details and Sample MCQs). Wording and options unchanged; no official answer key was issued, so the answer is inferred from: OpenStax 'Business Ethics', section 2.4 (p. 48); Week 4 lecture slides, Part Two

questions.stem: The Week 4 lecture opened with a dilemma in which two brothers both shoot at an intruder: one intends to hit him but misses; the other intends only to scare him but hits and kills him unintentionally. This dilemma was used primarily to illustrate:

options.text: The difference between descriptive and conceptual ethics.
The difference between moral licensing and moral compensation.
The difference between civil and criminal law.
The principle that self-defence is always morally justified.
The question of whether motivations (intentions) matter more than actions and their outcomes, or vice versa.

questions.explanation: The slide asks: 'Is an intention to kill / maim, but not succeeding, better or worse than accidentally killing / maiming someone? Do motivations matter more than actions or vice versa?' - the tension that separates consequentialist from non-consequentialist thinking.
questions.source: Week 4 lecture slides, Part One (Introduction to Ethical Theories and Frameworks), slide 2

questions.stem: Three approaches to ethics were outlined in class. Which ONE of the following correctly describes them?

options.text: Descriptive: analysis of terms; Conceptual: what ought to be done; Normative: what is being done.
All three approaches are concerned only with what the law requires.
Descriptive: what ought to be done; Conceptual: what is being done; Normative: analysis of terms.
Descriptive: what ought to be done; Conceptual: analysis of terms; Normative: what is being done.
Descriptive: factual analysis of what is being done; Conceptual: analysis of terms such as rights, obligations, justice and responsibility; Normative (prescriptive): what ought to be done.

questions.explanation: Descriptive ethics is the scientific study of ethics (what is being done); conceptual ethics analyses terms like rights, obligations, justice, virtue, responsibility; normative (prescriptive) ethics asks what ought to be done, compared with what is being done.
questions.source: Week 4 lecture slides, Part One (Introduction to Ethical Theories and Frameworks), slide 3

questions.stem: A manager argues: 'Paying officials to speed up permits is normal practice in this country, so it is what we ought to do when we operate here.' This position is best described as:

options.text: Discourse ethics
Rule utilitarianism
Moral relativism
Moral absolutism
Descriptive ethics

questions.explanation: Moral relativism holds that moral codes are culturally formed and applies this in a normative way ('this is what ought to be done' here). The lecture warned that a wide-spread practice (e.g. corruption) does not mean it is morally acceptable.
questions.source: Week 4 lecture slides, Part One (Introduction to Ethical Theories and Frameworks), slide 4

questions.stem: With regard to moral absolutism and moral relativism, as discussed in class, which ONE of the following is FALSE?

options.text: Moral relativism is 'normative' because it makes a value judgement about what ought to be done in a given culture.
Moral absolutism holds that there is 'right' and 'wrong', as objective qualities, rationally decided.
A wide-spread practice does not mean that it is morally acceptable.
Multinational corporations are increasingly abandoning consistent codes of conduct in favour of separate ethical rules for each country.
People may hold the same moral standards but disagree on the 'facts' informing a moral scenario, as in the climate-change debate.

questions.explanation: The slide notes the opposite: an increasing trend for MNCs and large corporations to try to apply consistent codes of business nationally and internationally. It also distinguishes relativism of judgement from relativism of standards.
questions.source: Week 4 lecture slides, Part One (Introduction to Ethical Theories and Frameworks), slide 4

questions.stem: According to the lecture, the normative approach to ethics found in most business literature tends to have:

options.text: A purely descriptive orientation, avoiding any assumptions about human nature.
A religious orientation, based on Judeo-Christian teaching alone.
An Asian orientation, with a collectivist approach in which the family comes first.
An 'Anglo-American' orientation, with an individualist approach in which capitalism is taken as a given.
No particular orientation, as it is culturally neutral.

questions.explanation: The slide: the normative approach 'tends to be an Anglo-American orientation in business literature; individualist approach (capitalism as a given)', with specific assumptions about the world and human nature (in economics: opportunistic, bounded rationality - Williamson and others).
questions.source: Week 4 lecture slides, Part One (Introduction to Ethical Theories and Frameworks), slide 5

questions.stem: Which ONE of the following correctly distinguishes egoism from utilitarianism, as presented in class?

options.text: Both focus only on the intention behind an action, not on its results.
Egoism focuses on social outcomes for the community; utilitarianism focuses on outcomes for the decision-maker.
Egoism focuses on duty; utilitarianism focuses on character.
Egoism is a non-consequentialist theory; utilitarianism is a consequentialist theory.
Egoism focuses on the outcome(s) for the decision-maker; utilitarianism focuses on social outcomes for the whole community (the 'Greatest Happiness' principle).

questions.explanation: Both are consequentialist. Egoism is more focussed on outcomes for the decision-maker (free to make own choices, though these might not be in one's interests); utilitarianism focuses on social outcomes for the whole community.
questions.source: Week 4 lecture slides, Part One (Introduction to Ethical Theories and Frameworks), slide 6

questions.stem: The quotation 'an action is morally right if and only if it produces at least as great a balance of value over disvalue as any available action' (Arnold, 2020) was used in class to define:

options.text: Justice theory
Virtue ethics
Egoism
Deontology
Utilitarianism

questions.explanation: This is the definition of utilitarianism given on the slide.
questions.source: Week 4 lecture slides, Part Two (Utilitarianism), slide 3

questions.stem: A company is deciding whether to use a supplier that employs children. One manager says: 'Let's just weigh up the costs and benefits to everyone affected in this one particular case.' Another says: 'We should ask what would happen in the long run if child labour were generally accepted in cases like this.' The two managers are applying, respectively:

options.text: Act utilitarianism and rule utilitarianism.
Descriptive ethics and normative ethics.
Egoism and enlightened egoism.
Rule utilitarianism and act utilitarianism.
Deontology and virtue ethics.

questions.explanation: Act utilitarianism is a 'one-off' calculation of a particular case; rule utilitarianism looks at multiple cases of actions and considers the long run (e.g. child labour in general).
questions.source: Week 4 lecture slides, Part Two (Utilitarianism), slide 3

questions.stem: Which of the following is / are criticisms or limitations of utilitarianism that were raised in class?

options.text: It is open to the subjectivity of the analyst.
There is a problem of quantification and of apportioning costs and benefits.
Minorities can get over-looked, or penalised, as the majority tends to benefit in 'greater good' analysis.
a) and b) above
a), b) and c) above

questions.explanation: The slide describes utilitarianism as closest to cost-benefit analysis in economics (e.g. a mining project: environmental impact v. jobs), open to subjectivity, with problems of quantification and of minorities being over-looked or penalised.
questions.source: Week 4 lecture slides, Part Two (Utilitarianism), slide 4

questions.stem: According to the core textbook reading, Jeremy Bentham created a 'hedonic calculus' in order to:

options.text: Rank human rights in order of importance.
Measure the utility of proposed actions according to conditions such as intensity, duration, certainty and the probability that a certain consequence would result.
Measure the moral character of the person carrying out an action.
Calculate the punishment appropriate for each type of crime.
Demonstrate that pleasure cannot be measured.

questions.explanation: Bentham wanted to reduce utility to a single index measured in 'utils', providing a reasoned basis for judgements of value rather than subjectivity, intuition or opinion.
questions.source: Core Reading 5: OpenStax 'Business Ethics' (2018), section 2.4 Utilitarianism (pp. 44-50), p. 46

questions.stem: According to the core textbook reading (and the lecture slides based on it), utilitarianism as developed by Bentham has four characteristics. Which ONE of the following is NOT one of them?

options.text: Universality
Objectivity
Quantifiability
Spirituality
Rationality

questions.explanation: The textbook lists universality, objectivity, rationality (not based in metaphysics or theology) and quantifiability (reliance on utility). Bentham rejected religious authority.
questions.source: Core Reading 5: OpenStax 'Business Ethics' (2018), section 2.4 Utilitarianism (pp. 44-50), p. 45; Week 4 lecture slides, Part Two (Utilitarianism), slide 5

questions.stem: With regard to Jeremy Bentham's utilitarianism, as set out in the core textbook reading and the lecture, which ONE of the following is FALSE?

options.text: Bentham strongly defended the idea of natural rights as the foundation of morality.
Bentham believed people seek pleasure and avoid pain, regardless of character.
It emphasises the consequences of an act rather than the character of the actor or the actor's motivation.
Social morals and government legislation should aim to produce the greatest happiness for the greatest number of people.
It was criticised for being mechanistic, turning people into utility functions and confusing morality with law.

questions.explanation: Bentham railed against natural rights as 'rhetorical nonsense, nonsense upon stilts'. Omitting natural rights was one of the criticisms of his system - it was Mill who later brought natural rights together with utility.
questions.source: Core Reading 5: OpenStax 'Business Ethics' (2018), section 2.4 Utilitarianism (pp. 44-50), pp. 45-47; Week 4 lecture slides, Part Two (Utilitarianism), slide 5

questions.stem: According to the core textbook reading, how did John Stuart Mill's version of utilitarianism differ from Jeremy Bentham's?

options.text: Mill sought to humanise Bentham's system, offering a synthesis of utility and human rights that protected everyone's rights, particularly the minority's.
Mill argued that the state should intervene in a person's life for their own good.
Mill made utilitarianism more mechanistic by adding further numerical formulas.
Mill rejected utilitarianism entirely in favour of Kant's categorical imperative.
Mill argued that only the happiness of the majority matters.

questions.explanation: Dissatisfied with Bentham's mechanistic approach, Mill wrote that 'human nature is not a machine ... but a tree', and introduced the harm principle to protect individual freedom. His synthesis would eventually underpin neoclassical economic principles.
questions.source: Core Reading 5: OpenStax 'Business Ethics' (2018), section 2.4 Utilitarianism (pp. 44-50), pp. 47-48; Week 4 lecture slides, Part Two (Utilitarianism), slide 6

questions.stem: The core textbook reading identifies limitations of Mill's 'harm principle'. Which of the following is / are among them?

options.text: There has never been a satisfactory definition of 'harm' - what one person finds harmful another may find beneficial.
It makes no provision for emotional or cognitive harm.
It requires the state to intervene whenever a person may harm themselves.
a) and b) above
a), b) and c) above

questions.explanation: The textbook notes that 'harm' has never been satisfactorily defined (raising questions about suicide, euthanasia and drug addiction) and that the approach makes no provision for emotional or cognitive harm. Option c) contradicts the harm principle itself - a person's own good 'is not a sufficient warrant'.
questions.source: Core Reading 5: OpenStax 'Business Ethics' (2018), section 2.4 Utilitarianism (pp. 44-50), p. 48; Week 4 lecture slides, Part Two (Utilitarianism), slide 6

questions.stem: The core textbook reading discusses the role of utilitarianism in contemporary business. Which ONE of the following reflects the textbook's view?

options.text: A cost-benefit analysis that considers only shareholders is a complete utilitarian calculus.
Business leaders never use utilitarian reasoning, as it is purely a theory of government.

Whenever business leaders take stock of what is to be gained and lost in a significant decision (e.g. a cost-benefit analysis) they make a utilitarian determination, although a simple cost-benefit analysis is arguably not a utilitarian calculus unless it considers all stakeholders and a full accounting of externalities.
