Utilitarianism cannot be applied to decisions such as store closings or layoffs.
Utilitarianism requires businesses to ignore numbers and rely on intuition.

questions.explanation: The textbook notes utilitarianism is used frequently in decisions on expansion, store closings, hiring and layoffs, but that a true utilitarian calculus would include all stakeholders, externalities, worker preferences and community and environmental effects.
questions.source: Core Reading 5: OpenStax 'Business Ethics' (2018), section 2.4 Utilitarianism (pp. 44-50), p. 48

questions.stem: In the lecture on egoism, Adam Smith's 'invisible hand of competition' was linked to the phrase 'egoist practices for utilitarian results' (Beauchamp and Bowie, 1997). This means that:

options.text: Companies should pursue the public good directly rather than their own interests.
Egoism and utilitarianism are both non-consequentialist theories.
Governments must plan production so that the greatest number benefit.
Self-interested behaviour always harms society.

When producers pursue their own interests in a competitive market, those who serve consumers poorly will go out of business (or improve) in the longer run, so more people end up served by better goods and services.

questions.explanation: Egoism has been used to advocate free markets and reduced government control (Milton Friedman): competition gives consumers free choice, and self-interested producers who serve consumers well survive, giving the argument a utilitarian focus.
questions.source: Week 4 lecture slides, Part Three (Egoism), slide 3

questions.stem: Which of the following is / are issues with egoism as an ethical philosophy that were raised in class?

options.text: A philosophy based on pursuing personal desire treats very different behaviours as morally 'equal'.
One person's egoism might impact on others' ability to achieve their choices (e.g. sustainability).
Adam Smith was writing when businesses were quite small and tended to be privately owned, so he did not need to address trans-national corporations.
a) and b) above
a), b) and c) above

questions.explanation: The 'Egoism - Issues' slide lists all three, along with the point that acting on immediate desires might not be beneficial and that growing social inequality and market domination by large corporations suggest markets are not functioning as the philosophy assumes.
questions.source: Week 4 lecture slides, Part Three (Egoism), slide 4

questions.stem: 'Enlightened egoism', as described in class, differs from simple egoism in that it:

options.text: Applies only to governments rather than to individuals or companies.
Puts the interests of society ahead of the interests of the decision-maker.
Is a non-consequentialist theory based on duty.
Takes a long-term perspective on one's own interests, rather than acting on immediate desires.
Rejects the idea that people should pursue their own interests.

questions.explanation: Acting on immediate desires (e.g. drinking, gambling) might not be in one's interest; enlightened egoism takes a long-term perspective on self-interest.
questions.source: Week 4 lecture slides, Part Three (Egoism), slide 4

questions.stem: The 'Selling a Kidney' dilemma discussed in class involved a very poor person who is offered approx. 3,000 euro (a few years' income) to be flown abroad to 'donate' a kidney. Which ONE of the following best reflects how this dilemma was discussed?

options.text: It was used to explain the difference between descriptive and conceptual ethics.
It was presented as a clear-cut case with an official 'right' answer under every ethical theory.
A consequentialist argument can be made that both the seller's family and the recipient benefit, but the case raises concerns about exploitation of the poor, deception and the risk of lasting injury.
It was concluded that the commercial sale of kidneys is legal in most countries.
It was used to show that egoism and utilitarianism always reach opposite conclusions.

questions.explanation: The slide notes that some 'donors' have been cheated and left permanently damaged while others appear unharmed, and asks whether the person should be allowed to do this 'as it is their health and family'. In class it was noted that Iran is the only country that allows the commercial sale of kidneys.
questions.source: Week 4 lecture slides, Part Three (Egoism), slide 2; Lecture 4 class notes

questions.stem: In the video shown in class (first 15 minutes of Michael Sandel's Harvard lecture 'The Moral Side of Murder'), students are asked about a runaway trolley car. Most would turn the trolley to kill one person rather than five, but most would NOT push a large man off a bridge to stop the trolley, even though one person dies and five are saved in both cases. As discussed in class, this suggests that:

options.text: Moral reasoning is entirely determined by the law.
The two cases are different because more people die in the second case.
People never consider consequences when making moral decisions.
People's moral reasoning is not based on consequences alone - the nature of the act itself, and directly using a person as a means, also matter.
People are consistently utilitarian in their moral reasoning.

questions.explanation: The first response reflects consequentialist reasoning (one death is better than five); the reluctance to push the man shows that non-consequentialist considerations - the act itself and treating someone as a means - also shape our judgements.
questions.source: Week 4 lecture slides, Part One (Introduction to Ethical Theories and Frameworks), slide 7 (Sandel video); Lecture 4 class notes

questions.stem: According to the lecture, Jeremy Bentham and John Stuart Mill are both associated with utilitarianism, which was described as being closest to which tool used in economics and business?

options.text: Cost-benefit analysis
Game theory
Stakeholder mapping
Break-even analysis
SWOT analysis

questions.explanation: The slide: utilitarianism is 'closest to cost-benefit analysis in Economics', using 'utility' as a measure - e.g. a mining project's environmental impact versus the jobs it creates.
questions.source: Week 4 lecture slides, Part Two (Utilitarianism), slide 4

chapters.title: Week 5 · Ethical Frameworks (2): Non-consequentialist Theories
chapters.description: Kant and deontology, virtue ethics, rights theories, Rawls, discourse ethics, Bauman and resolving moral disagreements, with the textbook readings on deontology and justice theory. Includes official sample 10. Keep answer shuffling OFF.

questions.stem: According to Rawl’s ‘difference principle’, discussed in class:

options.text: No one in society should ever be treated differently when considering how the economy is structured, and hierarchies in companies and organisations should be as flat as possible.
Inequality in society is unacceptable and all economic systems should ensure everyone is given an equal share of the rewards of production.
Economic inequality in society is acceptable once the advantages that result from this inequality (such as a new productivity policy) benefit the most disadvantaged groups proportionately.
Ethical values can be interpreted differently when considering cultural factors, but any difference must be clearly indicated by management.
A difference of opinion is not a valid basis for adhering to accepted ethical frameworks

questions.explanation: Official sample question (answer inferred - no official key supplied). The slide: 'inequality is acceptable once everyone benefits from the causes of this' - e.g. a policy that increases productivity and still adds wealth to owners but, proportionately, gives more return to the least-paid workers.
questions.source: Official MG2008 lecturer sample question 10 (2026 Exam Instructions, Details and Sample MCQs). Wording and options unchanged; no official answer key was issued, so the answer is inferred from: Week 5 lecture slides, Part Three, 'Justice Theory - John Rawls'

questions.stem: Non-consequentialist theories, as introduced in the Week 5 lecture, hold that:

options.text: An action is right if it serves the long-term interests of the decision-maker.
There are basic universal principles of right and wrong, and one should behave according to duty / rules and others' rights regardless of the consequences in a particular situation.
Moral codes are culturally formed, so whatever is widely practised is acceptable.
Only the outcomes of an action are relevant to judging it.
An action is right if it produces the greatest happiness for the greatest number.

questions.explanation: The slide: basic universal principles of right and wrong; ethics of rights (preserve others' rights) and ethics of duty (behave according to duty / rules); 'behave regardless of consequences; the outcomes in a particular situation are not relevant'.
questions.source: Week 5 lecture slides, Part One (Kantian Ethics), slide 1

questions.stem: Which of the following is / are elements of Immanuel Kant's 'categorical imperative', as presented in class?

options.text: Universality - act as if your action were to become a universal law; no one is special or 'above the law'.
Human dignity - treat all humans as an end and not (merely) as a means.
Utility - choose the action that produces the greatest balance of pleasure over pain.
a) and b) above
a), b) and c) above

questions.explanation: The slide lists consistency, acting on the basis of goodwill rather than self-interested motives, human dignity and universality. Maximising pleasure over pain is utilitarian, which Kant rejected.
questions.source: Week 5 lecture slides, Part One (Kantian Ethics), slide 2

questions.stem: The 'New York Times Test', referred to in the lecture on Kantian ethics, asks:

options.text: Whether an action would be legal in the state of New York.
Whether a company's advertising has been reviewed by an independent journalist.
Whether the majority of newspaper readers would benefit from the action.
Whether you would be comfortable with your action, and your reasons for it, appearing on the front page of a newspaper.
Whether a company is large enough to be reported on in the national press.

questions.explanation: As explained in class, the test is a practical check on universality: if you would not be comfortable with the full story of what you did and why being examined publicly, you should reconsider. The lecturer noted the meaning of this test has been examined before.
questions.source: Week 5 lecture slides, Part One (Kantian Ethics), slide 2; Lecture 5 class notes

questions.stem: A shop owner is always scrupulously honest with customers. When asked why, she says: 'Because honesty pays - customers come back when they trust you.' According to the Kantian analysis presented in class, her behaviour is:

options.text: An example of treating customers as ends in themselves, regardless of her motive.
Fully moral, because the outcome is good for everyone.
Immoral, because she is making a profit.
Moral, because she is acting out of kindness.
A prudential decision rather than a moral one, as 'honesty pays' is not an appropriate moral motivation.

questions.explanation: The slide: ''honesty pays', 'being good is good for business' is not an appropriate motivation - this is a prudential decision, not a moral one.' For Kant the motive (acting from duty) is what matters.
questions.source: Week 5 lecture slides, Part One (Kantian Ethics), slide 4

questions.stem: Paula is a manager who feels no particular sympathy for a struggling employee, but she gives him the extra support he is entitled to under company policy because she believes she has a duty to do so. Her colleague Mark gives the same support to another employee purely because he feels sorry for her. According to the strict Kantian account presented in class:

options.text: Paula's action reflects the appropriate moral motive, because kind-heartedness and compassion are not valid motives morally - only adhering to duty matters.
Neither action has moral worth, because both produce the same outcome.
Mark's action is moral only if the employee benefits more than he does.
Both actions are immoral, because employees are being treated as a means.
Mark's action has greater moral worth, because compassion is the highest moral motive.

questions.explanation: The slide: 'Kind-heartedness and compassion are not valid motives, morally - only adhering to the duty required at a point in time matters. Act with reason and not intuition or emotion.' The lecturer indicated that scenarios distinguishing duty from sympathy have been examined.
questions.source: Week 5 lecture slides, Part One (Kantian Ethics), slide 4; Lecture 5 class notes

questions.stem: Kant is often quoted as saying 'never treat another person merely as a means to your own goals'. According to Arnold (2020), as discussed in class, this means that:

options.text: People may be treated purely as a means provided the overall outcome is positive.
Employment is always unethical, because the employee is a means to the employer's profit.
Only customers, and not employees, must be treated as ends.

Kant did not say categorically that others may never be treated as a means, but rather not exclusively so - for example, an employment contract freely entered into, with fair remuneration and good treatment, is acceptable.
The principle applies to individuals but can never be applied in business.

questions.explanation: The word 'merely' matters: the objection is to treating people exclusively as a means. A freely entered exchange with fair remuneration and good treatment respects the person as an end as well.
questions.source: Week 5 lecture slides, Part One (Kantian Ethics), slides 3-4

questions.stem: Which ONE of the following was NOT given in class as a criticism of Kant / deontology?

options.text: It is too rigid and can be hard to apply in all situations (e.g. 'never tell a lie').
Loyalty to a co-worker might conflict with loyalty to a supervisor, so one could end up treating one of them as a means to an end.
It allows minorities to be penalised for the benefit of the majority.
It is too narrow - 'apply to all people in all situations' - when a manager might face a different set of obligations than a worker.
It does not consider partial motivation, such as the treatment of a loved one over others we do not know.

questions.explanation: Over-looking or penalising minorities for the 'greater good' is a criticism of utilitarianism. The criticisms of Kant were rigidity, being too rational, being too narrow, conflicting loyalties and ignoring partial motivation; deontology is increasingly supplemented by more contemporary theories such as rights theories.
questions.source: Week 5 lecture slides, Part One (Kantian Ethics), slide 5

questions.stem: According to the core textbook reading, in its initial form Kant described the categorical imperative as:

options.text: 'Good actions come from good persons.'
'The greatest happiness of the greatest number is the measure of right and wrong.'
'The only purpose for which power can be rightfully exercised over any member of a civilized community, against his will, is to prevent harm to others.'
'Act only according to that maxim whereby you can, at the same time, will that it should become a universal law.'
'Justice is fairness.'

questions.explanation: The textbook quotes this from the Groundwork of the Metaphysic of Morals (1785). 'Categorical' means unconditional. The other quotations relate to Bentham, Mill, virtue theory and Rawls.
questions.source: Core Reading 5: OpenStax 'Business Ethics' (2018), section 2.5 Deontology (pp. 50-53), p. 51

questions.stem: According to the core textbook reading on deontology, which ONE of the following is true of Kant?

options.text: He believed that individuals have no free will to accept or reject the categorical imperative.
He believed that an objective calculus was needed for ethical action.
He was primarily concerned with the consequences of actions and the harm caused to one's individual interests.
He focused on motives and the willingness of individuals to act for the good of others, even though that action might result in personal loss.
He believed that the purpose of ethics was to attain happiness.

questions.explanation: 'Doing something for the right reason was much more important to Kant than any particular outcome.' He rejected Bentham's calculus, held that individuals still have free will to accept or reject the imperative, and asked not how to attain happiness but how to become worthy of it.
questions.source: Core Reading 5: OpenStax 'Business Ethics' (2018), section 2.5 Deontology (pp. 50-53), pp. 50-52

questions.stem: The core textbook reading uses the story of Jean Valjean in 'Les Miserables', who steals a loaf of bread to feed his sister's starving family, to illustrate that:

options.text: Under Kantian ethics breaking the law is always immoral, whatever the motive.
There can be a gap between the legal and the moral: Valjean broke the law, but in a Kantian framework his motives and good will towards others would be taken into account.
Utilitarianism would always condemn theft.
Virtue ethics has no place in business.
Rawls's difference principle requires the redistribution of bread.

questions.explanation: The textbook says that under conventional legal reasoning Valjean is guilty, but 'according to Kantian ethics, Valjean may have been ethical in stealing bread for his family, particularly because the action was grounded in good will and provided benefit to others more than to himself'.
questions.source: Core Reading 5: OpenStax 'Business Ethics' (2018), section 2.5 Deontology (pp. 50-53), p. 52

questions.stem: According to the core textbook reading, why do most companies NOT adhere to strict Kantian theories?

options.text: Because Kantian ethics only applies to governments.
Because Kantian ethics is illegal in most jurisdictions.
Because they look to the outcome of their decisions rather than focusing on motives or intentions.
Because Kant believed companies had no ethical obligations.
Because Kantian ethics forms the foundation of cost-benefit analysis, which companies avoid.

questions.explanation: The textbook notes that, unlike utilitarianism (the foundation of most cost-benefit analysis), Kantian ethics is not easily applied; unconditional ethics is also a challenge for a global organisation operating across very different cultures.
questions.source: Core Reading 5: OpenStax 'Business Ethics' (2018), section 2.5 Deontology (pp. 50-53), p. 53

questions.stem: Which ONE of the following best describes virtue ethics, as presented in class?

options.text: Morality is determined by stakeholders reaching consensus through discussion.
Morality consists of following universal rules regardless of the consequences.
Morality consists of maximising the balance of pleasure over pain.
Morality's primary function is the cultivation of a virtuous character; 'good actions come from good persons', with the focus on habitual patterns of behaviour rather than one-off acts.
Morality is whatever a culture agrees it to be.

questions.explanation: Virtue ethics (Plato / Aristotle) is an approach based on character and integrity: do not just consider actions; look at habitual patterns. Aristotle saw a virtuous character as neither natural nor unnatural but cultivated, like a language.
questions.source: Week 5 lecture slides, Part Two (Virtue Ethics), slides 1-2

questions.stem: An employee does her job for the pay and fulfils every requirement of her contract, but detests the work and does not care about the company or its customers. According to virtue theory, as discussed in class:

options.text: She is acting immorally and should be dismissed.
She is virtuous, because she fulfils all of her duties.
She would not be considered virtuous, because virtue involves more than acting appropriately according to rules - a cultivated character leads one to act from virtuous feelings and desires.
Virtue theory has nothing to say about her, as it applies only to leaders.
She is virtuous, because the outcome for customers is the same.

questions.explanation: The slide contrasts virtue theory with Kantian ethics: more than just acting appropriately according to rules, the cultivation of virtuous character leads one to act according to feelings and desires which are virtuous. Doing a job for the pay but detesting it 'would not be considered virtuous'.
questions.source: Week 5 lecture slides, Part Two (Virtue Ethics), slide 1

questions.stem: With regard to virtue ethics, as presented in class, which ONE of the following is FALSE?

options.text: Aristotle distinguished intellectual virtues (wisdom) from moral virtues (such as honesty, patience and courage).
Its main strength is that it provides a clear and detailed code of conduct for every situation.
It is still strongly associated with some African-based cultures (ubuntu: 'I am because of who we all are') and with Confucianism.
Business characteristics like competitiveness or 'toughness' should not be confused with virtues like integrity, courage, truthfulness and compassion.
In a commercial setting it might more often be applied to professionals such as doctors and lawyers.

questions.explanation: The absence of a clear code of conduct is listed as a draw-back, along with the questions of which community's ideal of 'good practice' to draw on, cultural context, how to translate virtuous traits into action and the need for knowledge and judgement.
questions.source: Week 5 lecture slides, Part Two (Virtue Ethics), slides 1-3

questions.stem: In rights theories, as presented in class, a 'positive right' and a 'negative right' are distinguished. Which ONE of the following is correct?

options.text: A positive right is a right not to be interfered with; a negative right is an obligation to provide a benefit.
There is no difference - the two terms are used interchangeably.

A positive right may create an obligation to provide certain benefits or services (e.g. insurance); a negative right concerns non-interference (e.g. whether employers can stop employees partaking in unhealthy activities in their own time).
Positive rights are legal rights; negative rights are illegal.
Positive rights are held by companies; negative rights are held by individuals.

questions.explanation: Positive rights raise the question of whose responsibility it is to provide them (State, private companies?); negative rights concern being left alone, with the corresponding obligation on others not to interfere.
questions.source: Week 5 lecture slides, Part Three (Rights Theories, Discourse Ethics and Resolving Moral Differences), slides 1-2

questions.stem: With regard to rights theories, as presented in class, which of the following is / are TRUE?

options.text: 'Natural rights' (life, freedom, property, speech) are associated with John Locke, with a later shift to 'human rights'.
Rights theories can be attractive to MNCs, as they can offer a trans-national and trans-cultural set of ethical norms.
A clear and universally agreed hierarchy of rights determines which right takes precedence when rights conflict.
a) and b) above
a), b) and c) above

questions.explanation: The slides state that rights theory lacks theoretical methodology and that there is 'no clear hierarchy of rights provided to date; what takes precedence?'. It is also described as predominantly based on a Western view of morality.
questions.source: Week 5 lecture slides, Part Three (Rights Theories, Discourse Ethics and Resolving Moral Differences), slides 1-2

questions.stem: John Rawls's 'original position' exercise (with its 'veil of ignorance') asks us to consider:

options.text: What rules the most powerful stakeholders would agree to in open discussion.
What a virtuous person would do in the same circumstances.
What societal structure and sharing of resources and power we would agree to if we did not know where we were to be born, or to what social / socio-economic group, race or gender.
What the original founders of a company intended its purpose to be.
What action would produce the greatest happiness for the greatest number.

questions.explanation: Behind the veil of ignorance people imagine they have no identity regarding age, sex, ethnicity, education, income and so on, which reduces bias and self-interest when deciding what is fair.
questions.source: Week 5 lecture slides, Part Three (Rights Theories, Discourse Ethics and Resolving Moral Differences), slide 3; Core Reading 6: OpenStax 'Business Ethics' (2018), section 2.6 A Theory of Justice (pp. 54-58), p. 55

questions.stem: According to the core textbook reading, Rawls's justice theory contains three principles. These are:

options.text: Utility, objectivity and quantifiability.
An 'original position', a 'veil of ignorance' and unanimity of acceptance of the original position.
Universality, human dignity and goodwill.
Descriptive, instrumental and normative.
Liberty, equality and fraternity.

questions.explanation: The textbook lists these three principles together with five procedural steps (entering the contract, agreeing unanimously, including basic conditions such as freedom of speech, maximising the welfare of the most disadvantaged, and ensuring the stability of the contract).
questions.source: Core Reading 6: OpenStax 'Business Ethics' (2018), section 2.6 A Theory of Justice (pp. 54-58), p. 55

questions.stem: In the core textbook reading, Rawls's example of 'pure procedural justice' involves a cake being shared among several people. According to Rawls, the best way to divide the cake fairly is to:

options.text: Let the majority vote on who gets which slice.
Sell the slices to the highest bidders.
Have the person slicing the cake take the last piece.
Give the largest slice to the hungriest person.
Give the largest slice to the person who baked it.

questions.explanation: If the person cutting takes the last piece, they have an incentive to make the slices equal - what matters is an independent standard of what is just and a procedure for implementing it.
questions.source: Core Reading 6: OpenStax 'Business Ethics' (2018), section 2.6 A Theory of Justice (pp. 54-58), p. 55

questions.stem: According to the core textbook reading on justice theory, who is described as perhaps the most compelling critic of Rawls, and what did he argue?

options.text: Milton Friedman, who argued that justice is the business of business.
Immanuel Kant, who argued that fairness is not a duty.
John Locke, who argued that there are no natural rights.
Jeremy Bentham, who argued that justice cannot be quantified.
Robert Nozick, who argued that the power of the state may never ethically be used to deprive someone of property they have legally obtained or inherited in order to distribute it to others in need.

questions.explanation: Nozick, Rawls's colleague at Harvard, wrote a direct rebuttal of Rawlsian justice theory. The textbook also asks whether focusing on the worst off dampens initiative, innovation and creativity.
questions.source: Core Reading 6: OpenStax 'Business Ethics' (2018), section 2.6 A Theory of Justice (pp. 54-58), p. 56

questions.stem: With regard to Rawls's theory of justice, as covered in the lecture and the core textbook reading, which ONE of the following is FALSE?

options.text: Rawls frequently used the expression 'justice as fairness'.
Rawls sought to maximise total wealth for society, in line with the utilitarian thinking of his time.
Rawls's concept of fairness was a political one that relied on the state to take care of the most disadvantaged.
The second principle includes equality of opportunity for all positions, with necessary training provided.
Citizens' equal basic liberties (thought, speech, vote, fair trial, personal property) have priority over economic policy.

questions.explanation: The textbook: Rawls 'sought not to maximize wealth, which was a utilitarian goal, but to establish justice as the criterion by which goods and services were distributed'. His theory was offered as an alternative to the dominant utilitarianism of the time.
questions.source: Core Reading 6: OpenStax 'Business Ethics' (2018), section 2.6 A Theory of Justice (pp. 54-58), p. 54; Week 5 lecture slides, Part Three (Rights Theories, Discourse Ethics and Resolving Moral Differences), slide 3

questions.stem: Discourse ethics, as presented in class, is best described as an approach in which:

options.text: The various stakeholders meet to discuss and resolve issues and reach consensus, with the most powerful stakeholders not being given a disproportionate say.
The option that benefits the majority of stakeholders is always chosen.
Each individual follows his or her own conscience without consulting others.
A single universal code of ethics is applied in the same way in every culture.
The most senior manager decides what is ethical after consulting the law.

questions.explanation: Discourse ethics is a more practical approach for inter-cultural contexts, where standard normative theories may not work. Its draw-backs: it is time consuming and assumes participation by all relevant stakeholders.
questions.source: Week 5 lecture slides, Part Three (Rights Theories, Discourse Ethics and Resolving Moral Differences), slide 4

questions.stem: Bauman (1993), as discussed in class, argued for a pluralistic approach to ethics. Which of the following reflect(s) his position?

options.text: Universal codes can never be found.
Rational approaches deny the real source of morality, which is rooted in a subjective, emotional 'moral impulse' ('gut feel').
Decision-makers should stay at a distance from those affected, so that emotion does not cloud their judgement.
a) and b) above
a), b) and c) above

questions.explanation: Bauman argued employees can become 'distanced' from moral situations, especially in large corporations; decision-makers should be present and interact with the actors to develop their own moral sense of the situation rather than taking a prescriptive approach ('think local - act local').
questions.source: Week 5 lecture slides, Part Three (Rights Theories, Discourse Ethics and Resolving Moral Differences), slide 5

questions.stem: Two colleagues are arguing about whether their company treats staff 'equally'. It emerges that one means 'everyone gets identical treatment' and the other means 'everyone is treated fairly, taking account of differences'. According to the lecture on solving moral disagreements, this suggests that:

options.text: The disagreement cannot be resolved, as it is a difference of fundamental moral values.
The disagreement may be conceptual rather than moral, and could be eased by establishing definitional clarity about the terms being used.
The more senior colleague's view should prevail.
One of the colleagues must be acting immorally.
The issue should be settled by a utilitarian calculation.

questions.explanation: Ways to ease conflict: obtain objective information where possible; establish definitional clarity (it could be a conceptual rather than a moral difference); and analyse arguments and positions for inconsistencies.
questions.source: Week 5 lecture slides, Part Three (Rights Theories, Discourse Ethics and Resolving Moral Differences), slide 6; Lecture 5 class notes

chapters.title: Week 6 · Stakeholder Theory, CSR and Corporate Governance
chapters.description: Corporations and shareholder primacy, stakeholder theory, CSR and its critics, Irish corporate governance, the WRC, Labour Court and protected disclosures, with Core Readings 7, 8 and 9. Includes official samples 4 and 8. Keep answer shuffling OFF.

questions.stem: In terms of Stakeholder Theory, which of the following is NOT considered to be a type of stakeholder:

options.text: Diffused
Normative
Enabling
Participative
Functional

questions.explanation: Official sample question (answer inferred - no official key supplied). The textbook (Figure 3.4) groups stakeholders as enabling, functional, normative and diffused. 'Participative' is not one of the categories.
questions.source: Official MG2008 lecturer sample question 4 (2026 Exam Instructions, Details and Sample MCQs). Wording and options unchanged; no official answer key was issued, so the answer is inferred from: OpenStax 'Business Ethics', section 3.2 'Defining Stakeholder Categories' (Reading 9); Week 6 lecture

questions.stem: ‘Enlightened Self-interest’ means that companies act in a way that is considered ‘enlightened’ (beneficial to others / to society) but that is also of commercial benefit to the company itself because:

options.text: It can enhance long-term revenue, such as by keeping loyal customers and / or good employees.
It can help maintain a social licence that makes it easier to operate, such as having the support of the local community
It can help to manage risk and uncertainty, such as by influencing legislation in a pro-active way
A and B above
A, B and C above

questions.explanation: Official sample question (answer inferred - no official key supplied). The CSR slide lists under 'enlightened self-interest': enhance long-term revenues, reduce costs, manage risk and uncertainty (forestall or influence legislation), and maintain the social licence to operate. All three statements are on that list.
questions.source: Official MG2008 lecturer sample question 8 (2026 Exam Instructions, Details and Sample MCQs). Wording and options unchanged; no official answer key was issued, so the answer is inferred from: Week 6 lecture slides, 'Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR)' (Crane and Matten, 2016)

questions.stem: In the lecture introducing stakeholder theory, 'limited liability' was explained as meaning that:

options.text: Shareholders are liable for all of the debts of the company.
A company can only be sued up to the value of its annual profits.
Directors cannot be held liable for anything a company does.
In the event of business failure, an investor's losses cannot exceed the amount they paid for their share of ownership - although profits are unlimited.
A company's profits are limited by law to a fixed percentage of its capital.

questions.explanation: The slide: losses cannot exceed the amount anyone paid for their share of ownership, 'but allowed unlimited profits' - prompting the question of whether corporations owe a duty to society for the protection afforded them.
questions.source: Week 6 lecture slides, Part One (Stakeholder Theory Introduction), slide 2

questions.stem: With regard to corporations / limited companies, as presented in class, which ONE of the following is FALSE?

options.text: They are defined in terms of legal status and ownership of assets.
They are notionally 'owned' by shareholders but exist independently of them.
They are considered 'artificial persons' in law, able to enter contracts, be sued and pay taxes.
They are regarded as independent of any employee, manager or investor, with perpetual succession.
Shareholders personally own the company's assets and are liable for all of its losses.

questions.explanation: The slide notes that shareholders may not be liable for losses, or own the assets - the corporation is a separate artificial person that exists independently of them.
questions.source: Week 6 lecture slides, Part One (Stakeholder Theory Introduction), slide 3

questions.stem: Which ONE of the following correctly describes the relationship between shareholders and stakeholders?

options.text: The terms mean the same thing.
All shareholders are stakeholders, but not all stakeholders are shareholders.
All stakeholders are shareholders, but not all shareholders are stakeholders.
Shareholders and stakeholders are two entirely separate groups.
Only employees and customers can be stakeholders.

questions.explanation: All shareholders are stakeholders because they are affected by a company's actions, but stakeholders also include many who hold no shares. Traditionally shareholders were given pre-eminence, but that priority is weakening.
questions.source: Week 6 lecture slides, Part One (Stakeholder Theory Introduction), slide 4

questions.stem: In Dodge v. Ford Motor Company (1919), discussed in class in relation to the principle of shareholder primacy:

options.text: Ford wanted to improve quality, lower car prices, expand production and improve employee conditions, but lost - the court held that the company must operate primarily in the profit-maximising interests of shareholders.
The Dodge brothers were prevented from suing because they were competitors.
The court established the 'business judgment rule', protecting Ford's decision.
Ford won, establishing that a company may put employees and customers ahead of shareholders.
The court held that corporations may object to legislation on religious grounds.

questions.explanation: Dodge v. Ford is the classic statement of shareholder primacy: Ford lost.
questions.source: Week 6 lecture slides, Part One (Stakeholder Theory Introduction), slide 7

questions.stem: The 'business judgment rule', as discussed in class, is best described as:

options.text: A rule that assumes office-holders are acting in the interests of shareholders, even if some decisions are not optimal, so that courts should not interfere in management unless fraud or a breach of faith has taken place - allowing some latitude from shareholder primacy.
A rule that gives stakeholders the same legal rights as shareholders.
A rule that makes directors personally liable for any loss suffered by shareholders.
A rule that managers must always choose the option that maximises short-term profit.
A rule that requires every business decision to be approved by a court.

questions.explanation: The rule indemnifies office-holders from losses and frivolous law suits. It is illustrated by Shlensky v. Wrigley (1968).
questions.source: Week 6 lecture slides, Part One (Stakeholder Theory Introduction), slide 8

questions.stem: In Shlensky v. Wrigley (1968), discussed in class, the owner of the Chicago Cubs decided not to install lighting for night-time baseball, out of concern for the impact on the surrounding neighbourhood. Shareholders believed this caused a significant loss of revenue. What was the outcome?

options.text: The case was settled before a judgment was given.
The court ruled that neighbourhood residents were the legal owners of the club.
Wrigley won - the courts decided they should not interfere in a corporation's management unless fraud or a breach of faith had taken place.
The court ordered the club to compensate the local residents.
Wrigley lost, and was ordered to install lights to maximise shareholder returns.

questions.explanation: Wrigley won, an application of the business judgment rule that allows latitude from strict shareholder primacy.
questions.source: Week 6 lecture slides, Part One (Stakeholder Theory Introduction), slide 8

questions.stem: Which ONE of the following statements, quoted in the lecture on stakeholder theory, is attributed to Jack Welch, former CEO of General Electric?

options.text: 'Being good is good for business.'
Shareholder value maximisation as a strategy is 'a dumb idea' and 'your main constituencies are your employees, your customers and your products'.
'Corporations aren't people ... they're bundles of contracts.'
'A business that makes nothing but money is a poor business.'
'The business of business is business.'

questions.explanation: The other quotations belong to Milton Friedman, Henry Ford, Anita Roddick and Robert Reich respectively.
questions.source: Week 6 lecture slides, Part One (Stakeholder Theory Introduction), slide 10

questions.stem: Evans and Freeman (1993), cited in class, proposed two principles. Which ONE of the following correctly states them?

options.text: The Principle of Corporate Rights: corporations have an obligation not to violate the rights of others; and the Principle of Corporate Effect: corporations are responsible for the effects of their actions on others.
The Principle of Shareholder Primacy and the Business Judgment Rule.
The Principle of Corporate Rights: corporations have the same rights as individuals; and the Principle of Corporate Effect: corporations must maximise their effect on profits.
The Principle of Utility and the Harm Principle.
The Difference Principle and the Principle of Equal Opportunity.

questions.explanation: These two principles underpin the stakeholder view that corporations owe obligations beyond their shareholders.
questions.source: Week 6 lecture slides, Part One (Stakeholder Theory Introduction), slide 11

questions.stem: Graham Kenny (HBR, 2014) proposed five questions to identify key stakeholders. According to the answers shown in class, a group is a KEY stakeholder when:

options.text: It has a fundamental impact on the organisation, the organisation can identify what it wants from it, the relationship is dynamic, the organisation cannot exist without or easily replace it, and it has not already been identified through another relationship.
It holds shares in the organisation, regardless of its impact.
It has already been identified through another relationship, such as a trade union representing employees.
It has no interest in the relationship growing.
The organisation can exist without it or easily replace it.

questions.explanation: The answers are YES, YES, YES, NO, NO: fundamental impact; identifiable wants; dynamic relationship; cannot exist without / easily replace; not already identified through another relationship.
questions.source: Week 6 lecture slides, Part Two (Stakeholder Theory and CSR), slide 4

questions.stem: Three approaches to stakeholder claims were presented in class. A firm that 'considers stakeholders as an end in themselves, with intrinsic needs, and not as a means to another end' is taking which approach?

options.text: The normative approach
The diffused approach
The descriptive approach
The instrumental approach
The enabling approach

questions.explanation: Descriptive: weigh and balance all stakeholder claims and address fairly. Instrumental: connect stakeholder claims with financial outcomes (the 'bottom line'). Normative: stakeholders as ends in themselves - described as the most ethical approach.
questions.source: Week 6 lecture slides, Part Two (Stakeholder Theory and CSR), slide 6; Core Reading 9: OpenStax 'Business Ethics' (2018), Chapter 3 (pp. 67-82)

questions.stem: A retailer decides to improve conditions for its suppliers' workers solely because research shows that doing so will reduce supply disruptions and improve profits. In terms of the approaches to stakeholder claims, this is best described as:

options.text: An instrumental approach
A deontological approach
A normative approach
A descriptive approach
A diffused approach

questions.explanation: The instrumental approach connects stakeholder management with financial outcomes: managing stakeholder interests is useful because it contributes to a positive bottom line.
questions.source: Week 6 lecture slides, Part Two (Stakeholder Theory and CSR), slide 6; Core Reading 9: OpenStax 'Business Ethics' (2018), Chapter 3 (pp. 67-82)

questions.stem: According to the core textbook reading (OpenStax, Chapter 3), stakeholders can be grouped into four categories. Which ONE of the following pairings is correct?

options.text: Diffused stakeholders - suppliers and employees.
Functional stakeholders - NGOs, voters and mass media organisations.
Functional stakeholders - those who influence inputs (suppliers, employees, unions) and outputs (customers, distributors, retailers).
Normative stakeholders - stockholders, legislatures, government regulators and boards of directors.
Enabling stakeholders - competitors and peers who influence the norms of the industry.

questions.explanation: Enabling: stockholders, legislatures, regulators, boards (they permit the firm to function). Functional: inputs and outputs. Normative: competitors and peers. Diffused: NGOs, voters and mass media, with less direct relationships but potential for meaningful impact.
questions.source: Core Reading 9: OpenStax 'Business Ethics' (2018), Chapter 3 (pp. 67-82), section 3.2

questions.stem: In the core textbook reading (OpenStax, Chapter 3), Samsung's decision to recall its faulty washing machines and repay customers, rather than simply issuing a warning, is used to illustrate the difference between:

options.text: Shareholder primacy and the business judgment rule.
An 'ethical maximum' (the strongest possible action to behave ethically) and an 'ethical minimum' (the least a company might do that complies with the law).
Positive and negative rights.
Enabling and functional stakeholders.
Descriptive and normative ethics.

questions.explanation: The textbook says Samsung acted at an ethical maximum; offering the warning and nothing more would have been the ethical minimum. Businesses that adhere only to laws and ethical minimums can develop poor reputations and people can be harmed.
questions.source: Core Reading 9: OpenStax 'Business Ethics' (2018), Chapter 3 (pp. 67-82), section 3.1

questions.stem: The core textbook reading (OpenStax, Chapter 3) describes Johnson & Johnson's response to the 1982 Chicago Tylenol poisonings. Which ONE of the following reflects that account?

options.text: The company permanently discontinued the Tylenol brand.
The company denied responsibility and kept the product on sale outside Cook County.
The company voluntarily removed all Tylenol products from the market, even though the poisoning was limited to one area - an extreme action based on the ethics in its corporate credo.
The company was forced by a court to recall the product.
The company blamed its retailers and sued them.

questions.explanation: Seven people died after taking capsules laced with cyanide. Johnson & Johnson's wide recall of a flagship product reassured the public, and the industry followed with tamper-proof packaging.
questions.source: Core Reading 9: OpenStax 'Business Ethics' (2018), Chapter 3 (pp. 67-82), section 3.2 (Cases from the Real World)

questions.stem: Carroll's (1991) 'pyramid of corporate social responsibility', shown in class, sets out four levels of responsibility. From the base of the pyramid to the top, these are:

options.text: Philanthropic, ethical, legal, economic
Ethical, legal, economic, philanthropic
Economic, ethical, philanthropic, legal
Economic, legal, ethical, philanthropic
Legal, economic, philanthropic, ethical

questions.explanation: Carroll's pyramid places economic responsibilities (be profitable) at the base, then legal (obey the law), ethical (do what is right, just and fair) and, at the top, philanthropic responsibilities (be a good corporate citizen).
questions.source: Week 6 lecture slides (Corporate Social Responsibility - Canvas Notes), slide 1 (Carroll, 1991)

questions.stem: In addition to 'enlightened self-interest', a 'moral argument' for CSR was presented in class (Crane and Matten, 2016). Which of the following is / are part of that moral argument?

options.text: Externalities, such as pollution and resource depletion.
The power argument - 'with great power comes great responsibility'.
The dependency argument - corporations depend on wider society for survival and profitability, and so owe something in return.
a) and b) above
a), b) and c) above

questions.explanation: The moral argument for CSR rests on externalities, power and dependency. Reducing costs and enhancing revenues belong to the 'enlightened self-interest' argument.
questions.source: Week 6 lecture slides (Corporate Social Responsibility - Canvas Notes), slide 2

questions.stem: The term 'halo effect' was used in class, in a quotation from Byars et al. (2019) on the emergence of CSR. It refers to:

options.text: The tendency of consumers to say they care about ethics but buy on price.
The legal protection given to directors against frivolous law suits.
The practice of deflecting criticism of a company's ethical record through cause-based advertising.
The collective benefits of social, environmental and charitable programmes that can add value to the business - for example, consumers taking CSR spending as an indirect indicator of product quality.
The tendency of leaders to believe that rules do not apply to them.

questions.explanation: The quotation notes that such programmes 'often create shareholder value rather than take away from it', and consumers are often more willing to buy products as an indirect way of donating to a good cause. Friedman, by contrast, warned that corporations pursuing a social agenda might ultimately lead to a form of corporate autocracy.
questions.source: Week 6 lecture slides (Corporate Social Responsibility - Canvas Notes), slide 3

questions.stem: In the lecture on CSR, Coca-Cola was used as an example to test a company's stated commitment to stakeholders and sustainability against its conduct. Which of the following was / were raised in class?

options.text: In Chiapas, Mexico, residents drink on average more than two litres of soda a day, while a Coca-Cola plant has permits to extract more than 300,000 gallons of water a day in a town where water is scarce.
Coca-Cola's sponsorship of the Cop27 climate summit was criticised as 'greenwashing', given that it is one of the world's biggest plastic polluters.
Coca-Cola was accused of propping up Swaziland's absolute monarch.
a) and b) above
a), b) and c) above

questions.explanation: All three examples were shown after the company's own stakeholder-engagement statement, alongside health data on sugary drinks (e.g. approx. 10 teaspoons of added sugar in a can of cola against a WHO recommendation of no more than 6 a day).
questions.source: Week 6 lecture slides (Corporate Social Responsibility - Canvas Notes), slides 9-13

questions.stem: In 2022 Yvon Chouinard gave away almost all of the stock in Patagonia, a company often cited as representing more ethical values, to fight climate change. The article shown in class (Quartz, 2022) pointed out that:

options.text: The gift was reversed after a shareholder revolt.
The gift was illegal under U.S. corporate law.
The proceeds would be used to buy out competitors.
The arrangement was also a convenient way to avoid taxes, allowing the family to effectively maintain control of the company while almost entirely avoiding gift tax.
The company would be closed down within five years.

questions.explanation: The article called it 'a masterful bit of corporate manoeuvering': a $3 billion gift would normally attract about $1.2 billion in gift tax. The example invites a critical look even at companies with strong ethical reputations.
questions.source: Week 6 lecture slides (Corporate Social Responsibility - Canvas Notes), slide 17

questions.stem: Waterstones was discussed in class in relation to three shops (including 'Southwold Books') that it opened in 2017. The ethical issue raised was that:

options.text: The company closed the shops without notice to staff.
The shops were unbranded, appearing to be independent local bookshops, which rivals described as dishonest - although the company denied any 'subterfuge'.
The shops were opened without planning permission.
The shops sold counterfeit books.
The shops refused to employ local staff.

questions.explanation: Only a handwritten notice in the window stated the owner's true identity. Local competitors complained that Waterstones had 'crept in under the guise of a nice, independent book-store'.
questions.source: Week 6 lecture slides (Corporate Social Responsibility - Canvas Notes), slides 22-23

questions.stem: According to Robert Reich, in the core reading 'Why corporate social responsibility is BS', corporations will only change their ways when:

options.text: Their chief executives personally decide to be socially responsible.
Consumers ask them to.
They are required by law to change - and even then only when the penalty times the probability of getting caught is higher than the profits from continuing anyway.
Their shareholders vote for more spending on CSR.
They sign voluntary codes of conduct.

questions.explanation: Reich argues CEOs 'won't do anything that hurts their bottom lines' and that 'soothing promises of social responsibility are intended to forestall such laws'.
questions.source: Core Reading 7: 'Why corporate social responsibility is BS' (Robert Reich, The Guardian, 2021)

questions.stem: In the core reading 'Why corporate social responsibility is BS', Robert Reich uses the example of the Business Roundtable. What is his point?

options.text: After issuing a widely praised 2019 statement committing to all stakeholders, the Roundtable lobbied intensely against a bill containing the very priorities it claimed to support, because of the tax increases needed to fund it.
The Roundtable lobbied in favour of higher corporate taxes.
The Roundtable's 2019 statement of commitment to 'all of our stakeholders' proved that a new era of CSR had begun.
The Roundtable refused to make any public statement about stakeholders.
The Roundtable disbanded after its members disagreed about CSR.

questions.explanation: Reich contrasts the Roundtable's statements with its 'significant, multifaceted campaign' against Biden's $3.5tn reconciliation bill. Business did not fight the infrastructure bill because that spending helps the bottom line.
questions.source: Core Reading 7: 'Why corporate social responsibility is BS' (Robert Reich, The Guardian, 2021)

questions.stem: With reference to the core reading 'Why corporate social responsibility is BS' (Reich), which ONE of the following is FALSE?

options.text: Reich concludes that voluntary CSR is the most effective way to tackle climate change and inequality.
Reich argues that if we want corporate behaviour to align better with public needs, laws must change.
Reich argues that corporations are not people but 'bundles of contracts', so are not capable of emotions such as greed.
Reich describes corporate lobbyists, lawyers and PR people as forming, in effect, a 'fourth branch of government'.
Reich argues that talk of CSR masks the growing share of the economy going to corporate profits and the declining share going to wages.

questions.explanation: Reich calls 98 per cent of CSR 'rubbish' and concludes that the answer is to ignore talk of CSR and push for laws, including laws to reduce the power of big money in politics.
questions.source: Core Reading 7: 'Why corporate social responsibility is BS' (Robert Reich, The Guardian, 2021)

questions.stem: According to the core reading 'Cigarette-style warning labels should be on everyday food, say campaigners', why does the British Heart Foundation (BHF) argue that warning labels would have to be MANDATORY?

options.text: Because simply asking profit-driven food companies to voluntarily reformulate their products to make them healthier does not work.
Because voluntary labels are more expensive to produce.
Because the food industry has asked for mandatory labelling.
Because consumers do not read voluntary labels.
Because EU law already requires it.

questions.explanation: The BHF said the voluntary approach, taken by governments between 2010 and July 2024, does not work. The measures in the article are campaigners' proposals, not enacted law.
questions.source: Core Reading 8: 'Cigarette-style warning labels should be on everyday food, say campaigners' (The Guardian, 2024)

questions.stem: Which of the following measures was / were proposed by health campaigners in the core reading 'Cigarette-style warning labels should be on everyday food, say campaigners'?

options.text: New taxes (a levy) on salty and sugary products.
A ban on junk food sponsorship of sport.
Outlawing 'buy one get one free' offers in supermarkets.
a) and b) above
a), b) and c) above

questions.explanation: The BHF also proposed extending the junk food advertising ban to billboards and radio. It estimated the measures could save as many as 11,000 lives a year by 2035. The Food and Drink Federation responded that businesses had invested more than £160m since 2023 in healthier products.
questions.source: Core Reading 8: 'Cigarette-style warning labels should be on everyday food, say campaigners' (The Guardian, 2024)

questions.stem: With regard to corporate governance in Ireland, as presented in class (White and McLoughlin, 2025), which ONE of the following is FALSE?

options.text: Every Irish public company must have at least two directors.
A body corporate (another company) may act as a director of an Irish company.
A private company limited by shares may have a sole director, but must also have a separate company secretary.
It is derived from a combination of corporate law, statutory regulations and codes, the codes being for the most part non-binding.
The primary legislation relating to companies is the Companies Act 2014 (as amended).

questions.explanation: A body corporate is prohibited from becoming a director of an Irish company. The principal leadership role is performed by the board of directors; larger companies generally combine executive and non-executive directors.
questions.source: Lecture slides: Corporate Governance, WRC and Protected Disclosures, slide 1

questions.stem: With regard to the Workplace Relations Commission (WRC) and the Labour Court, as covered in class, which ONE of the following is correct?

options.text: Appeals from the Labour Court are heard by the WRC.
The Labour Court's recommendations in industrial relations disputes are binding, but its employment-rights determinations are not.
The Labour Court is a court of law whose decisions in industrial relations disputes are always legally binding.
The WRC only hears unfair dismissal cases and provides no other services.

The WRC provides services such as mediation, conciliation, inspections and first-instance adjudication of employment-rights complaints; its adjudication decisions can be appealed to the Labour Court, whose determinations on such appeals are legally binding.

questions.explanation: The WRC (established under the Workplace Relations Act 2015) promotes good workplace relations and compliance, and offers mediation, conciliation, advice, inspection and adjudication. The Labour Court (1946) is an industrial relations tribunal, not a court of law: a 'court of last resort' whose recommendations in industrial relations disputes are non-binding, but whose determinations on employment-rights appeals are binding.
questions.source: Lecture slides: Corporate Governance, WRC and Protected Disclosures, slides 2-8; Lecture 6 class notes

questions.stem: Under the Protected Disclosures Act 2014 (as amended in 2022), as discussed in class, a 'protected disclosure' is best described as:

options.text: Any complaint that an employee makes about how they are treated by their manager.
A confidential report that a company makes to its shareholders.
A disclosure made to the media about something heard outside of work.
A disclosure of information which a worker reasonably believes tends to show relevant wrongdoing, which came to their attention in a work-related context.
A disclosure that has been proven to be true by an independent investigation.

questions.explanation: The test is reasonable belief, not proof. Relevant wrongdoings include offences, failure to comply with legal obligations, miscarriages of justice, dangers to health and safety, environmental damage, misuse of public funds and concealment of such matters.
questions.source: Lecture slides: Corporate Governance, WRC and Protected Disclosures, slides 9-11; Lecture 6 class notes

questions.stem: Niamh works in the accounts department of a manufacturing company. She has a poor relationship with her manager, who she feels constantly undermines her in meetings. Separately, she notices invoices that she reasonably believes show the company is illegally dumping chemical waste. With regard to protected disclosures, as discussed in class, which ONE of the following is correct?

options.text: The waste-dumping concern may be the subject of a protected disclosure, but the interpersonal grievance with her manager should be dealt with through internal grievance procedures.
Both matters are suitable for a protected disclosure.
Only the grievance with her manager is suitable for a protected disclosure.
The waste dumping can only be reported if she can first prove it beyond doubt.
Neither matter is suitable for a protected disclosure.

questions.explanation: Environmental damage reasonably believed and encountered in a work-related context is a relevant wrongdoing. Personal grievances and interpersonal conflicts are not what the legislation is for - and certainty is not required, only reasonable belief.
questions.source: Lecture slides: Corporate Governance, WRC and Protected Disclosures, slides 9-11; Lecture 6 class notes

questions.stem: With regard to protected disclosures ('whistleblowing') in Ireland, as discussed in class, which ONE of the following is FALSE?

options.text: A worker is only protected if the wrongdoing they reported is later proven to have taken place.
If a worker claims they were penalised for making a protected disclosure, the burden is on the employer to show that its action was justified on other grounds.
A disclosure may be made about wrongdoing that has occurred, is occurring or is likely to occur.
Protection extends beyond current employees to groups such as contractors, agency workers, trainees, volunteers, job applicants, shareholders and board members.
Transparency International Ireland runs a 'Speak Up' helpline offering free support to those considering a disclosure.

questions.explanation: A worker who reasonably believed the information showed wrongdoing remains protected even if the concern turns out to be mistaken. Protection from dismissal and penalisation is the purpose of the Act.
questions.source: Lecture slides: Corporate Governance, WRC and Protected Disclosures, slides 10-13; Lecture 6 class notes

chapters.title: Week 7 · Consumerism and Well-being
chapters.description: Critique of consumerism, GDP and the well-being gap, alternative measures (World Happiness Report, GNH, triple bottom line, de-growth) and Core Readings 10 (Pretty et al.), 11 (marketing and hedonism) and 12 (TOMS). Includes official sample 7. Keep answer shuffling OFF.

questions.stem: According to Pretty et al. (2016), in the article ‘Improving Health and Well-being Independently of GDP’ (a core reading for the module and also discussed in a lecture), the authors present a list of the increasing negative externalities (costs) associated with six key variables that should contribute to well-being (such as ‘healthy food’, ‘active mind’ etc.) and a ‘counterbalance’ of positive outcomes related to each of these variables.  For instance, an indicator of a negative externality for ‘healthy food’ is increasing obesity levels in adults and children and a countertrend for ‘healthy food’ would be a greater understanding of food sources and sustainability of agriculture.  At the end of the study they conclude that “on balance” their ‘scorecard’ for the six factors overall is:

options.text: Very clear, with each factor showing greater improvements overall (in terms of the countertrends) versus the costs of the negative externalities.
Very clear, with each factor showing greater losses (in terms of the negative externalities) overall than the benefits of the improvements (countertrends).
Mixed, but with most factors in substantial deficit (in terms of negative externalities versus positive countertrends).
Mixed, but with most factors in a slight surplus (in terms of positive countertrends versus negative externalities)
Mixed, with half the factors in surplus and the other half in deficit in terms of the balance of negative externalities and positive countertrends.

questions.explanation: Official sample question (answer inferred - no official key supplied). The conclusion states: 'Our scorecard for the six sustainable lifestyle and behavioural choices ... is mixed. Most appear to be in substantial deficit, suggesting an opportunity for health and financial benefits through action and policy.'
questions.source: Official MG2008 lecturer sample question 7 (2026 Exam Instructions, Details and Sample MCQs). Wording and options unchanged; no official answer key was issued, so the answer is inferred from: Pretty et al. (2016), Conclusions

questions.stem: According to Pretty et al. (2016), in the core reading 'Improving Health and Well-being Independently of GDP', what is the relationship between GDP and well-being?

options.text: Well-being falls as GDP rises, even in the poorest countries.
Well-being depends only on the rate of GDP growth, not its level.
Increases in GDP beyond a threshold of basic needs do not lead to further increases in well-being.
GDP has no relationship with well-being at any level of income.
Well-being rises in direct proportion to GDP at every level of income.

questions.explanation: At low per capita GDP, well-being increases with rising GDP; after a threshold it becomes much less dependent on GDP (the 'consumption cliff and affluent uplands' shape). The authors' explanation is that material consumption also produces negative health externalities.
questions.source: Core Reading 10: Pretty et al. (2016), 'Improving Health and Well-being Independently of GDP', abstract

questions.stem: Pretty et al. (2016) identify six factors critical for health and well-being. Which ONE of the following is NOT one of the six?

options.text: High disposable income
Healthy food
Active body
Attachment to meaningful possessions
Contact with nature and green / blue space

questions.explanation: The six factors are healthy food; active body; healthy mind; links with community and family; contact with nature and green / blue space; and attachment to meaningful possessions. The paper's argument is precisely that well-being can improve independently of income (GDP).
questions.source: Core Reading 10: Pretty et al. (2016), 'Improving Health and Well-being Independently of GDP'; Week 7 lecture slides (Consumerism; factors other than GDP leading to well-being), slide 39

questions.stem: In the model proposed by Pretty et al. (2016), well-being would increase 'regardless of levels of GDP' if:

options.text: Governments capped household incomes at the level of basic needs.
All consumption of goods and services were to stop.
Material consumption (MC) continued to grow, with greener products simply added on top.

Environmentally sustainable consumption (ESC) were increasingly substituted for material consumption (MC), and sustainable behaviours involving non-material consumption (SBs-NMC) became more prevalent.
Health services were funded entirely by taxes on consumption.

questions.explanation: The key word is substitution: ESC and SBs-NMC (e.g. gardening, walking, volunteering, community activities) replace damaging material consumption, building natural, social and human capital.
questions.source: Core Reading 10: Pretty et al. (2016), 'Improving Health and Well-being Independently of GDP', abstract and Figures 3a-3b

questions.stem: Pretty et al. (2016) estimate the annual health costs in the UK of the 'negative consumption externalities' of modern material consumption lifestyles. Which ONE of the following reflects their estimate?

options.text: £62 million to the National Health Service and £184 million to the wider economy.
£184 billion to the National Health Service and £62 billion to the wider economy.
No costs could be estimated, as the externalities cannot be measured.

£62 billion to the National Health Service and £184 billion to the whole economy, across conditions such as mental ill-health, dementia, obesity, physical inactivity, diabetes, loneliness and cardiovascular disease.
£620 billion to the National Health Service alone.

questions.explanation: These are the totals for seven major conditions associated with modern material consumption lifestyles; the authors argue a 'dividend' is available if substitution could limit their prevalence.
questions.source: Core Reading 10: Pretty et al. (2016), 'Improving Health and Well-being Independently of GDP', abstract and conclusions

questions.stem: The lecture on consumerism referred to the 'GDP and well-being gap'. Which of the following points was / were made?

options.text: Well-being remains stable once a certain level of affluence is attained, at both personal and national levels.
National gains in well-being are off-set by negative externalities associated with high levels of material consumption, such as obesity, diabetes and social isolation.
There are rapidly diminishing marginal returns of happiness with increasing income.
a) and b) above
a), b) and c) above

questions.explanation: All three points appear on the slide, leading to the conclusion that there is a 'need to redefine the concept of prosperity'.
questions.source: Week 7 lecture slides (Consumerism; factors other than GDP leading to well-being), slide 16

questions.stem: In the lecture on consumerism, a quotation from Chandler Burr's book on the perfume industry was used. It stated that:

options.text: About 97 per cent of the price of a perfume is the cost of its ingredients.
Only about 3 per cent of the price of a perfume in the shop is 'the smell'; the rest is packaging, advertising and margins.
Consumers can reliably tell expensive perfumes from cheap ones.
Advertising accounts for less than 3 per cent of the price of a perfume.
Perfume is the only luxury product that is priced at its cost of production.

questions.explanation: The quotation illustrates how much of what consumers pay for is psychological (brand, image, identity) rather than functional value.
questions.source: Week 7 lecture slides (Consumerism; factors other than GDP leading to well-being), slide 12; Lecture 7 class notes

questions.stem: The World Happiness Report, discussed in class, uses six factors to explain differences in national happiness scores. Which ONE of the following lists includes only factors from the Report?

options.text: GDP per capita, military strength, population size, climate, religion and language.
People, planet, profit, power, politics and prosperity.
Inflation, unemployment, interest rates, exports, imports and government debt.
Healthy food, active body, healthy mind, community links, contact with nature and meaningful possessions.
GDP per capita, social support, healthy life expectancy, freedom to make life choices, generosity and perceptions of corruption.

questions.explanation: These six explanatory factors are compared against 'Dystopia', an imaginary country with the world's least-happy people, used as a benchmark. Option c) lists the six factors of Pretty et al. (2016).
questions.source: Week 7 lecture slides (Consumerism; factors other than GDP leading to well-being), slides 24-26

questions.stem: According to the findings of the World Happiness Report presented in class, which ONE of the following is FALSE?

options.text: City dwellers are on average happier than those in rural areas, especially in less happy countries.
People like living in communities and societies with less inequality of well-being, and where trust in other people and public institutions is high.
The happiest countries are those that care least about sustainable development.
People in high-trust communities are more resilient in the face of challenges such as illness, unemployment and low income.
People are happier in green spaces, especially when accompanied by family or friends.

questions.explanation: The Report found that the happiest countries are those which also care about sustainable development and do more to try to meet the SDGs.
questions.source: Week 7 lecture slides (Consumerism; factors other than GDP leading to well-being), slide 28

questions.stem: Gross National Happiness (GNH), as discussed in class, was introduced as an alternative to GDP by:

options.text: The Government of Costa Rica, in 2000.
The World Bank, in 1945.
The United Nations, in 2015.
The King of Bhutan, in the mid-1970s.
The Government of Denmark, in the 1990s.

questions.explanation: King Jigme Singye Wangchuck said GDP was less important because it could not deliver happiness and well-being. Bhutan has remained a reasonably equitable and sustainable society with a high proportion of happy people despite relatively low per capita income.
questions.source: Week 7 lecture slides (Consumerism; factors other than GDP leading to well-being), slide 38

questions.stem: Which of the following were given in class (in the discussion of Gross National Happiness) as limitations of GDP as a measure of progress?

options.text: It does not distinguish between GDP from good development and GDP from bad development.
It does not value natural, human and social capital.
It does not value free time, leisure or unpaid work.
a) and b) above
a), b) and c) above

questions.explanation: All three are listed on the slide (source: Asian Development Bank). GNH policies take into account equality, family integrity, health, gender equity and satisfying jobs, among other things.
questions.source: Week 7 lecture slides (Consumerism; factors other than GDP leading to well-being), slide 38

questions.stem: The 'Triple Bottom Line', referred to in the lectures, is also known as:

options.text: Economic, Legal, Ethical
People, Planet, Profit
Descriptive, Instrumental, Normative
Reduce, Reuse, Recycle
Profit, Price, Promotion

questions.explanation: The triple bottom line asks businesses to account for social (people), environmental (planet) and economic (profit) performance.
questions.source: Week 7 lecture slides (Consumerism; factors other than GDP leading to well-being), slide 37; Week 12 lecture slides, slide 19

questions.stem: 'De-growth', as presented in the lecture on consumerism, is best described as:

options.text: A call for every country, rich and poor, to reduce its output by the same percentage.
A critique of growth that calls for the abolishment of economic growth as a social objective, pointing towards societies that use fewer natural resources and organise and live differently.
A strategy of doing less of the same economic activity while leaving everything else unchanged.
A policy of reducing wages in order to reduce consumption.
A recession caused by a fall in consumer spending.

questions.explanation: D'Alisa et al. (2014): 'De-growth does not call for doing less of the same ... In a de-growth society everything will be different'. They accept that poorer countries of the Global South still need to grow to satisfy basic needs. Serge Latouche called 'sustainable development' an oxymoron.
questions.source: Week 7 lecture slides (Consumerism; factors other than GDP leading to well-being), slides 40-41

questions.stem: In the de-growth literature quoted in class (D'Alisa et al., 2014), growth is described as a 'zero-sum game' in relation to positional competition. This means that:

options.text: The economy can never grow in real terms.
Growth in one country must be matched by a recession in another.
Growth eliminates competition for status.
Growth always benefits the poor more than the rich.
Everyone wants growth in order to raise their position, but as everyone rises together no one gets better off in relative terms, and growth makes positional goods more expensive.

questions.explanation: 'These are the social limits of growth: growth can never satisfy positional competition; it can only make it worse.'
questions.source: Week 7 lecture slides (Consumerism; factors other than GDP leading to well-being), slide 41

questions.stem: According to the core reading 'Marketing, the Consumer Society and Hedonism' (O'Shaughnessy and O'Shaughnessy, 2002), which ONE of the following best reflects the authors' conclusion about whether marketing is 'guilty as charged' of creating a hedonistic consumer society?

options.text: Marketing should be banned in order to end materialism.
Hedonism was invented by twentieth-century advertising agencies.
Marketing has been more of a facilitator than a manufacturer of the consumer society - the charge against it is overstated.
Marketing has no connection whatsoever with consumption.
Marketing is solely responsible for creating the consumer society and its hedonistic lifestyle.

questions.explanation: The paper examines the common assumption that marketing is responsible for the consumer society and concludes that, in relation to hedonism, marketing 'has been in the role more of facilitator than of manufacturer'. Anti-materialism has a long tradition that pre-dates modern marketing.
questions.source: Core Reading 11: O'Shaughnessy and O'Shaughnessy (2002), 'Marketing, the Consumer Society and Hedonism'

questions.stem: The core reading 'Marketing, the Consumer Society and Hedonism' distinguishes different forms of hedonism. Which ONE of the following is correct?

options.text: Universal hedonism claims that each person should pursue only his or her own pleasure.
Psychological hedonism claims that pleasure is what we ought to pursue; ethical hedonism claims that pleasure is the only possible object of desire.
Both forms claim that pleasure should be avoided.

Psychological hedonism claims that pleasure is the only possible object of desire, because all motivation is based on the prospect of pleasure; ethical hedonism claims that pleasure is what we ought to pursue.
Hedonism is the view that duty is the only good in life.

questions.explanation: Hedonism is the view that pleasure (including the avoidance of pain) is the only good in life. Universal hedonism, which lies behind utilitarianism, argues that everyone ought to act to bring about the most pleasure for the greatest number.
questions.source: Core Reading 11: O'Shaughnessy and O'Shaughnessy (2002), 'Marketing, the Consumer Society and Hedonism'

questions.stem: With reference to the core reading 'Marketing, the Consumer Society and Hedonism', which ONE of the following is FALSE?

options.text: The authors observe that the thrust of most of the world's religions is anti-materialistic.
The authors argue that seeking pleasure directly is the surest way to achieve happiness.
The authors note that consumer culture and consumerism generally get a bad press.
The authors consider the image of marketing to be important because it influences recruitment and social acceptance of the profession.
The authors link criticism of consumerism with criticism of globalisation.

questions.explanation: The authors make the opposite point: seeking pleasure directly is commonly not the best way to achieve happiness.
questions.source: Core Reading 11: O'Shaughnessy and O'Shaughnessy (2002), 'Marketing, the Consumer Society and Hedonism'

questions.stem: According to the core reading on TOMS ('Buying TOMS shoes is a terrible way to help poor people'), when TOMS worked with an outside research team to evaluate the impact of its shoe donations, the researchers found that:

options.text: School attendance and self-esteem improved significantly among children who received shoes.
The children refused to wear the shoes.
The donations eliminated foot disease in the communities studied.
The children liked the shoes and used them, but there was no significant improvement in their school attendance or self-esteem.
The donations doubled the income of local shoe sellers.

questions.explanation: The data also suggested the children spent a bit less time on homework and were slightly more likely to feel dependent on outside aid.
questions.source: Core Reading 12: 'Buying TOMS shoes is a terrible way to help poor people' (Amanda Taub, Vox, 2015)
