questions.stem: In the core reading on TOMS, the author argues that 'buy one, give one' products make 'two really big logical leaps'. These are:

options.text: That cash will be wasted, and that goods will be valued.
That the hardships poor children face are due to their lack of shoes, and that giving them shoes is therefore the best way to address those problems.
That charity is always wasteful, and that business is always efficient.
That shoes are cheap to make, and that they are easy to ship.
That poor children want shoes, and that Western consumers want to buy them.

questions.explanation: The author argues neither assumption is correct: people's problems are almost always more complicated than the lack of an inexpensive consumer item.
questions.source: Core Reading 12: 'Buying TOMS shoes is a terrible way to help poor people' (Amanda Taub, Vox, 2015)

questions.stem: The author of the core reading on TOMS suggests an alternative approach to in-kind donations. Which ONE of the following best reflects her argument?

options.text: Aid should be given only to governments.
Companies should donate two items for every one sold.
Charities should never give goods of any kind, as cash is always best.
Consumers should stop trying to help poor people altogether.

Giving poor people cash should be considered, since they know more about their own needs than donors do - although cash is not necessarily always best (e.g. vaccinations or bednets may be better provided directly).

questions.explanation: She cites research (e.g. Blattman's Uganda study, GiveDirectly) and argues every charity should ask whether it could achieve more by distributing cash. Reports of donated TOMS turning up in local markets suggest recipients turn shoes into cash - inefficiently.
questions.source: Core Reading 12: 'Buying TOMS shoes is a terrible way to help poor people' (Amanda Taub, Vox, 2015)

questions.stem: With reference to the core reading on TOMS, which ONE of the following is FALSE?

options.text: The author says that a desire to help people in need is a good thing.
The author concludes that TOMS shoes have been shown to lift recipients out of poverty.
The author argues that 'buy one, give one' messaging emphasises the importance of the person doing the helping over the person being helped.
The author describes TOMS as an accessory company that markets itself like a charity.
The author argues that such models can promote a view of the world's poor as helpless and passive.

questions.explanation: The article concludes: 'Your TOMS shoes look great with that outfit. But they're not going to save the world.' In class it was added that flooding markets with free goods can hurt local sellers.
questions.source: Core Reading 12: 'Buying TOMS shoes is a terrible way to help poor people' (Amanda Taub, Vox, 2015); Lecture 7 class notes

questions.stem: In the lecture on consumerism, examples such as Innocent smoothies, Naked Juice and Ben & Jerry's were used to make which point?

options.text: These brands had all been found guilty of using child labour.
Brands with a wholesome or progressive image are often owned by large multinationals (e.g. Coca-Cola, PepsiCo, Unilever), a fact that is not obvious to many consumers.
Small independent companies are always more ethical than large ones.
Consumers always check who owns a brand before buying.
Multinationals are legally prohibited from owning health-food brands.

questions.explanation: Ben & Jerry's was founded in 1978 and is now owned by Unilever; the lecture also showed a U.S. lawsuit alleging its 'happy cows' marketing was deceptive. The parent's name is usually kept off the brand.
questions.source: Week 6-7 lecture slides (CSR Canvas Notes, slides 19-21; Consumerism, slides 31-34); Lecture 7 class notes

chapters.title: Week 8 · The Fortune at the Bottom of the Pyramid
chapters.description: Global wealth distribution, marketing to the poor, the requirements for serving BOP markets, and the Prahalad v. Karnani debate (Core Readings 13 and 14). Keep answer shuffling OFF.

questions.stem: The 'Bottom of the Pyramid' (BOP) proposition, associated with C.K. Prahalad, is best summarised as the idea that:

options.text: The world's poor represent a large untapped market, and companies that design products and business models to serve them can both make profits and help reduce poverty and economic isolation.
Only governments can provide goods and services to people on very low incomes.
The poor should be encouraged to save rather than to consume.
The poor should be helped mainly through aid and charitable donations from rich countries.
Multinational companies should withdraw from poor countries to protect local culture.

questions.explanation: Hammond and Prahalad describe the world's 4 billion poor as 'the largest untapped consumer market on Earth': 'Getting it right can both generate big profits and help end economic isolation throughout the developing world' - 'doing well by doing good'.
questions.source: Core Reading 13: Hammond and Prahalad (2004), 'Selling to the Poor', Foreign Policy; Week 8 lecture slides, Part One (The Fortune at the Bottom of the Pyramid - Canvas Notes), slides 1 and 25

questions.stem: The lecture on the Bottom of the Pyramid used the example of small sachets and small pack sizes (e.g. shampoo and detergent sachets, a 200 ml Coca-Cola bottle at 10 rupees in India). Which of the following points was / were made in relation to this approach?

options.text: A low unit price makes a product affordable to people who are paid, and spend, day to day.
A low upfront price does not necessarily mean good value per unit - the customer may pay more per gram or per millilitre than someone buying in bulk.
Plastic sachets have created a significant waste and pollution problem.
a) and b) above
a), b) and c) above

questions.explanation: The slides cited a Reuters investigation: sachets 'allowed companies to tap millions of low-income customers ... but also unleashed a global pollution crisis'. In class the access benefit was weighed against unit value and environmental cost.
questions.source: Week 8 lecture slides, Part One (The Fortune at the Bottom of the Pyramid - Canvas Notes), slides 14 and 17; Lecture 8 class notes

questions.stem: A 2022 Reuters investigation into plastic sachets, shown in class, reported which ONE of the following about Unilever?

options.text: It had stopped selling sachets in all developing countries.
It had invented a fully biodegradable sachet that solved the waste problem.
It had privately fought to derail bans on sachets, despite saying publicly that it wanted to 'get rid of' them.
It had been fined by the United Nations for plastic pollution.
It had never sold products in sachets.

questions.explanation: Unilever, a pioneer in selling sachets, was reported to have lobbied privately against bans on the packaging while publicly saying it wanted to get rid of it - a gap between stated values and conduct.
questions.source: Week 8 lecture slides, Part One (The Fortune at the Bottom of the Pyramid - Canvas Notes), slide 14

questions.stem: With regard to the requirements for successfully serving Bottom of the Pyramid markets, as presented in class, which ONE of the following is FALSE?

options.text: Serving these markets often requires sophisticated and demanding solutions.
Co-creation reduces investment risk.
Products should simply be cheaper, lower-quality versions of western products.
Solutions should be co-created with consumers, drawing on local knowledge.
An 'eco-system' of partners is needed.

questions.explanation: The 'Co-create Solutions' slide states: 'Not just cheaper versions of western products' - 'lean business' should create world-class, safe products, and consumers should be seen as co-creators of solutions.
questions.source: Week 8 lecture slides, Part One (The Fortune at the Bottom of the Pyramid - Canvas Notes), slides 19-22

questions.stem: In the context of the Bottom of the Pyramid, the 'new concept of scale' presented in class refers to:

options.text: Reducing the number of products sold to a single item.
Selling only to the wealthiest 10% of consumers in a country.
Decentralised origination with centralised processing and marketing - for example Amul Dairies (10,000 villages, 2.2 million farmers) and Jaipur Rugs (40,000 contract weavers).
Building the largest possible factory in one location.
Exporting all production to developed countries.

questions.explanation: Very large numbers of small producers supply a central organisation that handles processing and marketing.
questions.source: Week 8 lecture slides, Part One (The Fortune at the Bottom of the Pyramid - Canvas Notes), slide 23

questions.stem: The phrase 'creative capitalism', referred to in the lecture on the Bottom of the Pyramid, is associated with:

options.text: Milton Friedman
Muhammad Yunus
Aneel Karnani
Bill Gates
Andrew Rugasira

questions.explanation: The slide lists 'creative capitalism - Bill Gates' under sustainability: the role of business in tackling social and environmental challenges.
questions.source: Week 8 lecture slides, Part One (The Fortune at the Bottom of the Pyramid - Canvas Notes), slide 24

questions.stem: According to the slide on 'Approach to Market Development' at the Bottom of the Pyramid, success should be assessed using 'different measures'. This means:

options.text: Looking only at the profit margin on each unit sold.
Looking at change in life-style rather than just income, with a focus on areas such as education and health-care.
Looking only at the number of sachets sold.
Looking at how closely the product resembles the version sold in western markets.
Looking only at sales volumes and market share.

questions.explanation: The slide: 'Different measures - change in life-style, rather than income; focus on education and health-care; be sensitive to different decision-criteria'.
questions.source: Week 8 lecture slides, Part One (The Fortune at the Bottom of the Pyramid - Canvas Notes), slide 24

questions.stem: In the core reading 'Selling to the Poor', Hammond and Prahalad open with the example of ITC's 'e-Choupals' in India. What does this example illustrate?

options.text: A microfinance bank lending to women.
A charity distributing free computers to farmers.

A network of Internet-connected computers in farming villages that let soy farmers check fair market prices and sell directly to ITC for more than they previously received - showing how access to information can raise incomes.
A scheme for selling sachets of shampoo.
A government scheme to guarantee crop prices.

questions.explanation: Farmers bypassed local auction markets and received about $6 more per ton; the network also let them buy inputs at a saving. The authors present it as 'the beginnings of consumer market power at the poorest level of Indian society'.
questions.source: Core Reading 13: Hammond and Prahalad (2004), 'Selling to the Poor', Foreign Policy

questions.stem: According to Hammond and Prahalad in 'Selling to the Poor', which of the following is / are 'myths' or mistaken assumptions that prevent companies from serving poor customers?

options.text: That the poor have no money.
That the poor resist new products and services.
That the poor are value-conscious consumers.
a) and b) above
a), b) and c) above

questions.explanation: The authors argue that leaders have 'uncritically accepted the myth that the poor have no money' and that the poor resist new products, when in truth they are rarely offered products designed for their circumstances. That the poor are value-conscious consumers is the authors' own claim, not a myth they reject.
questions.source: Core Reading 13: Hammond and Prahalad (2004), 'Selling to the Poor', Foreign Policy

questions.stem: In the passage from Hammond and Prahalad (2004) quoted in class, the authors argue that:

options.text: Access to new products, expanded choices and increased purchasing power improve one's quality of life, and the exercising of collective consumer market power forces attention to the needs of poor people.
Consumer culture always harms the poor.
The poor should not be allowed to buy non-essential goods.
Only local firms can sell to the poor.
Multinationals should stay out of poor countries because critics are right that they exploit the poor.

questions.explanation: The quotation acknowledges critics who condemn multinationals for 'preaching the gospel of consumer culture to the poor' and for exploitation, but argues that access, choice and purchasing power improve quality of life.
questions.source: Week 8 lecture slides, Part One (The Fortune at the Bottom of the Pyramid - Canvas Notes), slide 25; Core Reading 13: Hammond and Prahalad (2004), 'Selling to the Poor', Foreign Policy

questions.stem: In 'The Mirage of Marketing to the Bottom of the Pyramid', Karnani (2007) argues that the BOP proposition is 'riddled with fallacies'. What alternative does he propose?

options.text: That multinationals should lend money to the poor at commercial rates.
That the private sector has no role to play in alleviating poverty.
That aid should replace trade entirely.
That companies should sell even more consumer goods to the poor in smaller packages.

That, rather than viewing the poor primarily as consumers, the focus should be on the poor as producers - buying from the poor - since the only way to alleviate poverty is to raise the real income of the poor.

questions.explanation: Karnani: 'Creating opportunities for steady employment at reasonable wages is the best way to eradicate poverty.'
questions.source: Core Reading 14: Karnani (2007), 'The Mirage of Marketing to the Bottom of the Pyramid', California Management Review

questions.stem: Karnani (2007) disputes Prahalad's estimate of the size of the BOP market. Which ONE of the following reflects Karnani's argument?

options.text: There are no poor people left in the world, so there is no BOP market.

Prahalad's claim of a $13 trillion BOP market grossly over-estimates its size: based on average consumption of about $1.25 per day by 2.7 billion poor people, the market is around $1.2 trillion at PPP - and even that is an over-estimate.
The BOP market is even larger than the $13 trillion that Prahalad claims.
The BOP market cannot be estimated at all.
The BOP market is exactly as large as Prahalad claims, but too risky to serve.

questions.explanation: Karnani argues that the BOP market is fairly small and not very profitable for most big companies, given low purchasing power and the high costs of distribution to dispersed customers.
questions.source: Core Reading 14: Karnani (2007), 'The Mirage of Marketing to the Bottom of the Pyramid', California Management Review

questions.stem: Karnani (2007) describes the 'single-serve revolution' (e.g. shampoo sold in sachets) as 'a dud'. His argument is that:

options.text: Sachets are too expensive for companies to produce.
Small packages are illegal in most developing countries.
The poor refuse to buy products in sachets.
Sachets are always cheaper per use than large packs.
Selling in small packages does not increase real affordability; the only way to increase real affordability is to reduce the price per use.

questions.explanation: Small packages offer convenience and help cash-flow, but do not make the product cheaper per use. Similarly he argues that providing credit does not change the affordability of a product, even if it provides some other value.
questions.source: Core Reading 14: Karnani (2007), 'The Mirage of Marketing to the Bottom of the Pyramid', California Management Review

questions.stem: The quotation 'The poor surely have a right to buy televisions; the issue is whether it is in their self-interest to buy televisions' was used in class. Who made this statement, and what does it reflect?

options.text: C.K. Prahalad - arguing that the poor should be prevented from buying luxury goods.
Muhammad Yunus - arguing that microcredit should fund televisions.
Milton Friedman - arguing that free choice always maximises welfare.
Samuel Klein - defending Casas Bahia's credit sales.
Aneel Karnani - questioning whether selling consumer goods to the poor actually improves their welfare, even though they have the right to choose.

questions.explanation: Karnani warns against romanticising the poor as 'value-conscious consumers': the poor, like others, often make choices not in their own self-interest (he cites spending on alcohol and tobacco).
questions.source: Week 8 lecture slides, Part One (The Fortune at the Bottom of the Pyramid - Canvas Notes), slide 26; Core Reading 14: Karnani (2007), 'The Mirage of Marketing to the Bottom of the Pyramid', California Management Review

questions.stem: With reference to Karnani's article 'The Mirage of Marketing to the Bottom of the Pyramid', which ONE of the following is FALSE?

options.text: He argues that the BOP proposition is both logically flawed and inconsistent with the evidence.
He argues that a by-product of the BOP proposition is a de-emphasis of the role of the state in providing basic services and infrastructure.
He argues that we should not romanticise the poor as 'creative and resilient entrepreneurs'.
He argues that large multinational companies selling to the poor is the single best way to eradicate poverty.
He criticises the marketing of the skin-whitening cream 'Fair & Lovely', which Hammond and Prahalad had cited positively.

questions.explanation: That is the BOP proposition Karnani is attacking. He asks whether it is 'a harmless illusion or a dangerous delusion', and favours raising incomes through employment and buying from the poor.
questions.source: Core Reading 14: Karnani (2007), 'The Mirage of Marketing to the Bottom of the Pyramid', California Management Review

questions.stem: Which ONE of the following best captures the difference between Hammond and Prahalad ('Selling to the Poor') and Karnani ('The Mirage of Marketing to the Bottom of the Pyramid')?

options.text: Hammond and Prahalad see the poor mainly as producers; Karnani sees them mainly as consumers.
Hammond and Prahalad oppose multinational involvement; Karnani supports it without reservation.
Both argue that aid is the only solution to poverty.
Both argue that the BOP market is worth $13 trillion.
Hammond and Prahalad emphasise the poor as consumers who benefit from access and choice; Karnani emphasises the poor as producers who need higher real incomes.

questions.explanation: This is the central distinction between the two core readings for the week, as emphasised in class.
questions.source: Core Reading 13: Hammond and Prahalad (2004), 'Selling to the Poor', Foreign Policy; Core Reading 14: Karnani (2007), 'The Mirage of Marketing to the Bottom of the Pyramid', California Management Review; Lecture 9 class notes

questions.stem: In the lecture on the Bottom of the Pyramid, a washing machine designed for the Indian market (around 125 euro) was discussed. Which ONE of the following reflects how this example was used?

options.text: As an example of a product that failed because the poor do not want appliances.

As an example of a product adapted to local conditions that may free up time (often women's time) for paid work or education - a possible benefit, to be weighed against the cost of repayments on a very low income.
As an example of a product that should not be sold to the poor.
As an example of a product given away free by a charity.
As proof that buying a washing machine lifts a family out of poverty.

questions.explanation: The lecturer presented a possible mechanism rather than a guaranteed outcome, and linked the question of credit and affordability to the Casas Bahia case.
questions.source: Week 8 lecture slides, Part One (The Fortune at the Bottom of the Pyramid - Canvas Notes), slide 12; Lecture 8 class notes

questions.stem: Global wealth data shown in the Bottom of the Pyramid lecture indicated which ONE of the following?

options.text: The bottom half of the world's population hold about half of the world's wealth.
Global inequality has been eliminated since 2000.
Wealth is spread fairly evenly across the world's adult population.
The richest 1% of the population hold close to half of the world's wealth, while the bottom half hold less than 1%.
No country outside Europe and North America has a significant number of millionaires.

questions.explanation: The slides quoted household wealth reports: half of the world's wealth in the hands of 1% of the population; the bottom half accounted for less than 1% of global wealth while the richest 1% owned 45%. China now has the most people in the top 10% of the global wealth distribution.
questions.source: Week 8 lecture slides, Part One (The Fortune at the Bottom of the Pyramid - Canvas Notes), slides 4 and 10

chapters.title: Week 9 · Micro-finance, Kiva and Fairtrade
chapters.description: Micro-finance and Grameen Bank, Project Shakti, Kiva and its critics, Fairtrade and its critics, plus Core Readings 15 (Rugasira), 16 (Kiva), 17 (Nestle) and 18 (KitKat). Keep answer shuffling OFF.

questions.stem: With regard to Grameen Bank, as presented in the lecture on micro-finance, which ONE of the following is FALSE?

options.text: It has over 10 million borrowers.
It lends small amounts to people who are excluded from conventional banking.
It was founded in 1976 in Bangladesh.
The great majority (97%) of its borrowers are men.
It is associated with Muhammad Yunus.

questions.explanation: The slide states that 97% of borrowers are female. Grameen has 2,568 branches, covers over 81,000 villages and had lent over $35 billion by September 2022.
questions.source: Week 8/9 lecture slides, Part Two (Micro-finance, Grameen Bank, Fair-trade, Kiva - Canvas Notes), slide 3; Lecture 9 class notes

questions.stem: Micro-finance, as discussed in class, is best described as:

options.text: Large loans from international banks to governments of developing countries.
A system of grants that never have to be repaid.
A system of insurance for small farmers.
The provision of small loans to people who lack access to conventional banking, with the aim of supporting income-generating activity.
Loans that are only available to multinational companies operating in poor countries.

questions.explanation: The lecture distinguished the social-development purpose of micro-finance from commercial lenders who borrow its language while charging very high interest, and stressed that capital alone does not guarantee a viable enterprise.
questions.source: Week 8/9 lecture slides, Part Two (Micro-finance, Grameen Bank, Fair-trade, Kiva - Canvas Notes), slides 1-6; Lecture 9 class notes

questions.stem: 'Project Shakti', discussed in the lecture on micro-finance, is an initiative in which:

options.text: A fair-trade organisation certifies village-made soap.
Hindustan Unilever provides micro-credit and training to underprivileged women in India's villages so that they can become entrepreneurs who promote and distribute Unilever's hygiene products.
Grameen Bank lends money to women to buy mobile phones.
The Indian government provides free hygiene products to rural villages.
Kiva lenders fund Indian farmers directly through a website.

questions.explanation: The slide describes social benefits (access to hygiene products, an income for the women) and business benefits (an expanded distribution network reaching hard-to-reach populations) - over 45,000 entrepreneurs covering approx. 100,000 villages.
questions.source: Week 8/9 lecture slides, Part Two (Micro-finance, Grameen Bank, Fair-trade, Kiva - Canvas Notes), slide 7

questions.stem: Project Shakti can be seen as an example of a company 'doing well by doing good'. From an ethical perspective, as discussed in class, which ONE of the following is the most accurate assessment?

options.text: The scheme is unethical because women should not be entrepreneurs.
The commercial benefit to Unilever proves that the scheme has no social value.
The social benefits described prove that Unilever has no commercial motive.
The scheme is a form of charity with no business rationale.
A commercial benefit does not automatically invalidate a social benefit, but equally a positive corporate story does not by itself establish that welfare has improved.

questions.explanation: The lecturer neither dismissed the scheme nor presented its benefits as proven - the module's approach is to test claims against outcomes.
questions.source: Week 8/9 lecture slides, Part Two (Micro-finance, Grameen Bank, Fair-trade, Kiva - Canvas Notes), slide 7; Lecture 9 class notes

questions.stem: Kiva's website, shown in class, invites people to 'lend as little as $25'. According to the criticisms of Kiva in the core reading and discussed in class, which ONE of the following is correct?

options.text: Kiva guarantees that borrowers pay no interest.
Kiva is not in fact peer-to-peer: the loans featured have typically already been made by local microfinance institutions (MFIs), and Kiva users are effectively refinancing them.
Kiva is a pure peer-to-peer lender: the money goes directly from the lender to the borrower featured on the website.
Kiva charges lenders interest on the money they provide.
Kiva lends only to large companies.

questions.explanation: The reading notes that Kiva does not charge interest itself, 'leaving that part to the MFIs it works with', which receive interest-free capital while charging borrowers interest.
questions.source: Core Reading 16: 'The Kiva Fairytale' (Hugh Sinclair) - criticisms of Kiva; Lecture 9 class notes

questions.stem: With reference to the core reading on the criticisms of Kiva ('The Kiva Fairytale'), which of the following criticisms is / are made by the author?

options.text: Kiva provides heart-warming stories and photos but fails to discuss the interest rate that the poor are charged.
Independent academics have been unable to find convincing evidence that microcredit has an overall positive impact on poverty reduction.
Kiva is less efficient at getting money from the investor to the poor person than specialised microfinance funds.
a) and b) above
a), b) and c) above

questions.explanation: The author claims Kiva spent $0.13 for every $1 loaned in 2012, making typical specialised funds 6 or 7 times more efficient, and quotes David Roodman's summary of the impact of microcredit on poverty: 'zero'.
questions.source: Core Reading 16: 'The Kiva Fairytale' (Hugh Sinclair) - criticisms of Kiva

questions.stem: The core reading on the criticisms of Kiva includes a number of 'Editor's notes'. What is the significance of these?

options.text: They state that Kiva has since closed down.
They confirm that Kiva accepts all of the author's criticisms.
They show that the article was written by Kiva's founders.
They record that Kiva disputes several of the author's claims and has provided responses - so the article presents the author's criticisms rather than undisputed facts.
They add further criticisms from the New York Times.

questions.explanation: For example, Kiva disputes the claim that its approach to poverty alleviation does not work, the efficiency comparison, and the claim that field partners are deserting it.
questions.source: Core Reading 16: 'The Kiva Fairytale' (Hugh Sinclair) - criticisms of Kiva

questions.stem: According to the core reading on the criticisms of Kiva, why is Kiva's publication of low default rates questioned?

options.text: Because the banks (MFIs) themselves report default rates substantially higher than Kiva's, suggesting either that Kiva weeds out non-performing clients better than the bank can, or that the bank covers losses itself to keep the interest-free capital flowing.
Because Kiva does not publish any default rates.
Because borrowers are not required to repay Kiva loans.
Because Kiva's default rates are higher than those of commercial banks.
Because default rates are irrelevant to lenders.

questions.explanation: The author also criticises Kiva for citing out-of-date portfolio yields rather than actual interest rates, under-stating the real cost to the poor. In class it was stressed that repayment alone does not show that borrowers are better off.
questions.source: Core Reading 16: 'The Kiva Fairytale' (Hugh Sinclair) - criticisms of Kiva; Lecture 9 class notes

questions.stem: The Fairtrade label, according to the core reading on KitKat, guarantees that:

options.text: Farmers own a share of the company that buys their produce.
The farmers behind a product get a set minimum price as well as a financial bonus (premium).
The retailer makes no profit on the product.
The product has been processed and packaged in the country where it was grown.
The product is organic and free from pesticides.

questions.explanation: The label is seen on products including chocolate, coffee and bananas.
questions.source: Core Reading 18: ''Profoundly disappointing': KitKat cuts ties with Fairtrade' (The Guardian)

questions.stem: According to the core reading 'KitKat cuts ties with Fairtrade', what did Nestle decide to do?

options.text: To pay farmers double the Fairtrade minimum price.
To set up its own cocoa farms in Switzerland.
To end its 10-year association with Fairtrade for KitKat and instead source cocoa from farms on Rainforest Alliance terms.
To stop buying cocoa from West Africa altogether.
To move all of its brands to Fairtrade certification.

questions.explanation: Nestle said it was harmonising its certification internationally (it already used Rainforest Alliance for Aero and Yorkie) and that the decision was not taken to save money. The Fairtrade Foundation called it 'profoundly disappointing' and said farmers in Ivory Coast were 'devastated'.
questions.source: Core Reading 18: ''Profoundly disappointing': KitKat cuts ties with Fairtrade' (The Guardian)

questions.stem: With reference to the core reading 'KitKat cuts ties with Fairtrade', which ONE of the following is FALSE?

options.text: Nestle said it would provide financial support to help farmers certify with the Rainforest Alliance.
Nestle acknowledged that the move would have an impact on some farmers.
Nestle said the decision had been taken in order to reduce the amount it spends on cocoa.
The article notes that other companies, such as Sainsbury's for its own-brand tea, had also moved away from Fairtrade labelling.
The head of the Fairtrade Foundation warned that thousands of farmers would be hit by the move.

questions.explanation: Nestle said the decision 'had not been taken to save money' and that it would spend the same amount on cocoa from its farmers over the next year.
questions.source: Core Reading 18: ''Profoundly disappointing': KitKat cuts ties with Fairtrade' (The Guardian)

questions.stem: In the core reading 'Fair trade is not the solution', Andrew Rugasira (founder of Good African Coffee, Uganda) describes Fairtrade as:

options.text: The most sustainable model for developing African farming communities.
A scheme that pays farmers too much and distorts the market.
A model that he copied directly for his own company.
A government programme that should be made compulsory.
'Compassionate consumption' - a Western kind of charity model that cannot develop farming communities by adding pennies to pounds of coffee while the roasting and packing is done overseas.

questions.explanation: Rugasira argues Fairtrade is 'well-meaning but ... misguided' and can distract from the real, structural issues.
questions.source: Core Reading 15: 'Fair trade is not the solution' (interview with Andrew Rugasira, New African, 2013); Week 8/9 lecture slides, Part Two (Micro-finance, Grameen Bank, Fair-trade, Kiva - Canvas Notes), slide 16

questions.stem: Andrew Rugasira, in the core reading 'Fair trade is not the solution', contrasts the annual value of the coffee that producers sell (about $25bn) with the value of the coffee traded and sold in Western markets (about $128bn). What point is he making?

options.text: That coffee prices are too low for Western consumers.
That the real profit margins go to companies in the developed world, because producers are at the lower end of the value chain and value is added (roasting, packing, branding) elsewhere.
That Fairtrade has succeeded in transferring most of the value to farmers.
That coffee should no longer be exported from Africa.
That African farmers produce too much coffee.

questions.explanation: 'No economy has developed without value addition.' His own company roasts and packs in Uganda to keep more of the value there.
questions.source: Core Reading 15: 'Fair trade is not the solution' (interview with Andrew Rugasira, New African, 2013); Week 8/9 lecture slides, Part Two (Micro-finance, Grameen Bank, Fair-trade, Kiva - Canvas Notes), slide 16

questions.stem: According to Andrew Rugasira in the core reading 'Fair trade is not the solution', which of the following is / are among the real, structural barriers facing African producers and entrepreneurs?

options.text: Non-tariff barriers, such as stringent and shifting standards for access to export markets.
Difficulty in raising capital - he visited 36 banks without securing a loan.
Poor infrastructure and high transport costs.
a) and b) above
a), b) and c) above

questions.explanation: He notes that it took him two-and-a-half years and 14 trips to get his product on sale in the UK, that only 4% of bank loans in Uganda go to agriculture, and that moving a container from Mombasa to Kampala costs more than shipping it from Dubai to Mombasa.
questions.source: Core Reading 15: 'Fair trade is not the solution' (interview with Andrew Rugasira, New African, 2013)

questions.stem: In class, a video of the researcher Peter Griffiths criticising Fairtrade was shown. Which ONE of the following reflects the arguments attributed to him?

options.text: That Fairtrade has eliminated poverty among coffee farmers.
That only a small share of the extra price paid by consumers may reach the producing country, and that guaranteed prices can weaken the incentive to improve quality.
That Fairtrade should be made compulsory for all coffee.
That consumers should pay more for Fairtrade products.
That all of the Fairtrade premium paid by consumers reaches the farmer.

questions.explanation: The lecturer presented this as one researcher's position, noting that Fairtrade organisations would offer counter-arguments - the aim being to question the accepted narrative that 'fair trade is good' rather than to settle the debate.
questions.source: Lecture 9 class notes (Fairtrade, value capture and structural barriers); Lecture 1 class notes

questions.stem: According to the core reading on Nestle, what did the company publicly disclose about its supply chain in Thailand?

options.text: That it had closed all of its operations in Thailand.
That it had found forced labour in its seafood supply chain, and that slave labour was involved in the production of its Fancy Feast cat-food brand.
That it had been using child labour in its own factories.
That it had found no evidence of labour abuse.
That it would no longer audit its suppliers.

questions.explanation: The disclosure followed a year-long investigation (carried out by Verite) and was described by many as ground-breaking, a move into 'a new era of self-policing' of supply chains.
questions.source: Core Reading 17: Nestle (The Guardian articles on forced labour disclosure and water bottling)

questions.stem: The core reading on Nestle describes the company as being in an 'unfortunate position'. Why?

options.text: Because it had been forced to disclose the findings by a court order.
Because its disclosure caused its sales to collapse.
Because its investigation found no problems, which nobody believed.
Because it had been banned from selling cat food.

Because it was disclosing slavery in one part of its operations (Thai seafood) while at the same time fighting through the courts to fend off accusations that child slavery exists in another, more profitable, part of its business (cocoa in the Ivory Coast).

questions.explanation: Critics quoted in the article argue that 'it's easy to own up to something that has already been uncovered' and that self-reporting could be a tactic to deflect litigation.
questions.source: Core Reading 17: Nestle (The Guardian articles on forced labour disclosure and water bottling)

questions.stem: The core reading on Nestle also covers the company's bottled-water operations in the United States. Which ONE of the following reflects that part of the reading?

options.text: Nestle only bottles water that it imports from Switzerland.
All of Nestle's water permits have been cancelled.

Nestle extracted millions of gallons of spring water from a national forest in California while paying the US Forest Service and state practically nothing, and critics describe it as targeting struggling communities.
Nestle pays the full market price for all the water it extracts from public land.
Nestle has been praised by conservationists for restoring dried-up creeks.

questions.explanation: The article raises the question of whether water should be commodified and sold by private industry or is a basic human right.
questions.source: Core Reading 17: Nestle (The Guardian articles on forced labour disclosure and water bottling)

questions.stem: The slide headed 'Cultural Pollution?' in the lecture on micro-finance and Fairtrade raised which ONE of the following ethical questions?

options.text: Whether plastic sachets pollute rivers.
Whether the spread of global consumer brands damages local cultures - and, in turn, who gets to decide what a culture should preserve.
Whether coffee farming pollutes the soil.
Whether advertising should be allowed on television.
Whether micro-finance loans are used to buy alcohol.

questions.explanation: In class a student challenged the lecturer's regret at the arrival of Western fast-food brands in Delhi, arguing that local people should be able to choose for themselves - culture is constantly changing.
questions.source: Week 8/9 lecture slides, Part Two (Micro-finance, Grameen Bank, Fair-trade, Kiva - Canvas Notes), slide 18; Lecture 9 class notes

chapters.title: Week 10 · 'Big' Tobacco, Oil, Pharma and Food
chapters.description: Ethics in industry: tobacco marketing and denial, the OxyContin / opioid crisis, ultra-processed food and food-industry concentration, plus Core Readings 19 (plastics in Africa) and 20 (ILSI). Keep answer shuffling OFF.

questions.stem: In the lectures on ethics in industry, tobacco was presented as a model for a recurring pattern of corporate behaviour that can also be seen in other industries. Which ONE of the following best describes that pattern?

options.text: Hand responsibility for product safety entirely to consumers from the outset.

Promote a product as beneficial or safe; when evidence of harm emerges, deny or cast doubt on it, using sponsored scientists, public relations and lobbying; reassure customers and influence government; face accountability only much later.
Promote a product; when evidence of harm emerges, publish it promptly; withdraw the product; compensate those affected.
Avoid promoting any product until independent regulators have confirmed that it is harmless.
Sell a harmful product only in countries where it is illegal.

questions.explanation: The lecturer used the pattern as an analytical comparison for pharmaceuticals (OxyContin), food and social media, while cautioning that similarity is not proof that every company behaves identically.
questions.source: Lecture 10 class notes (A recurring pattern of corporate harm); Lecture 9 class notes

questions.stem: According to the Centres for Disease Control and Prevention data shown in the lecture on Big Tobacco, which ONE of the following is FALSE?

options.text: Cigarette smoking causes more than 480,000 deaths each year in the United States - nearly one in five deaths.
The risk of dying from cigarette smoking has fallen to almost zero in the U.S. over the last 50 years.
Cigarette smoking is the leading preventable cause of death in the United States.
Smoking causes about 90% of all lung cancer deaths.
More than 10 times as many U.S. citizens have died prematurely from cigarette smoking than have died in all the wars fought by the United States.

questions.explanation: The slide states that the risk of dying from cigarette smoking has increased over the last 50 years in the U.S. Worldwide, tobacco use causes approx. 8 million deaths per year.
questions.source: Week 10 lecture slides, Part One (Ethics in Industry - Big Tobacco), slides 6-8

questions.stem: In 2018, cigarette and smokeless tobacco companies spent over $9 billion on advertising and promotional expenses in the United States. According to the data shown in class, the great majority (over 90%) of cigarette company marketing expenditure went on:

options.text: Price discounts paid to retailers and wholesalers to reduce the price of cigarettes to consumers, and promotional allowances paid to retailers and wholesalers.
Social media influencers.
Health warnings on packaging.
Sponsorship of medical research.
Television and radio advertising.

questions.explanation: Three categories - price discounts (about $7.2 billion) and promotional allowances to retailers and to wholesalers - accounted for 92.4% of cigarette company marketing spend: restrictions on advertising have pushed promotion into other forms.
questions.source: Week 10 lecture slides, Part One (Ethics in Industry - Big Tobacco), slides 11-12

questions.stem: The lecture on Big Tobacco described how tobacco marketing has been targeted at particular racial / ethnic communities in the United States. Which of the following examples was / were given?

options.text: The targeting of African American communities with menthol cigarettes, including tobacco-sponsored hip-hop bar nights.
Marketing to Hispanics and American Indians / Alaska Natives using brand names such as Rio, Dorado and American Spirit.
Sponsorship of Chinese and Vietnamese New Year festivals in Asian American communities.
a) and b) above
a), b) and c) above

questions.explanation: All three examples are from the CDC material shown in class.
questions.source: Week 10 lecture slides, Part One (Ethics in Industry - Big Tobacco), slides 13-14

questions.stem: A documentary on the tobacco industry shown in class described a statement published by tobacco companies in the 1950s (the 'Frank Statement') that reassured the public about smoking. The ethical point drawn from this was that:

options.text: The industry's public reassurance contrasted with its internal knowledge of harm and its efforts to create doubt about the science.
The industry was unaware of any health risks at the time.
The statement admitted that nicotine was addictive.
The industry voluntarily withdrew cigarettes from sale.
Governments had forced the industry to publish the statement.

questions.explanation: The documentary linked a 1953 meeting of tobacco executives with a public relations firm to a coordinated strategy; later litigation by U.S. states led to the 1998 Master Settlement Agreement and the disclosure of internal documents.
questions.source: Lecture 9 class notes (Big Tobacco: promotion, manufactured doubt and accountability)

questions.stem: The lecturer noted that smoking has declined in many Western countries following regulation. What point was made about the tobacco industry's response?

options.text: The industry has largely ceased to exist.
The industry has been nationalised in most countries.
The industry now sells only nicotine-free products.
The industry has stopped all marketing worldwide.
The industry has expanded in markets with weaker regulation and growing populations, particularly in the Global South, and into other products.

questions.explanation: Stricter rules in one market do not eliminate the activity; firms may redirect promotion or expand where controls are weaker - a pattern the lecturer also linked to food companies.
questions.source: Lecture 10 class notes; Lecture 9 class notes

questions.stem: OxyContin, discussed in the lecture on Big Pharma, was manufactured by which company, owned by which family?

options.text: Johnson & Johnson, owned by the Johnson family
Purdue Pharma, owned by the Sackler family
Cargill, owned by the Cargill family
Novo Nordisk, owned by the Jorgensen family
Pfizer, owned by the Pfizer family

questions.explanation: Purdue Pharma, owned by the billionaire Sackler family, made the prescription painkiller OxyContin.
questions.source: Week 10 lecture slides, Part Three (Big Pharma and the OxyContin Crisis), slide 9

questions.stem: In 2019 Purdue Pharma filed for bankruptcy. According to the report shown in class, the lawsuits against the company alleged that it had:

options.text: Falsely promoted OxyContin by downplaying the risk of addiction.
Refused to supply painkillers to hospitals.
Tested its drugs on patients without consent.
Sold counterfeit medicines.
Failed to pay its taxes.

questions.explanation: The company faced more than 2,000 lawsuits, including from nearly all U.S. states; the filing was partly aimed at halting them. The opioid crisis claimed nearly 400,000 lives between 1999 and 2017.
questions.source: Week 10 lecture slides, Part Three (Big Pharma and the OxyContin Crisis), slide 9; Week 3 lecture slides, p. 47

questions.stem: With regard to the OxyContin / opioid crisis, as covered in class, which ONE of the following is FALSE?

options.text: Richard Sackler told a bankruptcy court that he, his family and the company accepted full responsibility for the opioid crisis.
Victims of the opioid crisis formally confronted members of the Sackler family at a hearing in 2022.
The consulting firm McKinsey issued a rare apology for its role, having discussed ways for Purdue to 'turbocharge' sales of OxyContin.
A settlement plan would see the Sackler family give up ownership of the company and contribute billions of dollars.
McKinsey was reported to have proposed that Purdue pay distributors rebates for overdoses linked to the pills they sold.

questions.explanation: Asked whether he, his family and the company bear responsibility for the opioid crisis, Richard Sackler gave a one-word answer for each: 'No'. The lecturer linked this to earlier material on how people separate their self-image from the harm they cause.
questions.source: Week 10 lecture slides, Part Three (Big Pharma and the OxyContin Crisis), slides 10-14; Lecture 10 class notes

questions.stem: In the OxyContin case, how did the company's route to the consumer differ from that of the tobacco industry, as discussed in class?

options.text: The company relied on celebrity endorsements on television.

Doctors stood between the company and the patient, so the company marketed through medical authority - paid medical advocates, conferences, sponsored education and targeting of high-prescribing doctors.
OxyContin was sold directly to consumers in supermarkets.
OxyContin was never promoted at all.
OxyContin was only available in hospitals to terminally ill patients.

questions.explanation: The slow-release formulation was promoted as carrying little risk of addiction - the reassurance that was the marketing claim under scrutiny. The case raises the question of shared responsibility between manufacturers, prescribers and pharmacists.
questions.source: Lecture 10 class notes (OxyContin: marketing through medical authority)

questions.stem: According to the definitions presented in class (Poti et al., 2018), 'ultra-processed foods' are:

options.text: Foods with salt, oil or sugar added that remain recognisable as modified versions of unprocessed foods, such as canned vegetables or cheese.
Fresh fruit and vegetables that have been washed and packaged.
Foods that have been certified as organic.
Multi-ingredient industrial formulations, including sugar-sweetened beverages, packaged breads, cookies, savoury snacks, candy, ice cream, breakfast cereal and pre-prepared frozen meals.
Any foods that have been cooked at home.

questions.explanation: Option a) describes 'processed foods'. The majority of energy intake in high-income countries now comes from ultra-processed foods and beverages.
questions.source: Week 10 lecture slides, Part Two (Ultra-processed Food and Health), slides 3-4

questions.stem: With regard to ultra-processed foods (UPFs), which of the following was / were presented in class?

options.text: Recent research provides fairly consistent support for an association between UPF intake and obesity and related cardiometabolic outcomes.
An umbrella review (Dai et al., 2024) reported that not a single study found an association between UPF intake and a beneficial health outcome.
The American population consumes over half of its calories from ultra-processed food sources.
a) and b) above
a), b) and c) above

questions.explanation: The slides also noted that 73% of food on U.S. grocery shelves is ultra-processed. The lecturer cautioned that reported associations are not, by themselves, proof of causation.
questions.source: Week 10 lecture slides, Part Two (Ultra-processed Food and Health), slides 3-7; Lecture 10 class notes

questions.stem: According to Grover (2024), cited in the lecture on ultra-processed food, it costs about $0.55 to produce 100 calories of ultra-processed food compared with $1.45 for unprocessed food. The ethical implication drawn in class was that:

options.text: Ultra-processed food is a luxury that only wealthier households can afford.
Low-income households face a real affordability constraint, so high consumption of ultra-processed food cannot be put down simply to a lack of willpower.
Ultra-processed food is healthier because it is cheaper.
Unprocessed food should be taxed to make prices equal.
Food companies make no profit on ultra-processed food.

questions.explanation: UPFs are cheap, shelf-stable and calorie-dense; at-risk groups, including low-income families, consume them at a higher rate.
questions.source: Week 10 lecture slides, Part Two (Ultra-processed Food and Health), slide 7; Lecture 10 class notes

questions.stem: The research on sugar cited in class (Ahmed et al., 2013, 'Sugar addiction: pushing the drug-sugar analogy to the limit') concluded that:

options.text: Sugar and sweetness can induce reward and craving comparable in magnitude to those induced by addictive drugs, which may explain why many people have difficulty controlling consumption of foods high in sugar.
Sugar addiction has been proven to be identical to cocaine addiction in humans.
Sugar has no effect on the brain's reward system.
Sugar reduces the desire to eat.
Only laboratory rats, and never humans, respond to sugar.

questions.explanation: The evidence in humans is limited by the difficulty of comparing different types of reward, but is supported by experimental research in rats. The lecturer cautioned against treating the comparison as proof of identical addiction.
questions.source: Week 10 lecture slides, Part Two (Ultra-processed Food and Health), slide 2; Lecture 10 class notes

questions.stem: A joint investigation by the Guardian and Food and Water Watch (2021) into the U.S. food system, shown in class, found that:

options.text: Consumer choice is largely an illusion - a few powerful transnational companies dominate every link of the food supply chain, despite shelves full of different brands.
Food-industry jobs are among the best paid in the country.
Farmers receive most of every dollar spent in the supermarket.
Thousands of independent companies compete in every food category, giving consumers genuine choice.
The food industry spends nothing on political contributions.

questions.explanation: For 85% of groceries analysed, four firms or fewer controlled more than 40% of the market; only 15 cents of every dollar goes to farmers; and at least half of the 10 lowest-paid jobs are in the food industry.
questions.source: Week 10 lecture slides, Part Two (Ultra-processed Food and Health), slides 10-13

questions.stem: The lecture referred to the weight-loss / diabetes drugs Ozempic and Wegovy (Novo Nordisk). What ethical or business issue did this raise in relation to the food industry?

options.text: The drugs have been banned because they harm food sales.
Medicines that reduce appetite may reduce sales of snack and confectionery products, showing how the commercial interests of the food and pharmaceutical industries can overlap and conflict.
The drugs are made from ultra-processed food.
Food companies own the patents on the drugs.
Food companies and pharmaceutical companies have identical incentives.

questions.explanation: Novo Nordisk expects 'a multibillion-dollar market with nearly a billion potential patients'. The lecturer also noted that diet-related illness itself creates demand for pharmaceutical treatment.
questions.source: Week 10 lecture slides, Part Three (Big Pharma and the OxyContin Crisis), slide 4; Lecture 10 class notes

questions.stem: According to the core reading 'Big Oil Is in Trouble. Its Plan: Flood Africa With Plastic', why are oil companies 'racing to make more plastic'?

options.text: Because African governments have asked for more plastic.
Because governments are paying them to do so.
Because recycling has eliminated the supply of used plastic.
Because plastic has been shown to reduce carbon emissions.
Because the climate crisis and falling demand threaten the fossil fuel business, so producers are seeking new uses for an oversupply of oil and gas.

questions.explanation: The industry has spent more than $200 billion on chemical and manufacturing plants in the U.S. over the past decade. But many markets are already awash with plastic, and few countries are willing to be dumping grounds for the world's plastic waste.
questions.source: Core Reading 19: 'Big Oil Is in Trouble. Its Plan: Flood Africa With Plastic' (New York Times, 2020)

questions.stem: According to the core reading 'Big Oil Is in Trouble. Its Plan: Flood Africa With Plastic', what was the American Chemistry Council lobbying for in relation to Kenya?

options.text: For U.S. trade negotiators to press Kenya to reverse its strict limits on plastics (including its plastic-bag ban) and to continue importing foreign plastic waste.
For Kenya to build plastic recycling plants at its own expense.
For the U.S. to stop exporting plastic waste to Africa.
For Kenya to introduce a stricter ban on plastic bags.
For a global treaty to end plastic production.

questions.explanation: Kenya passed a stringent law against plastic bags in 2017 and signed a global agreement to stop importing plastic waste. The council's letter anticipated that Kenya could become 'a hub for supplying U.S.-made chemicals and plastics to other markets in Africa'.
questions.source: Core Reading 19: 'Big Oil Is in Trouble. Its Plan: Flood Africa With Plastic' (New York Times, 2020)

questions.stem: With reference to the core reading 'Big Oil Is in Trouble. Its Plan: Flood Africa With Plastic', which ONE of the following is FALSE?

options.text: The lobbying became known because the industry announced its proposals at a public press conference in Nairobi.
The American Chemistry Council's members include the petrochemical operations of Exxon Mobil, Chevron and Shell.
The article notes that industries typically have a strong voice in shaping trade policy.
In 2019, American exporters shipped more than 1 billion pounds of plastic waste to 96 countries, ostensibly to be recycled.
After China closed its ports to most plastic trash in 2018, exporters looked for new destinations, and exports to Africa rose sharply.

questions.explanation: The proposals came to light through documents reviewed by The New York Times - it was behind-the-scenes lobbying, which alarmed environmental groups in Kenya.
questions.source: Core Reading 19: 'Big Oil Is in Trouble. Its Plan: Flood Africa With Plastic' (New York Times, 2020)

questions.stem: According to the core reading 'A Shadowy Industry Group Shapes Food Policy Around the World', the International Life Sciences Institute (ILSI) is:

options.text: An independent university research centre funded by governments.
A trade union for scientists working in the food industry.
A United Nations agency responsible for food safety.
A consumer campaign group that lobbies for warning labels on food.

An American non-profit, created by a top Coca-Cola executive, that is almost entirely funded by agribusiness, food and pharmaceutical companies, and which critics say acts as a front group for its corporate members.

questions.explanation: ILSI has branches in 17 countries and around 400 corporate members (including Coca-Cola, PepsiCo, DuPont, General Mills and Danone) providing its $17 million budget. It championed tobacco interests during the 1980s and 1990s.
questions.source: Core Reading 20: 'A Shadowy Industry Group Shapes Food Policy Around the World' (New York Times, 2019)

questions.stem: In the core reading on ILSI, what happened in India that 'enraged health advocates'?

options.text: The World Health Organization took over India's food regulator.
The government banned all packaged food.
After postponing red warning labels on unhealthy packaged food, the government appointed an ILSI trustee and former adviser to Nestle to head the expert panel reviewing the proposed labelling system.
Coca-Cola withdrew from the Indian market.
ILSI published research showing that sugar is harmful.

questions.explanation: Critics argued that 'the regulated cannot be the regulators'; under Indian law seats on such panels are reserved for independent experts.
questions.source: Core Reading 20: 'A Shadowy Industry Group Shapes Food Policy Around the World' (New York Times, 2019)

questions.stem: With reference to the core reading 'A Shadowy Industry Group Shapes Food Policy Around the World', which ONE of the following is FALSE?

options.text: ILSI rejects allegations that it works to advance the interests of its corporate members.
In 2015 ILSI lost its special access to governing bodies at the World Health Organization.
In China, ILSI shares staff and office space with the agency responsible for combating obesity-related illness.
The candy maker Mars withdrew from ILSI, saying it could no longer support an organisation that funds 'advocacy-led studies'.
ILSI's China affiliate helped shape anti-obesity campaigns that stressed dietary changes over physical activity.

questions.explanation: The campaigns stressed physical activity over dietary changes - a strategy long espoused by Coca-Cola that critics say was designed to protect corporate profits.
questions.source: Core Reading 20: 'A Shadowy Industry Group Shapes Food Policy Around the World' (New York Times, 2019)

chapters.title: Week 11 · Big Tech: AI, Social Media and Food Classification
chapters.description: UPCOMING lecture - questions are based on the lecture decks on file (which may be updated when delivered) and on Core Readings 21 (Pringles / Subway VAT rulings) and 22 (Cambridge Analytica). Keep answer shuffling OFF.

questions.stem: In the lecture material on artificial intelligence, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is quoted as saying: 'You're not going to lose your job to AI; you're going to lose your job to ...'

options.text: '... a robot.'
'... your own employer's algorithm.'
'... someone who uses AI.'
'... a cheaper worker overseas.'
'... a government regulator.'

questions.explanation: Huang argues that AI should support and enhance human labour rather than simply replace it: 'some jobs will be lost' while 'many jobs will be created', with significant losses only 'if the world runs out of ideas'.
questions.source: Week 11 lecture slides, Part One (Artificial Intelligence) - deck on file; lecture not yet delivered at time of writing, slide 2

questions.stem: Geoffrey Hinton, the 'Godfather of AI' and 2024 Nobel Laureate, is quoted in the lecture material on AI. Which ONE of the following reflects his view?

options.text: AI investment is too small to matter.

AI can do tremendous good in areas such as health care and education, but tech giants cannot profit from their enormous investments unless human labour is replaced - the problem lies in how we organise society.
AI is like nuclear weapons - it is only good for bad things.
AI will create more jobs than it destroys, so there is nothing to worry about.
AI is mostly hype and will have little economic impact.

questions.explanation: Hinton: 'It's not like nuclear weapons, which are only good for bad things' but 'to make money you're going to have to replace human labor' - AI will 'create massive unemployment and a huge rise in profits', which he attributes to the capitalist system.
questions.source: Week 11 lecture slides, Part One (Artificial Intelligence) - deck on file; lecture not yet delivered at time of writing, slide 11

questions.stem: The lecture material on AI quotes the 2024 Nobel Laureate John Hopfield. What was his main concern?

options.text: That he is unnerved by a technology that is not well enough understood to know its limits, noting that there are very few examples of more intelligent things being controlled by less intelligent things.
That AI will never be as intelligent as humans.
That AI is too expensive for most companies.
That AI will reduce the profits of technology companies.
That AI research is progressing too slowly.

questions.explanation: Hopfield warned of 'catastrophe' if AI advances are not controlled.
questions.source: Week 11 lecture slides, Part One (Artificial Intelligence) - deck on file; lecture not yet delivered at time of writing, slide 9

questions.stem: Which of the following concerns about AI was / were raised in the lecture material?

options.text: Generative AI systems are prone to hallucinations and errors, and studies have documented instances of AI deceiving its human operators.
A study found that the great majority of companies running AI pilot studies saw little or no return on their investment.
Valuations of U.S. technology stocks show signs of being 'stretched', with the Central Bank warning of knock-on risks to the Irish economy.
a) and b) above
a), b) and c) above

questions.explanation: The slides cite an MIT study (95 per cent of companies found little or no return), safety concerns raised by Yoshua Bengio and others, and the Central Bank of Ireland's warning about exposure to a tech-led market downturn.
questions.source: Week 11 lecture slides, Part One (Artificial Intelligence) - deck on file; lecture not yet delivered at time of writing, slides 4 and 10

questions.stem: The critic Gary Marcus is quoted in the lecture material on AI. Which ONE of the following reflects his argument about 'AI hype'?

options.text: AI companies are certain to be profitable by 2030.
AI systems now fully understand how the world works.
Simply scaling up models with more training will inevitably produce human-level intelligence.
AI has already replaced most professional jobs.
Scaling has lost steam: much larger models have been only moderately better, and generative AI lacks the proper 'world models', common sense and reliability needed to build trustworthy agents.

questions.explanation: Marcus points out, for example, that large language models still make illegal moves in chess however many games they have been trained on.
questions.source: Week 11 lecture slides, Part One (Artificial Intelligence) - deck on file; lecture not yet delivered at time of writing, slide 6

questions.stem: Former Mozilla and Jawbone employee Aza Raskin, quoted in the lecture material on social media (BBC Panorama, 2018), designed which feature, now seen as highly habit-forming - and what did he say about it?

options.text: The 'like' button - he said it had no effect on behaviour.
The news feed - he said it was designed purely to inform users.
The 'share' button - he said it reduced time spent online.
Push notifications - he said they should be made compulsory.
Infinite scroll - he said he had not set out to addict people and now felt guilty, describing addictive design as 'behavioural cocaine' sprinkled over the interface.

questions.explanation: Raskin said designers were driven by the business models of the companies that employed them: 'the amount of time that people spend on your app has to go up'.
questions.source: Week 11 lecture slides, Part Two (Social Media / 'Big Tech') - deck on file; lecture not yet delivered at time of writing, slide 7

questions.stem: A U.S. study of young adults cited in the lecture material on social media (Primack et al.) found that:

options.text: Heavy social media use had no relationship with social isolation.
Social media use eliminated feelings of loneliness.
Only people over 60 were affected by social media use.
People who used social media most had the largest number of close friends.
More than two hours of social media use a day doubled the chances of a person experiencing social isolation.

questions.explanation: Those who visited sites 58 or more times per week were three times more at risk of isolation than those visiting fewer than nine times: sites designed to connect people 'are actually causing them to feel more alone'.
questions.source: Week 11 lecture slides, Part Two (Social Media / 'Big Tech') - deck on file; lecture not yet delivered at time of writing, slide 8

questions.stem: With regard to the Cambridge Analytica scandal, as covered in the lecture material on social media, which ONE of the following is correct?

options.text: Users' data was obtained by hacking into Facebook's servers.

A personality test app harvested the personal data of the people who installed it and of their Facebook friends, so that a small number of app users yielded data on a very large number of people without their consent.
The app collected data only from users in the United Kingdom.
The data was used exclusively for academic research.
Only data from users who gave explicit consent for political use was collected.

questions.explanation: In Australia, for example, only 53 people installed the 'This is Your Digital Life' app, but it harvested the data of about 311,127 people. The information was used predominantly for political advertising.
questions.source: Week 11 lecture slides, Part Two (Social Media / 'Big Tech') - deck on file; lecture not yet delivered at time of writing, slide 5; Core Reading 22: 'Cambridge Analytica: how did it turn clicks into votes?' (The Guardian, 2018)

questions.stem: According to research described in the lecture material on social media (The Guardian, 2018), what can Facebook 'likes' reveal about a person?

options.text: Only what products they have bought.
Only the person's age and location.
Nothing of significance, as 'likes' are trivial.

A few dozen 'likes' can give a strong prediction of which party a user will vote for, and can reveal sensitive personal information such as sexual orientation - even though few users 'like' pages that explicitly reveal those attributes.
Only the names of their friends.

questions.explanation: For example, less than 5% of users labelled as gay were connected with explicitly gay groups; the predictions came from patterns in apparently trivial 'likes'.
questions.source: Week 11 lecture slides, Part Two (Social Media / 'Big Tech') - deck on file; lecture not yet delivered at time of writing, slide 4

questions.stem: In the core reading on how Cambridge Analytica worked, the whistle-blower Christopher Wylie explains that, in building a predictive algorithm, the first step is to create a 'training set'. In this case that involved:

options.text: Interviewing politicians about their supporters.
Sending questionnaires to every Facebook user in the world.
Guessing personality types from profile photographs.
Getting a few hundred thousand people to complete a 120-question personality quiz, so that their answers (the 'target variables') could be related to their Facebook data (the 'feature set').
Buying voting records from governments.

questions.explanation: Survey-takers were paid a few dollars, had to log in with Facebook and approve access to the app developed by Dr Aleksandr Kogan; the app then harvested their data and that of their friends.
questions.source: Core Reading 22: 'Cambridge Analytica: how did it turn clicks into votes?' (The Guardian, 2018)

questions.stem: According to the core reading on Cambridge Analytica, the personality surveys profiled people using the 'five factors' or 'Ocean' model. Which ONE of the following lists the five factors?

options.text: Honesty, mercy, modesty, loyalty and patience.
Openness to experience, conscientiousness, extraversion, agreeableness and neuroticism.
Optimism, courage, empathy, ambition and narcissism.
Obedience, conformity, entitlement, attribution and nostalgia.
Openness, confidence, energy, altruism and nerve.

questions.explanation: The model clusters personality traits in ways that hold across cultures and time, which is what made it useful for profiling and for tailoring messages to particular personality types.
questions.source: Core Reading 22: 'Cambridge Analytica: how did it turn clicks into votes?' (The Guardian, 2018)

questions.stem: In the core reading on Pringles and VAT, why did Procter & Gamble argue in the British courts that Pringles were NOT potato chips (crisps)?

options.text: To be allowed to advertise Pringles as a health food.
To avoid having to list potato as an allergen.
Because most foods are exempt from VAT in Britain, but potato crisps and similar products made from the potato are not - so being classed as a crisp meant paying VAT.
Because the company wanted to pay a higher rate of tax.
Because potato crisps were banned from sale in schools.

questions.explanation: P&G argued that Pringles did not 'contain enough potato to have the quality of potatoness' (about 42% potato) and had 'a shape not found in nature'.
questions.source: Core Reading 21: Pringles and Subway legal rulings for VAT

questions.stem: What was the final outcome of the Pringles case, according to the core reading?

options.text: Pringles were withdrawn from sale in Britain.
The case was dropped before any court ruled on it.
The courts finally ruled that Pringles are not potato crisps, so no VAT was due.
The European Court ruled that Pringles are a biscuit.
A lower court agreed with the company in 2008, but in 2009 the Court of Appeal reversed that decision, so Pringles are standard-rated for VAT.

questions.explanation: The Court of Appeal said the 'made from' question should be answered sensibly, in everyday English - 'more relevant and sensible' from 'a child consumer of crisps than ... a food scientist or a culinary pedant'.
questions.source: Core Reading 21: Pringles and Subway legal rulings for VAT

questions.stem: In 2020 Ireland's Supreme Court ruled on the bread used in Subway sandwiches. According to the core reading and the lecture, what did the court decide, and why?

options.text: That Subway must stop selling sandwiches in Ireland.
That Subway bread contained too little flour to be called bread.
That Subway bread was a health food and should be subsidised.
That Subway bread could not be defined as bread for VAT purposes, because its sugar content (about 10% of the weight of the flour) exceeds the 2% limit in the Value-Added Tax Act 1972.
That Subway bread is a staple food and exempt from VAT, because it is baked fresh.

questions.explanation: The Act distinguishes bread as a staple food from confectionery or fancy baked goods. The case arose from an appeal by Subway's Irish franchisee, Bookfinders Ltd, which had argued its bread should be zero-rated.
questions.source: Core Reading 21: Pringles and Subway legal rulings for VAT; Week 6-7 lecture slides (Subway slide)

questions.stem: Taken together, what do the Pringles and Subway cases (Core Reading 21) illustrate from a business ethics perspective?

options.text: That both companies won their cases.

That companies may argue for whatever classification of a product gives a tax advantage - one denying its snack is a potato crisp, another insisting its sugary bread is a staple - which can sit uneasily with how the products are marketed to consumers.
That food companies always describe their products in the same way to regulators, tax authorities and consumers.
That courts are not capable of ruling on food.
That VAT does not apply to food in Ireland or Britain.

questions.explanation: Both companies lost. The cases are legal classifications for tax, but they invite comparison between what companies tell the taxman and what they tell the customer.
questions.source: Core Reading 21: Pringles and Subway legal rulings for VAT

questions.stem: The lecture material on 'Big Tech' reports that Google spent some 15 years creating what a New York Times investigation (2024) called 'a culture of concealment'. This refers to:

options.text: Google hiding its search results from competitors.
Google refusing to publish its annual accounts.
Google telling employees to destroy messages, avoid certain words and copy in lawyers, making deletion the default in internal communications in order to reduce the risk from antitrust suits.
Google keeping its office locations secret.
Google concealing its ownership of YouTube.

questions.explanation: 'Even as the internet giant stored the world's information, it created an office culture that tried to minimize its own.'
questions.source: Week 11 lecture slides, Part Two (Social Media / 'Big Tech') - deck on file; lecture not yet delivered at time of writing, slide 6

questions.stem: The lecture material on social media refers to Facebook content moderators (2020). What ethical issue did their open letter raise?

options.text: That moderators were being replaced entirely by volunteers.
That moderators were refusing to remove harmful content.

That moderators - who are low-paid and not even directly employed by the firm - were doing psychologically toxic work reviewing violence and child abuse, and felt their lives were being put at risk to maintain profits during the pandemic.
That moderators were being paid too much.
That moderators had too little work to do.

questions.explanation: More than 200 moderators, including 114 working in Dublin for outsourcing firms, signed the letter - an example of a firm keeping responsibility at arm's length.
questions.source: Week 11 lecture slides, Part Two (Social Media / 'Big Tech') - deck on file; lecture not yet delivered at time of writing, slide 3

chapters.title: Week 12 · Sustainable Business and the UN SDGs
chapters.description: UPCOMING lecture - questions are based on the lecture deck on file (which may be updated when delivered): climate change, plastics, COP, the SDGs, the triple bottom line, the circular economy and B Corps. Keep answer shuffling OFF.

questions.stem: According to the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) Sixth Assessment report (2021), as presented in the lecture material on sustainability:

options.text: Global temperatures are expected to fall over the next few decades.
The climate has warmed by 5 degrees Celsius since 1750.
Warming will affect only polar regions.

Human emissions of heat-trapping gases have already warmed the climate by nearly 1.1 degrees Celsius since pre-industrial times, and the global average temperature is expected to reach or exceed 1.5 degrees C within the next few decades.
Human emissions have had no measurable effect on global temperature.

questions.explanation: The slide adds that these changes will affect all regions of Earth. Accompanying charts show rising CO2 emissions, global and sea temperatures and sea levels, and declining Arctic sea ice and Antarctic ice-sheets.
questions.source: Week 12 lecture slides (Sustainability - Environmental Impact of Business - UN SDGs) - deck on file; lecture not yet delivered at time of writing, slides 3-9

questions.stem: The lecture material on sustainability refers to the Alliance to End Plastic Waste (AEPW), set up in 2019 by companies including ExxonMobil, Dow, Shell, TotalEnergies and Chevron Phillips. According to data obtained by Greenpeace (2024):

options.text: The alliance diverted more plastic waste from the environment than its members produced.
The alliance's members had stopped producing plastic altogether.
The alliance was set up by environmental charities.
The alliance had recycled 90% of the world's plastic waste.
Five firms in the alliance produced around 1,000 times more new plastic in five years than the waste the alliance diverted from the environment.

questions.explanation: An OECD report cited on the same slide found that plastic waste more than doubled between 2000 and 2019, only 9% of which was ultimately recycled. The example invites the question of whether such alliances amount to greenwashing.
questions.source: Week 12 lecture slides (Sustainability - Environmental Impact of Business - UN SDGs) - deck on file; lecture not yet delivered at time of writing, slide 11

questions.stem: According to an OECD report cited in the lecture material on sustainability, approximately what share of the world's plastic waste is ultimately recycled?

options.text: About 30%
About 9%
About 75%
About 90%
About 50%

questions.explanation: Plastic waste grew from 156m tonnes in 2000 to 353m tonnes in 2019, of which only 9% was ultimately recycled. Plastic use and waste are projected to triple globally by 2060.
questions.source: Week 12 lecture slides (Sustainability - Environmental Impact of Business - UN SDGs) - deck on file; lecture not yet delivered at time of writing, slides 11-12

questions.stem: A report on the COP29 climate conference in Baku (2024), included in the lecture material on sustainability, found that:

options.text: At least 1,773 fossil fuel lobbyists were granted access - more passes than all of the delegates from the 10 most climate-vulnerable nations combined.
Lobbyists made up half of all attendees.
Fossil fuel companies paid the full cost of the conference.
No fossil fuel lobbyists were permitted to attend.
Climate-vulnerable nations outnumbered fossil fuel lobbyists by ten to one.

questions.explanation: The analysis came from the Kick Big Polluters Out coalition. The point connects to earlier material on corporate lobbying and power (e.g. pharmaceutical lobbyists in Washington, Coca-Cola's sponsorship of Cop27).
questions.source: Week 12 lecture slides (Sustainability - Environmental Impact of Business - UN SDGs) - deck on file; lecture not yet delivered at time of writing, slide 15

questions.stem: At COP29, many developing countries reacted with anger to a draft climate finance target of $250bn. According to the lecture material, their objection was that:

options.text: The money was to be paid by developing countries to developed countries.
The amount was far too generous.
The money would have to be repaid within one year.
The target applied only to European countries.
The amount was far below what is needed to help poorer countries shift to a low-carbon economy and adapt to the impacts of extreme weather.

questions.explanation: Developing countries dismissed the draft as a 'joke'; a deal was eventually reached, but they said it was not enough to avoid climate catastrophe.
questions.source: Week 12 lecture slides (Sustainability - Environmental Impact of Business - UN SDGs) - deck on file; lecture not yet delivered at time of writing, slide 16

questions.stem: The UN Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), covered in the final lecture, are best described as:

options.text: A legally binding treaty that fines companies for carbon emissions.
A set of 8 goals that apply only to developing countries.
