A set of 17 global goals adopted by UN member states in 2015, to be achieved by 2030, covering areas such as poverty, health, education, inequality, climate and responsible consumption.
A certification scheme for ethical companies run by B Lab.
A set of accounting standards for reporting profit.

questions.explanation: The slide notes that for exam purposes you need the key components, terms and concepts rather than every detailed element. The World Happiness Report material earlier in the module found that the happiest countries also do more to try to meet the SDGs.
questions.source: Week 12 lecture slides (Sustainability - Environmental Impact of Business - UN SDGs) - deck on file; lecture not yet delivered at time of writing, slides 17-18

questions.stem: The 'triple bottom line', referred to in the lecture material on sustainability, proposes that business performance should be assessed in terms of:

options.text: Shareholders, managers and employees.
Local, national and international sales.
Revenue, costs and profit.
People, Profit and Planet - social, economic and environmental performance.
Past, present and future earnings.

questions.explanation: The slide notes that the triple bottom line is 'also referred to as: People, Profit, Planet'.
questions.source: Week 12 lecture slides (Sustainability - Environmental Impact of Business - UN SDGs) - deck on file; lecture not yet delivered at time of writing, slide 19

questions.stem: On moving to a circular economy, the lecture material on sustainability quotes the World Economic Forum. Which ONE of the following reflects that quotation?

options.text: In a properly built circular economy the focus should be on avoiding the recycling stage at all costs - preventing waste from being created in the first place is the only realistic strategy.
A circular economy is impossible without burning waste for energy.
Recycling is the single most important stage of a circular economy.
A circular economy means increasing production so that more can be recycled.
A circular economy applies only to plastic.

questions.explanation: Prevention comes before recycling - consistent with the evidence in the same lecture that only a small share of plastic waste is actually recycled.
questions.source: Week 12 lecture slides (Sustainability - Environmental Impact of Business - UN SDGs) - deck on file; lecture not yet delivered at time of writing, slide 20

questions.stem: According to the lecture material on sustainability, which ONE of the following is a requirement for a company to become a certified 'B Corp'?

options.text: It must donate all of its profits to charity.
It must be a non-profit organisation.
It must have been in business for at least 50 years.
It must be listed on a stock exchange.
It must achieve a score of at least 80 on B Lab's Impact Assessment, make a legal commitment to be accountable to all stakeholders (not just shareholders) and agree to have its performance published.

questions.explanation: Companies must also apply for recertification every three years, or when there is a change of ownership or an initial public offering.
questions.source: Week 12 lecture slides (Sustainability - Environmental Impact of Business - UN SDGs) - deck on file; lecture not yet delivered at time of writing, slide 22

questions.stem: With regard to 'B Corps' and 'benefit corporations', as described in the lecture material on sustainability, which ONE of the following is correct?

options.text: They are exactly the same thing.
A benefit corporation is certified by B Lab; a B Corp is a legal form of company.

'B Corp' is a certification awarded by the non-profit B Lab to companies that meet certain standards of social and environmental performance, whereas a 'benefit corporation' is a type of company legally recognised in most U.S. states that operates for the benefit of stakeholders rather than simply shareholders.
A B Corp is a government agency; a benefit corporation is a charity.
Neither has anything to do with stakeholders.

questions.explanation: The slide notes the two are often confused. B Lab, based in the United States, was founded in 2006 and certified its first 82 corporations in 2007.
questions.source: Week 12 lecture slides (Sustainability - Environmental Impact of Business - UN SDGs) - deck on file; lecture not yet delivered at time of writing, slide 22

questions.stem: B Corp certification requires a company to be 'accountable to all stakeholders, not just shareholders'. Which earlier concept in the module does this requirement most directly challenge?

options.text: The categorical imperative (Kant).
Moral licence.
Shareholder primacy, as expressed in Milton Friedman's view that 'the business of business is business' and in Dodge v. Ford.
The harm principle (J.S. Mill).
The veil of ignorance (Rawls).

questions.explanation: A B Corp makes a legal commitment and changes its corporate governance structure so that directors must consider stakeholders - the opposite of treating shareholder profit as the sole responsibility of business.
questions.source: Week 12 lecture slides (Sustainability - Environmental Impact of Business - UN SDGs) - deck on file; lecture not yet delivered at time of writing, slide 22; Week 1 and Week 6 lecture slides

questions.stem: The lecture material on sustainability includes a 2024 report on air pollution in Delhi. What did it show?

options.text: That the pollution affected only rural areas outside the city.
That air pollution had been eliminated by a ban on cars.
That air pollution in Delhi is caused entirely by natural dust.
That pollution reached about 1,500 on the Air Quality Index - around 15 times the level the WHO considers satisfactory - leading authorities to shut schools and ban construction work.
That air quality in Delhi was better than World Health Organization guidelines.

questions.explanation: According to the WHO, air with AQI values above 300 is considered hazardous to health; Lahore had recorded levels above 1,000 weeks earlier.
questions.source: Week 12 lecture slides (Sustainability - Environmental Impact of Business - UN SDGs) - deck on file; lecture not yet delivered at time of writing, slide 10

chapters.title: Discussion Group 1 · Friedman v. Roddick and the Clothing-Sourcing Case
chapters.description: The first discussion group: Friedman and Roddick, and the case-study on sourcing sequinned blouses from suppliers using child labour. Keep answer shuffling OFF.

questions.stem: In preparation for the first discussion group, students were asked to consider Anita Roddick's claim that 'being good is good for business'. What question were they asked to consider about it?

options.text: Whether it proves that Milton Friedman was right.
Whether it applies only to cosmetics companies.
Whether it is illegal for a business to make such a claim.
Whether it means businesses should not make a profit.
Whether it is an 'ethical' position, or whether it is disingenuous, as the motivation is still profit and not 'being good' for the sake of it.

questions.explanation: The preparation sheet sets Roddick's claim against Friedman's position that business needs no ethical constraints beyond existing law. From a Kantian perspective, 'being good is good for business' is a prudential rather than a moral motive.
questions.source: Discussion Group One: Case-study One (sourcing low-cost clothing in South-east Asia) and preparation sheet; Week 2 lecture slides, slide 10

questions.stem: In the first discussion group case-study, you are sent by a low-cost European clothes retailer to source sequinned blouses in South-east Asia. What do you discover when you ask to see how and where the products are made?

options.text: That all production takes place in a modern, well-lit factory staffed by adults.
That the supplier has no workers and uses only machines.

That much of the production is 'out-sourced' to family units in poor villages, where children as young as 7 or 8 help their parents stitch sequins, and that teenage boys operate large steam presses in a run-down finishing facility.
That the blouses are imported from Europe and re-labelled.
That the agent has been stealing from your company.

questions.explanation: The children 'have never gone to school and probably never will', and boys of perhaps 14 or 15 work on steam presses in a dusty, poorly lit warehouse.
questions.source: Discussion Group One: Case-study One (sourcing low-cost clothing in South-east Asia) and preparation sheet

questions.stem: In the first discussion group case-study, how does the production manager respond when you say you cannot, in conscience, give his company the contract while it continues to employ children?

options.text: He agrees immediately to stop employing children.

He says you will not get the garments at the price you need if such changes were made, and that you would be further impoverishing the families of the younger workers, who rely on this income for survival.
He reports you to your employer.
He says the government will support the families through social welfare.
He offers to raise his prices so that he can pay adults.

questions.explanation: He laughs at the idea of social welfare - the government giving people money for 'doing nothing' - and says any inspection under a child-labour law could be solved with 'a good bottle of whiskey to the inspector'.
questions.source: Discussion Group One: Case-study One (sourcing low-cost clothing in South-east Asia) and preparation sheet

questions.stem: With reference to the first discussion group case-study (sourcing clothing in South-east Asia), which ONE of the following is FALSE?

options.text: The other suppliers you visit turn out to have much better conditions and no child workers.
You know that doing a good job is very likely to lead to promotion to a regional manager role, which you really want.
The region is the only one that can meet your target cost.
The agent is certified as an ethical provider, so your company will not be concerned about what you have seen.
The parents feel they earn more from this work than from farming, which is vulnerable to hurricanes and flooding.

questions.explanation: The other suppliers present 'the same scenario' - in fact the first supplier 'seems to offer their workers relatively better conditions and pay, and has fewer younger workers'. Walking away therefore does not obviously help the children.
questions.source: Discussion Group One: Case-study One (sourcing low-cost clothing in South-east Asia) and preparation sheet

questions.stem: In the first discussion group case-study, a colleague argues: 'Sign the contract. The families earn more than they would from farming, the children are at home with their parents, and if we walk away they will simply be poorer.' Another argues: 'Children have a right to an education and should never be used as a means to cheaper blouses, whatever the consequences.' The two colleagues are reasoning, respectively, from:

options.text: Descriptive ethics and conceptual ethics.
Egoism and moral relativism.
A Kantian position and a utilitarian position.
A consequentialist (utilitarian) position and a non-consequentialist (rights / Kantian) position.
Virtue ethics and discourse ethics.

questions.explanation: The first weighs outcomes for those affected (the lecture used this child-labour case as its example of an act-utilitarian calculation). The second appeals to rights (education, consent, a living wage) and to not treating people merely as a means.
questions.source: Discussion Group One: Case-study One (sourcing low-cost clothing in South-east Asia) and preparation sheet; Week 4 lecture slides (Utilitarianism); Week 5 lecture slides (Kant; Rights Theory in Business)

questions.stem: In the first discussion group case-study, you reflect that your own promotion depends on signing the contract, and that rival colleagues 'would have no qualms' about where the garments come from. If you decided to sign purely because of the benefit to your own career, your reasoning would be best described as:

options.text: Justice as fairness
Egoism
Deontology
Virtue ethics
Rule utilitarianism

questions.explanation: Egoism focuses on the outcome for the decision-maker. The case deliberately builds in personal incentives and pressures - rewards, competition and 'everyone does it' - of the kind discussed in the Week 2 lecture on why good people do bad things.
questions.source: Discussion Group One: Case-study One (sourcing low-cost clothing in South-east Asia) and preparation sheet; Week 4 lecture slides (Egoism); Week 2 lecture slides

questions.stem: The first discussion group case-study notes that your company buys through an agent who is 'certified as being an ethical provider', while production is out-sourced to village families and a run-down finishing plant. Which point from the stakeholder theory lecture does this best illustrate?

options.text: That diffused stakeholders have no influence.
That shareholders are the only stakeholders who matter.
That responsibility extends along the supply chain to suppliers' suppliers - certification of an immediate supplier does not settle what is happening further down the chain.
That the business judgment rule protects buyers.
That agents are enabling stakeholders.

questions.explanation: As discussed in class, retailers accused of using child labour often pointed to compliant direct suppliers while sub-contractors were the problem; companies are now expected to take responsibility for the whole chain.
questions.source: Discussion Group One: Case-study One (sourcing low-cost clothing in South-east Asia) and preparation sheet; Lecture 6 class notes (supply chain responsibility)

chapters.title: Discussion Group 2 · Casas Bahia — Marketing to the Poor
chapters.description: The second discussion group case-study on the Brazilian retailer Casas Bahia and its instalment-credit model. Includes official sample 6. Keep answer shuffling OFF.

questions.stem: With reference to the case-study, ‘Casas Bahia – Marketing to the Poor’, which one of the following is FALSE:

options.text: Casas Bahia, at the time of the case-study, was making around 90% of its revenues from credit sales.
Casa Bahia advertised that they offered lower credit rates than most other retailers, which was true.

Many customers were not financially literate (or interested) enough to distinguish between the cost of the products they bought with or without credit, as they were more concerned with the overall price they were paying and whether they could afford this or not. Casas Bahia has been criticised for possibly playing on this uncertainty.

As a sign of good-will, on one occasion in 2002, Samuel Klein offered all clients in arrears, nearly one million of them, a full pardon on their debt.  There was no immediate financial benefit to the company, but it was an effective marketing tool, as it brought back some customers who had defaulted previously.
Casas Bahia had a relatively low default rate on its credit sales generally, though it varied somewhat by product type.

questions.explanation: Official sample question (answer inferred - no official key supplied). The case states that the 2002 pardon 'worked as both a tax deduction measure and also as an effective marketing tool' - writing the old debts off reduced taxable income - so it is false that there was no immediate financial benefit. Over 90% of revenue came from credit sales; the average default rate was 8.5%, varying by product.
questions.source: Official MG2008 lecturer sample question 6 (2026 Exam Instructions, Details and Sample MCQs). Wording and options unchanged; no official answer key was issued, so the answer is inferred from: Casas Bahia case-study, 'The Business Model' section and footnote 15

questions.stem: According to the case-study 'Casas Bahia - Marketing to the Poor', who founded Casas Bahia, and how did he begin?

options.text: Samuel Klein, a Polish-born survivor of a Nazi concentration camp who emigrated to Brazil and began by selling blankets, bed linen and towels from a horse and cart to migrant labourers.
Michael Klein, a Brazilian banker who bought an existing chain of stores.
C.K. Prahalad, an American professor who opened a store as a research project.
A consortium of global electronics brands.
Muhammad Yunus, who opened a micro-finance bank in Sao Paulo.

questions.explanation: Klein opened his first store in 1958 in Sao Caetano do Sul, naming it after the home state (Bahia) of his first customers. He is quoted as saying: 'My talent is trusting the poor ... I was poor once.'
questions.source: Discussion Group Two case-study: 'Casas Bahia - Marketing to the Poor'

questions.stem: In the Casas Bahia case-study, customers paid their instalments using a passbook (the 'carne'), which was payable only at Casas Bahia stores, so customers had to come into a store every month. Why was this condition considered so important to the business?

options.text: Because Brazilian law prohibited payment by post.
Because customers did not trust banks.
Because it reduced the company's tax bill.
Because the company had no computer system.
Because it maintained a personal relationship with clients and exposed them to displays of the latest products, encouraging them to make further purchases (cross-selling).

questions.explanation: The case gives the example of a security guard's wife who came in to pay an instalment on a music system and left having bought cooking pots in four instalments: 'This tactic never failed to generate new sales.'
questions.source: Discussion Group Two case-study: 'Casas Bahia - Marketing to the Poor'

questions.stem: According to the Casas Bahia case-study, why were poor Brazilians largely unable to obtain credit elsewhere on reasonable terms?

options.text: Because Casas Bahia had a legal monopoly on credit.
Because banks generally closed their doors to those without a registered job or proof of regular income, while consumer credit companies ('financeiras') charged exorbitant interest rates.
Because the government provided free appliances.
Because credit was illegal in Brazil.
Because the poor did not want consumer goods.

questions.explanation: More than 40 million residents had no bank account, and financeiras charged as much as 14 per cent per month on personal loans. Casas Bahia's average interest rate was 4.13 per cent per month.
questions.source: Discussion Group Two case-study: 'Casas Bahia - Marketing to the Poor'

questions.stem: With reference to the Casas Bahia case-study, which ONE of the following is FALSE?

options.text: It sold only cheap, unbranded goods, as global brands refused to supply it.
Over 70 per cent of Casas Bahia's customers had no regular income.
Customer information, including notes on personality traits, was stored centrally and used to assess both creditworthiness and potential for further purchases.
A majority of its stores were located in some of the most deprived neighbourhoods.
A yellow preferred-client card given to punctual payers was regarded as a status symbol among Brazil's working class.

questions.explanation: A major attraction was the global brands it sold - Sony, Philips, Toshiba, Panasonic, Brastemp (Whirlpool) and others - bought in bulk at lower cost than competitors.
questions.source: Discussion Group Two case-study: 'Casas Bahia - Marketing to the Poor'

questions.stem: In the Casas Bahia case-study, Samuel Klein attributes the company's low default rate to the trust he placed in the poor, observing that 'the poorer the customer, the more punctual were his / her payments'. Which of the following other explanations or factors is / are also suggested by the case?

options.text: The poor had to guard their reputation, because defaulting would jeopardise their creditworthiness and access to credit.
Goods such as furniture were delivered and installed by the company, making them easy to repossess in the event of default.
A credit bureau check and an automated scoring process screened applicants, with about one-tenth rejected.
a) and b) above
a), b) and c) above

questions.explanation: The preparation questions ask whether the business succeeds only because Klein 'understands and trusts his customers'. The case shows other mechanisms too: furniture had a 4% default rate against up to 10% for portable items such as mobile phones and bicycles.
questions.source: Discussion Group Two case-study: 'Casas Bahia - Marketing to the Poor'

questions.stem: The Casas Bahia case-study includes a section headed 'The Criticism'. Which ONE of the following is a criticism made of the company in the case?

options.text: That it did not advertise enough.
That it refused to sell to the poor.

That, despite its much publicised low interest rates, the prices of its goods were inflated, so that the poor - who looked mainly at whether the monthly instalment fitted their budget - ended up paying more.
That it paid its staff below the minimum wage.
That it sold dangerous products.

questions.explanation: Critics also argued that the company took advantage of poor people's yearning for consumer goods, luring them into buying luxury items on credit at the expense of basic needs and savings. One customer said she did not know how much interest she was paying and wore broken sandals rather than miss an instalment.
questions.source: Discussion Group Two case-study: 'Casas Bahia - Marketing to the Poor'

questions.stem: Casas Bahia has been both praised and criticised. In terms of the debate between Prahalad and Karnani covered in the lectures, which ONE of the following is the most accurate statement?

options.text: Prahalad criticises Casas Bahia, whereas Karnani praises it.
Prahalad and Karnani both regard Casas Bahia as proof that selling to the poor eradicates poverty.
Neither author mentions Casas Bahia or retail credit.
Both argue that the poor should be prevented from buying on credit.

Prahalad cites Casas Bahia as a positive example of serving 'bottom of the pyramid' consumers, whereas Karnani's argument implies that access to credit and consumer goods does not by itself raise the real income of the poor.

questions.explanation: The case opens with a Prahalad quotation about seeing the poor as 'value-conscious consumers'. Karnani: 'providing credit does not change the affordability of a product' and 'the issue is whether it is in their self-interest'. A low default rate does not show that customers are better off.
questions.source: Discussion Group Two case-study: 'Casas Bahia - Marketing to the Poor'; Core Readings 13 and 14; Lecture 9 class notes

questions.stem: Maria earns the equivalent of $170 a month. A store offers her a television 'for just $15 a month over 15 months' and stresses its low interest rate; she is not told, and does not ask, the cash price or the total she will pay. She signs, pleased that the instalment fits her budget, and cuts back on food to keep up the payments. Applying the frameworks used in the Casas Bahia discussion, which ONE of the following is the most accurate assessment?

options.text: Only virtue ethics has anything to say about the sale.
There is no ethical issue, because she chose freely and the store broke no law.
A Kantian would approve of the sale provided the store makes a profit.
The sale is unethical under every framework, because the poor should never be sold televisions.

A consequentialist would weigh her enjoyment and access against the hardship of repayment, while a Kantian would ask whether she was treated merely as a means - which turns on whether she could give informed consent given what she was and was not told.

questions.explanation: The scenario mirrors the case: access and dignity on one side; affordability, disclosure and informed choice on the other. It also avoids the paternalism the lecturer warned against - who has the authority to deny the poor a television?
questions.source: Discussion Group Two case-study: 'Casas Bahia - Marketing to the Poor'; Lecture 8 and 9 class notes; Week 4-5 lecture slides

chapters.title: Discussion Group 3 · Addictive Junk Food and ILSI
chapters.description: The third discussion group: Moss (2013), 'The Extraordinary Science of Addictive Junk Food', and the critique of the International Life Sciences Institute (ILSI). The lecturer has said there will definitely be at least one exam question on this material. Keep answer shuffling OFF.

questions.stem: 'The Extraordinary Science of Addictive Junk Food' (Moss, 2013) opens with a meeting in Minneapolis in April 1999 of the men who controlled America's largest food companies. What happened at that meeting?

options.text: The companies agreed industry-wide limits on salt, sugar and fat.
The companies agreed to merge into a single corporation.

A Kraft vice president, Michael Mudd, warned about the obesity epidemic, drew a comparison with the tobacco industry and proposed that the industry act - but the head of General Mills, Stephen Sanger, rejected the idea, and the effort went no further.
Government regulators announced a tax on junk food.
The companies agreed to stop marketing to children.

questions.explanation: Sanger reportedly said 'Don't talk to me about nutrition', arguing that consumers buy what tastes good and that General Mills already acted responsibly by offering products for the health-conscious. Mudd had proposed, among other things, a code to guide the nutritional aspects of food marketing, especially to children.
questions.source: Discussion Group Three core reading: 'The Extraordinary Science of Addictive Junk Food' (Moss, New York Times, 2013)

questions.stem: In 'The Extraordinary Science of Addictive Junk Food', the 'bliss point', associated with the work of Howard Moskowitz, refers to:

options.text: The precise level of an ingredient such as sweetness at which consumers like a product the most - their optimum.
The legal limit for sugar in a soft drink.
The moment a consumer first sees an advertisement.
The price at which a product sells the most units.
The point at which a consumer feels full and stops eating.

questions.explanation: Moskowitz optimised products such as Dr Pepper and Prego spaghetti sauce by testing many variations. He told Moss: 'There's no moral issue for me ... I did the best science I could.'
questions.source: Discussion Group Three core reading: 'The Extraordinary Science of Addictive Junk Food' (Moss, New York Times, 2013)

questions.stem: According to 'The Extraordinary Science of Addictive Junk Food', 'sensory-specific satiety' is:

options.text: The tendency of consumers to prefer familiar brands.
The tendency of children to prefer sweet foods.
The feeling of fullness produced by high-fibre foods.
A legal standard for food labelling.

The tendency for big, distinct flavours to overwhelm the brain, which responds by depressing the desire to have more - so the most successful products are formulated to avoid a single overriding flavour.

questions.explanation: It became a guiding principle for the processed-food industry: products like Coca-Cola and Doritos owe their success to complex formulas that pique the taste buds without a single dominant flavour that tells the brain to stop eating.
questions.source: Discussion Group Three core reading: 'The Extraordinary Science of Addictive Junk Food' (Moss, New York Times, 2013)

questions.stem: In 'The Extraordinary Science of Addictive Junk Food', the food scientist Steven Witherly praises Cheetos for their 'vanishing caloric density'. This means that:

options.text: The snack melts down quickly in the mouth, so the brain thinks there are no calories in it and you can keep eating it.
Cheetos contain no calories.
Cheetos are high in fibre.
Cheetos are sold in ever smaller packs.
The calories in Cheetos disappear when they are cooked.

questions.explanation: 'If something melts down quickly, your brain thinks that there's no calories in it ... you can just keep eating it forever.'
questions.source: Discussion Group Three core reading: 'The Extraordinary Science of Addictive Junk Food' (Moss, New York Times, 2013)

questions.stem: According to 'The Extraordinary Science of Addictive Junk Food', which ONE of the following is true of Lunchables?

options.text: They were marketed only to elderly consumers.

They were developed by Bob Drane at Oscar Mayer (owned by Philip Morris) to reposition declining processed meats, were initially marketed to busy mothers, and later gained more sugar, salt and fat through added drinks and desserts.
They were created by a health charity to improve children's diets.
They always included fresh fruit and vegetables.
They were withdrawn after one year because they did not sell.

questions.explanation: Fresh components such as carrots were dropped because they did not suit a processed-food system needing weeks of transport and storage. Later marketing targeted children directly, with the message that Lunchables gave them control.
questions.source: Discussion Group Three core reading: 'The Extraordinary Science of Addictive Junk Food' (Moss, New York Times, 2013)

questions.stem: In 'The Extraordinary Science of Addictive Junk Food', Jeffrey Dunn, a former senior Coca-Cola executive, describes a visit to a poor neighbourhood (favela) in Brazil. What effect did it have on him?

options.text: He decided to double Coca-Cola's marketing budget in Brazil.
He proposed giving Coke away free.
He concluded that poor consumers could not afford soft drinks.
He decided that Coca-Cola should stop selling in Brazil.

He thought: 'These people need a lot of things, but they don't need a Coke', and it contributed to his decision to push the company towards healthier directions - after which he left and later marketed baby carrots using junk-food techniques.

questions.explanation: The company's strategy there was to repackage Coke into smaller, more affordable 6.7-ounce bottles at 20 cents each. Inside Coke, the biggest consumers were referred to as 'heavy users'.
questions.source: Discussion Group Three core reading: 'The Extraordinary Science of Addictive Junk Food' (Moss, New York Times, 2013)

questions.stem: With reference to 'The Extraordinary Science of Addictive Junk Food' (Moss, 2013), which ONE of the following is FALSE?

options.text: Moss argues that the obesity problem is simply a matter of poor willpower on the part of the consumer.
Food company executives competed for what they called 'stomach share'.
Our brains are described as loving sugar, fat and salt.
A former chief scientist at Frito-Lay, Robert Lin, had concerns about the company's reliance on salt.
Coca-Cola aimed not merely to beat rival brands but to outsell everything else people drank.

questions.explanation: Moss writes that it is 'not just a matter of poor willpower on the part of the consumer and a give-the-people-what-they-want attitude on the part of the food manufacturers', but of a conscious effort to get people hooked on foods that are convenient and inexpensive.
questions.source: Discussion Group Three core reading: 'The Extraordinary Science of Addictive Junk Food' (Moss, New York Times, 2013)

questions.stem: Students were asked to reflect, in the third discussion group, on the article 'The Extraordinary Science of Addictive Junk Food'. Which pair of questions were they asked to consider?

options.text: Whether the article was accurate, and whether its author should be sued.
Whether junk food should be banned, and who should enforce the ban.
Whether schools should serve Lunchables, and at what price.
What might be considered the ethical or unethical practices of large food producers discussed in the article, and to what extent consumers might need to take responsibility for their own behaviour.
How food companies could increase their sales, and which markets to enter.

questions.explanation: The same sheet states that there will definitely be at least one question on both the Casas Bahia case-study and this material in the final MCQ exam.
questions.source: Third Discussion Group details

questions.stem: For the third discussion group, students were asked to review and critique the International Life Sciences Institute (ILSI), starting from its own web-site. What was the main purpose of this exercise?

options.text: To apply for membership of the organisation.
To consider whether other information about the organisation alters the initial impression given by its own web-site, and what gives it credibility as an organisation addressing health and food.
To show that all scientific institutes are funded by governments.
To compare its logo with those of food companies.
To learn how to design a web-site for a scientific organisation.

questions.explanation: A scientific-sounding name, non-profit status, conferences and respected scientists lend credibility; independent sources report that ILSI was founded by a Coca-Cola executive and is funded almost entirely by food, agribusiness and pharmaceutical companies.
questions.source: Third Discussion Group details (ILSI critique) and Core Reading 20 (New York Times, 2019)

questions.stem: A health ministry sets up an expert panel to decide whether packaged food should carry warning labels. A trustee of an institute funded by major food companies is appointed to chair it. He says, sincerely, that he can achieve more by working with the industry than against it. In terms of the issues raised by the ILSI material, which ONE of the following is the most accurate assessment?

options.text: The only concern is that he is not paid enough.
The concern would disappear if the institute changed its name.
His appointment proves that warning labels are harmful.
There is no ethical concern, because he is sincere.

There is a conflict of interest that undermines the independence of the panel - 'the regulated cannot be the regulators' - even though it does not prove that he or every finding linked to the institute is wrong.

questions.explanation: This mirrors the Indian case in Core Reading 20. The appropriate critique focuses on funding, governance and transparency rather than assuming that every industry-funded result is false.
questions.source: Third Discussion Group details (ILSI critique) and Core Reading 20 (New York Times, 2019)
